By making the jays act exactly like people, Twain turns the joke on the reader: if the jays are this human, humans are this foolish. The story also shows Twain's rhetorical skill: the humor, dialect and deadpan delivery make Baker (and Twain) likable and believable, even while telling an impossible story.

Other important factors: From A Tramp Abroad (1880); Mark Twain, 1835-1910. A yarn is a long, exaggerated tale told as true; a tall tale and beast fable. The anthology's Introduction says Twain mastered the frontier humorous sketch and the fable rather than the short story, and calls "Bluejay Yarn" superb of its kind, linked to the Uncle Remus stories and later Thurber's fables. It bridges Romanticism and Regionalism / local color (setting-specific dialect and customs).

concepts.intro: A dark Romantic allegory set in Puritan Salem Village. Hawthorne's own ancestors took part in the Salem witch trials.
b: Intro: At sunset in Salem Village, Puritan Massachusetts, young Goodman Brown is leaving on a one-night "errand". His wife of three months, Faith, with pink ribbons in her cap, begs him to stay: "A lone woman is troubled with such dreams". He refuses and asks if she already doubts him. As he walks off he feels guilty ("what a wretch am I to leave her on such an errand!") and hints that the trip is evil, but promises himself that after this night he will cling to her skirts and follow her to heaven.

Middle: Deep in the dark forest he meets a traveler of about fifty, simply dressed and looking a lot like Brown, who says "You are late, Goodman Brown" ("Faith kept me back a while"). The man's staff looks like a great black snake that seems to twist like a living serpent. Brown wants to turn back, saying his family were honest Christians, but the traveler says he knew them well: he helped Brown's grandfather, a constable, whip a Quaker woman through Salem's streets, and gave Brown's father a torch to burn an Indian village in King Philip's War. He adds that deacons, selectmen and the governor's court are his friends. They see Goody Cloyse, the pious old woman who taught Brown his catechism. Brown hides, and she greets the traveler as "your worship", talks of witch ointments and a flying broomstick, and says a young man is to join their meeting tonight; the traveler lends her his staff and she vanishes. Brown sits down and refuses to go further, and the traveler leaves him the staff and disappears. Then Brown hears the minister and Deacon Gookin riding past, talking eagerly about the meeting and a young woman to be taken into communion. Brown looks up to heaven, but a dark cloud passes overhead carrying voices of townspeople, including Faith's, and a pink ribbon flutters down onto a branch. "My Faith is gone!" he cries. "There is no good on earth; and sin is but a name. Come, devil! for to thee is this world given." Laughing madly, he grabs the staff and races through the howling forest to the meeting: a rock altar in a clearing, lit by four burning pines, where the town's most respected people sit beside criminals and Indian priests. A dark figure calls the converts forward. Goody Cloyse and Martha Carrier lead in a veiled woman: Faith. The figure says "Welcome, my children, to the communion of your race" and "Evil is the nature of mankind", promising to reveal everyone's secret sins, and prepares to baptize them from a basin of what looks like blood.

End: Brown cries "Faith! Faith! look up to heaven, and resist the wicked one!" Instantly he is alone in the calm, silent forest, the rock cold and a twig dripping cold dew on his cheek. The next morning he walks into Salem Village. The minister blesses him, Deacon Gookin is praying, and Goody Cloyse is teaching a little girl her catechism, which Brown snatches the child away from. Faith runs out joyfully to meet him, pink ribbons and all, but he looks at her sternly and passes without a word. Hawthorne asks whether Brown only fell asleep and "dreamed a wild dream of a witch-meeting", and answers "Be it so if you will". Either way, Brown becomes "a stern, a sad, a darkly meditative, a distrustful, if not a desperate man". He can't stand to hear hymns or sermons, shrinks from Faith at night, and sees hypocrisy everywhere. When he dies an old man, followed to the grave by Faith, children, grandchildren and neighbors, they carve no hopeful verse on his tombstone, "for his dying hour was gloom".
Character: Goodman Brown: Protagonist. Young, naive, curious about evil, then bitter. Dynamic: he returns changed forever. Importance: every man who loses his faith in others.
Character: Faith: Brown's wife, with her pink ribbons. Importance: both a person and a symbol of his religious faith; "My Faith is gone!" works both ways.
Character: the traveler / the devil: Older man resembling Brown, with a serpent staff. Importance: the tempter; his claims make Brown doubt his family and church.

Characters: Goody Cloyse, the minister, Deacon Gookin: Respected Puritan leaders seen serving the devil. Importance: they expose the town's hypocrisy (Goody Cloyse and Martha Carrier are real Salem-trial names).
Point of view: Third person, limited mostly to Brown, so the reader shares his uncertainty about what is real.
Themes: Loss of innocence and faith; hypocrisy of the Puritans; the idea that evil lives in everyone; doubt that poisons a whole life.

Other important factors: Allegory and symbols (Faith; the pink ribbons for innocence; the forest for the moral wilderness; the serpent staff for evil); Biblical allusion (Eden, baptism and communion parodies); foreshadowing; deliberate ambiguity. The Introduction says Hawthorne added moral "specific gravity" and describes the story as a journey from light into darkness and back.

concepts.intro: Hawthorne's long autobiographical essay that introduces The Scarlet Letter. It is nonfiction blended with one big literary trick: Hawthorne claims the novel that follows is a true story he found, not one he invented.
b: Intro: Hawthorne describes his job as Surveyor of the Custom House in Salem, Massachusetts, where he inspects incoming ships' cargo and collects duties for the federal government. He is openly unimpressed with his co-workers: a crew of old, half-asleep political appointees who got their jobs through favoritism and do almost no real work. The most dignified is the elderly "Collector," a Revolutionary War veteran (based on General James Miller) who naps through most of the day but still commands respect.

Middle: Poking around in the building's dusty upper story, Hawthorne says he discovers a small bundle left by a former Surveyor named Jonathan Pue: old documents and a faded, moth-eaten scrap of scarlet cloth shaped like a capital letter "A," with gold embroidery. Pue's papers tell the story of a woman named Hester Prynne, who lived generations earlier. When Hawthorne holds the letter to his chest, he claims to feel it burn, "as if the letter were not of red cloth, but red-hot iron." He frames The Scarlet Letter as simply his retelling of Pue's manuscript, not his own invention. He also reflects at length on his Puritan ancestors, especially a stern early judge who persecuted Quakers and a witch-trial judge, and says he feels a kind of inherited guilt that his writing might be paying off.

End: Hawthorne loses his customs job when a change in presidential administration brings in a new political appointee to replace him — he jokes that he has been "guillotined," though, unlike a real beheaded victim, he survives it and can write about it afterward. Being pushed out of the practical, unimaginative world of the Custom House is what frees him to finally become a writer and finish the novel.

Character: Hawthorne (the narrator): The essay's first-person voice, blending the real Nathaniel Hawthorne with a partly invented persona. Importance: he sets up why the reader should trust the story that follows, and explains his own conflicted identity as both a Custom House officer and a writer.

Character: the Collector (based on General James Miller): An elderly, dignified Revolutionary War veteran who nominally runs the Custom House but naps through most of his duties. Importance: represents a fading, honorable past next to Hawthorne's more cynical, satirical view of the other officers.

Character: Jonathan Pue: A former Surveyor of the Custom House, long dead, whose old manuscript and the scarlet letter "A" Hawthorne claims to discover. Importance: the whole "found manuscript" conceit depends on him; he is Hawthorne's fictional source for Hester Prynne's story.

Character: Hawthorne's Puritan ancestors: Unnamed but based on real ancestors, including a judge who persecuted Quakers and a judge from the Salem witch trials. Importance: Hawthorne says he feels their harshness as a kind of family curse, and sees his writing as a way of answering for it.
Point of view: First person. Hawthorne writes as himself, an autobiographical essayist, though he mixes in the invented discovery of Pue's manuscript as if it were also true.

Themes: The tension between practical, commercial life (the Custom House) and the imaginative life of an artist; the weight of inherited guilt from Puritan ancestors; using a "found document" to make fiction feel authentic; gentle satire of government patronage jobs.

Other important factors: Genre: nonfiction essay, but built around an invented frame device (the discovered manuscript), a technique used to make an invented story feel like a rediscovered true one. Extended metaphor: losing his job as a political "guillotining." The scarlet letter "A" is introduced here as already strange and almost magical (it burns him) before the novel proper even begins. Hawthorne also describes his parlor at night, moonlight mixed with firelight, as the ideal condition for his imagination -- the mindset he needed to finally write the novel.
Important lines — Key passages from the essay, in order, for close-reading and presentation prep.

Lines 5-25 "It is a little… or his own.": Opening paragraph -- Hawthorne explains why he's writing another autobiographical sketch (he did one before, in "The Old Manse") and sets the ground rules for how personal an author may get without "violating either the reader's rights or his own."

Lines 26-55 "It will be…barbed arrows": Explains this sketch's real purpose (to explain how he got the manuscript and prove it's authentic), then describes the actual Custom-House building in Salem, including the American eagle over the door -- federal symbol, warns everyone off, "has no great tenderness."

Lines 56-86 "The pavement… Custom-House officers": Describes the mostly-empty, grass-grown Custom-House, the occasional busy morning when ships arrive, and introduces the row of old, half-asleep officers sitting around -- "Custom-House officers."

Lines 87-123 "Furthermore…to know": Describes his own office and desk, notes he's since been swept out of the job by political "reform," and begins reflecting on his strange, deep attachment to plain, unglamorous Salem.

Lines 124-153 "But the sentiment… with mine": Introduces his Puritan ancestor (persecuted Quakers) and that ancestor's son (a Salem witch-trial judge) -- his sense of inherited family guilt, and his ancestors' imagined scorn at him being "a writer of story-books."
Lines 154-181 "Planted… earth": Traces his family's generations in Salem (mostly sea captains) and how deeply the family became rooted -- literally buried -- in the town's soil.

Lines 182-214 "On emerging… to Paradise": Explains how he actually got the Surveyor job (a political appointment, "the President's commission"), meets his new staff of very old officers, and jokes that neither door of the Custom-House "opens on the road to Paradise."

Lines 215-248 "The greater part…any remedy": Most of his officers are Whigs, but he -- not a political operator -- doesn't fire them; describes their comic incompetence (missing real smuggling, over-fussing small things) with dry irony.

Lines 249-302 "Unless people… of the two": He grows genuinely fond of the old officers despite everything, then introduces the ancient, cheerful permanent Inspector -- pure appetite, "no soul, no heart, no mind" beyond his stomach.

Lines 303-333 "I used to… axe and handsaw": Continues the Inspector's portrait: he remembers old dinners in vivid detail but nothing else; the "chief tragic event" of his life was a famously tough goose he once tried to carve.

Lines 334-364 "But it is… alien weeds": Moves on to the Collector (General Miller) -- a once-great, now-frail soldier, described as hard to read as the ruined fortress of Ticonderoga, "overgrown... with grass and alien weeds."

Lines 365-413 "Nevertheless… desk": Gives the Collector real dignity -- a quiet, massive inner strength ("a deep, red glow, as of iron in a furnace") -- and pictures him as an old sword out of place among the office's inkstands and paper-folders.

Lines 414-458 "There was one… the change": Gives the Collector's famous battle motto, "I'll try, sir!," then introduces a totally different figure: the sharp, efficient "man of business" clerk who actually keeps the whole Custom-House running.

Lines 459-500 "Literature.. now writing": Hawthorne says he stopped caring about literature entirely while working there, valued only as "a tolerably good Surveyor of the Customs," and realizes how little his writing means to the people around him.

Lines 501-550 "In the second… skull itself": The key discovery scene: his own name is now famous only as a customs stamp on cargo; poking through attic barrels he finds an old parchment package -- Surveyor Jonathan Pue's actual royal commission and papers (Pue's exhumed remains, he notes, were basically just a skeleton and a well-preserved wig).

Lines 551-586 "They were documents… upon the floor": Describes Pue's private antiquarian notes, then the discovery of the scarlet cloth letter "A" itself -- and the famous moment Hawthorne holds it to his chest, feels it burn "as if the letter were not of red cloth, but red-hot iron," and drops it in shock.

Lines 587-609 "In the absorbing… the outline": He opens the roll of paper wrapped around the letter and finds Pue's manuscript telling Hester Prynne's story -- the passage where Hawthorne explicitly claims the novel is "authenticated" by a real document, while admitting he invented plenty of the details himself.

Lines 610-625 "This incident… I will": The whimsical ghost-of-Surveyor-Pue scene -- Hawthorne imagines Pue's ghost formally commissioning him to write up Hester Prynne's story. "Do this," says the ghost, "and the profit shall be all your own!" Hawthorne answers: "I will!"

Lines 626-654 "On Hester… many-hued description": Hawthorne obsessively paces the Custom-House halls thinking about Hester Prynne's story, annoying the old Inspector -- but his imagination stays dead. Says if he'd stayed in the job "through ten Presidencies," the novel never would have been written.

Lines 655-685 "If the imaginative… from me": The famous moonlight passage -- moonlight in a familiar room is the ideal condition for a writer's imagination, turning ordinary objects into "things of intellect." None of it worked on him: "An entire class of susceptibilities... was gone from me."

Lines 686-716 "It is my belief… of mankind": He reflects he might have written something better by capturing the old sea-captain Inspector's storytelling gift instead. Ends with his verdict on Custom-House work: it doesn't let a man "share in the united effort of mankind."

Lines 717-740 "An effect… manly character": The passage on leaning on "the mighty arm of the Republic" -- his theory that public office slowly destroys a man's self-reliance, comparing a government salary to "the Devil's wages."

Lines 741-777 "Here was… struck off": His fear of becoming like the old Inspector, then the political guillotine section -- Taylor's election, the Whigs sweeping Democrats from office. "My head was the first that fell!"

Lines 778-804 "In short… that fell / The moment… friendly one": Losing his job actually suits him -- he compares it to a man who wanted to commit suicide and got the "good hap to be murdered" instead.

Lines 806-828 "Meanwhile… literary man / Now it was… of quiet": Newspapers mock him as Irving's Headless Horseman; freed from the job, he becomes a writer again. Pue's old papers "came into play" -- this is where he actually starts writing the novel. Ends: "For I am in the realm of quiet!"

Lines 829-849 "The life of… without me / It may be… town pump": Final farewell to the Custom-House and Salem, naming the real merchants he worked among and saying the town won't miss him. Closes on the ironic Town Pump joke as his one hoped-for legacy.

concepts.intro: Everything around the six stories: devices and terms, the anthology intro, Romanticism, Emerson, the American Dream, how to answer analysis questions, the authors cheat sheet, handouts and the periods timeline. Each block starts with its own bold heading.
b: Words and tools (devices, terms and settings) — Every literary device and term for the unit in one place, followed by each story's setting.
Anthropomorphism: giving animals or living things human traits (the bluejays).
Personification: giving nonliving objects human traits (the House of Usher's "eye-like" windows).
Imagery: language that appeals to the senses.
Mood / Tone: mood is the feeling created for the reader; tone is the author's attitude toward the subject.
Setting: time and place.
Characterization: how the author reveals a character. Direct: the narrator tells you. Indirect (STEAL): Speech, Thoughts, Effect on others, Actions, Looks.
Round / flat, static / dynamic: round characters are complex, flat have one or two traits; static characters don't change, dynamic ones do (Goodman Brown).
Point of view: who narrates: first person, third limited, omniscient. A frame narrative is a story that holds another story.
Allusion: an indirect reference to a well-known person, place, text or event (the serpent staff and Eden).
Foreshadowing: hints about what comes next (the Mad Trist sounds).
Symbolism / Allegory: a symbol stands for a bigger idea; an allegory is a whole story whose characters and events stand for moral or political meanings.
Irony: verbal (saying the opposite of what you mean), situational (the opposite of what is expected), dramatic (the reader knows more than the character).
Juxtaposition: putting things side by side for effect (Baker's serious tone vs. an absurd story).
Metaphor / Simile / Hyperbole: direct comparison; comparison with like or as; exaggeration ("two tons" of acorns).
Diction / Syntax: word choice; sentence structure.
Dialect: speech showing a region or class (Jim Baker).
Ambiguity: an ending or event left open to more than one reading (Brown's dream).
Tall tale / Yarn / Fable: exaggerated story told as true; a beast fable uses animals to teach a point.
Gothic: horror plus romance in gloomy old buildings (Poe).
Spenserian stanza: nine lines, ABABBCBCC, last line longer (Keats).
Rhetorical appeals: ethos (credibility), logos (logic), pathos (emotion).
SOAPSTone: Speaker, Occasion, Audience, Purpose, Subject, Tone.
Setting: "Rip Van Winkle": a Dutch village and the Kaatskill (Catskill) Mountains on the Hudson, before and after the American Revolution (about 1770s to 1790s).
Setting: "The Eve of St. Agnes": a medieval castle on a freezing St. Agnes' Eve, January 20, during a loud feast; the lovers escape into a storm.
Setting: "The Fall of the House of Usher": the decaying Usher mansion beside a black tarn on a dull, soundless autumn day, ending on a stormy night.
Setting: "Baker's Bluejay Yarn": a lonely, empty log cabin in the woods of California (near Yosemite), told by a miner.
Setting: "Young Goodman Brown": Puritan Salem Village, Massachusetts, in the late 1600s; the dark forest at night, then the village next morning.
Introduction to Great American Short Stories — has its own section at the top of this unit (the first concept), with the editors' main claims in plain words.
Romanticism and Washington Irving — Romanticism is the frame for the whole unit. Irving's packet content is on the exam, so know the movement's vocabulary as well as the man.

Romanticism (late 18th to mid 19th century, per the Britannica handout) rejects the order, calm, harmony, balance and rationality of Classicism and late-18th-century Neoclassicism, and reacts against the Enlightenment, rationalism and physical materialism.

Romanticism emphasizes the individual, the subjective, the irrational, the imaginative, the emotional and the transcendental; it loves nature, exalts emotion over reason and the senses over intellect, and has a predilection for the exotic, mysterious, occult, monstrous and even satanic.
Classicism and Neoclassicism prized order, reason and restraint; Rationalism trusted reason above feeling. Romantic writers push back with intuition, mystery and the sublime.
Washington Irving (1783-1859) is often called the first American author to win international fame. "Rip Van Winkle" appeared in The Sketch Book (1819-20) under the pen name Geoffrey Crayon.
Irving frames the tale as papers left by the fictional historian Diedrich Knickerbocker, a playful fake-history frame (historiography: how history gets written).
Romantic markers to spot in the stories: dreamlike or supernatural events, wild nature, nostalgia for the past, a lone individual against society, and strong emotion.
Packet vocabulary to know: Classicism, Neoclassicism, Enlightenment, Rationalism, Transcendental, exaltation, predilection, occult, satanic, historiography.

English Romanticism began in the 1790s with Wordsworth and Coleridge's Lyrical Ballads; Wordsworth's 1800 Preface called poetry "the spontaneous overflow of powerful feelings". Blake was a third early poet; Keats, Byron and Shelley are the later high point; Scott is credited with the historical novel.

Gothic fiction combines horror and romance. Its origin is credited to Horace Walpole's The Castle of Otranto (1764, subtitled "A Gothic Story"); later examples include Mary Shelley's Frankenstein, Poe, and Stoker's Dracula. "Gothic" refers to the pseudo-medieval buildings where many of the stories take place.
Emerson and Transcendentalism — The Emerson handout (Lesson #5) is an excerpt from "The Transcendentalist". Bullet-point summary of the argument is on your notes.
Ralph Waldo Emerson (1803-1882) was the leading voice of American Transcendentalism, a Romantic movement that trusts intuition, individual conscience and nature over institutions and tradition.

From the excerpt: the materialist "takes his departure from the external world" and esteems a man as one product of it, respecting society, government, social art, luxury and "every mass". The idealist "takes his departure from his consciousness, and reckons the world an appearance".

The idealist's measure is metaphysical: the rank things take in his consciousness, not their size or appearance. "Mind is the only reality, of which men and all other natures are better or worse reflectors." Nature, literature and history are "subjective phenomena".

The idealist does not respect government, church, charities, property or the arts for themselves, only as symbols of the laws of being, and sees facts flowing outward "from an invisible, unsounded centre in himself". His thought "is the Universe".
Use the handout: quote how Emerson defines each side, then say what he means and how you know from his diction.
Connect to the unit: Rip resists social duties (individual vs. society); Goodman Brown loses faith in his community; Poe's Roderick lives inside his own mind; Keats prizes imagination.
Emerson is nonfiction (an essay/lecture), so you can also discuss purpose, audience, tone and ethos, logos and pathos in it.
The American Dream (James Truslow Adams) — How can we critically interpret the American Dream? Start with James Truslow Adams' definition.

James Truslow Adams popularized the phrase in The Epic of America (1931): a dream of a land where life is better, richer and fuller for everyone, with opportunity for each person according to ability or achievement.

Adams stresses that it is not just cars and high wages but a social order where each person can reach their fullest stature. Notice how diction like "better and richer and fuller" makes it about more than money.

Handout details: Adams wrote it in The Epic of America (1931, pp. 214-215); the dream is "for the European upper classes" hard to interpret, many Americans had "grown weary and mistrustful of it", and each person should be "recognized by others for what they are, regardless of the fortuitous circumstances of birth or position".

The handout also quotes the Declaration of Independence (life, Liberty and the Pursuit of Happiness), asks whether homesteaders, immigrants and World War II veterans pursued the same dream, and notes critics who say it became material prosperity or is out of reach for the working poor. Thomas Wolfe is quoted on "his shining, golden opportunity".
Ask of each story: whose version of the dream is shown, and who is left out or disillusioned?

Rip Van Winkle: freedom from duty and the birth of a new nation. Goodman Brown: the Puritan ideal of a godly community, undone by hypocrisy. Baker's yarn: folksy Western tall tale that pokes fun at human effort.
Definition is a moving target: consider how the dream has evolved and what it is not.
How to write and answer analysis questions — Most analysis questions ask how an author uses a device to convey a message.
Use direct text evidence and cite it (author, title, page or line). Explain how the exact words create the effect.
For multi-part questions, write ONE cohesive response that covers every part, using transitions to link them to your claim.
Effective paragraph basic structure: claim, evidence, commentary, and a link back to the claim. Use the template on the Effective Paragraph handout for multiple quotes.
Mood-of-the-text (MOT) routine: underline evidence, circle the key word that creates the feeling, label the mood, then explain how the words work together.
Pivotal questions are open-ended and text-based, not hunt-and-fetch: To what extent... In what ways... For what reasons... How is/does... and why is it significant?
SOAPSTone (Speaker, Occasion, Audience, Purpose, Subject, Tone) works on fiction and nonfiction; state purpose as a verb phrase (to warn, to satirize, to mourn).
Authors, dates and forms cheat sheet — A fast-recall table for the recognition questions. Dates are the standard publication years; check any date on your packet.
Irving (1783-1859): "Rip Van Winkle" (The Sketch Book, 1819-20). Romantic, satirical, folk-legend tone.
Keats (1795-1821): "The Eve of St. Agnes" (written 1819, published 1820). Narrative poem, Spenserian stanza.
Poe (1809-1849): "The Fall of the House of Usher" (1839). Gothic; contains "The Haunted Palace" and the "Mad Trist" of Ethelred.
Twain (1835-1910): "Baker's Bluejay Yarn" (1880). Humorous frame plus tall tale; anthropomorphism and dialect.
Hawthorne (1804-1864): "Young Goodman Brown" (1835). Dark Romanticism / Puritan allegory.
Emerson (1803-1882): "The Transcendentalist" (essay/lecture). Nonfiction; idealism vs. materialism.
Hawthorne (1804-1864): "The Custom House" (1850), the introductory essay to The Scarlet Letter. Nonfiction with an invented "found manuscript" frame.
Irving's life and impact (Lesson #1 handout) — The Irving handout is a Wikipedia biography with discussion questions. Expect accuracy-of-information and historical-context questions from it.

Washington Irving (April 3, 1783 - November 28, 1859) was born in Manhattan the same week New Yorkers learned of the British ceasefire that ended the Revolution. His mother named him for George Washington, whom he met at age six.

Boyhood trips up the Hudson, including the Catskill region (the setting of "Rip Van Winkle"), shaped him: he wrote that the Kaatskill Mountains had "the most witching effect on my boyish imagination". Tarrytown gave him Sleepy Hollow's Dutch customs and ghost stories.

Early writing: letters to the Morning Chronicle (1802) as Jonathan Oldstyle; the magazine Salmagundi (1807), which nicknamed New York "Gotham"; then A History of New-York by Diedrich Knickerbocker (1809), promoted with a hoax about the missing historian.

"Rip Van Winkle" is in The Sketch Book of Geoffrey Crayon, Gent. Irving wrote it overnight in Birmingham, England, staying with his sister Sarah and her husband Henry van Wart. He lived abroad for 17 years (1815-1832).

He served as U.S. Minister to Spain (1842-1846), lived at Sunnyside, and is buried in Sleepy Hollow cemetery (Dec 1, 1859). He encouraged writers such as Hawthorne, Melville, Longfellow and Poe, though Poe called him "much over-rated".

Legacy: called the first American man of letters and the first to earn a living by his pen; he advocated copyright protection, popularized "Gotham", is credited with the phrase "the almighty dollar", and helped shape the American image of St. Nicholas and Christmas. His Columbus biography also spread the flat-Earth myth.

Literary periods timeline (Literary Devices packet) — The last page of your Literary Terms packet gives a timeline and movement definitions. Historical-context questions can ask you to place a work in its period.
Puritanism 1620-1770s (plain style; obedience to God; journals, sermons, poems). Neoclassic 1770s to early 1800s (rationalism, the Age of Reason).
Romanticism early 1800s-1870s: a revolt against Rationalism. Realism 1850s-early 1900s. Regionalism 1884-early 1900s. Naturalism late 1800s-mid 1900s. Modernism 1920s-1945. Post-Modernism 1945 on.

Transcendentalism: a 19th-century movement in the Romantic tradition holding that every individual can reach ultimate truths through spiritual intuition, which transcends reason and sensory experience.
Rationalism: truth reached by reason instead of the authority of the past, the Church or an institution (also called Neoclassicism or the Age of Reason).

Plain style: writing that stresses simplicity and clarity, the main form of the Puritan writers. Regionalism / local color: emphasis on a specific setting's speech, customs and landscape, as in Twain's dialect.

Place the texts: Hawthorne's Puritan Salem is set in the 1600s but written in the 1830s Romantic period; Irving, Keats, Poe, Hawthorne and Emerson are Romantic-era writers; Twain (1880) bridges toward Realism and Regionalism.
A. A. Rubin's Poe-style poems (Lesson #2 handout) — Rubin, a former teacher turned professional poet, wrote these poems to imitate Edgar Allan Poe.
"Night Walkers" won first place in a Poe-style contest: a speaker whistling through a graveyard walks all night with a ghost until daybreak, when "all ghosts must go away".

"The Widow's Walk" (first published July 29, 2021 in Love Letters to Poe) uses the refrain "round and round she goes" and repeated end lines to create a haunting, hypnotic sound; children invent stories about the widow, and the dead husband follows her without knowing he is dead.

"The Widow's Walk (1849)" is set at Cold Spring Harbor: a widow paces the roof waiting for a husband whose ship sank; his ghost returns at night and leaves at dawn. The year 1849 is the year Poe died.
Recurring Poe-like elements: ghosts, graveyards, the pale moon, night's "dark inky gloom", refrain and repetition, and a supernatural companion. These echo Poe's Gothic style and mood.
Use for practice: identify allusion, refrain, imagery and mood in short poems, then connect them to Poe's Gothic style in "The Fall of the House of Usher".

traps: Mixing up anthropomorphism (animals or living things given human traits) with personification (nonliving objects given human traits). The bluejays are anthropomorphism; the House of Usher's "eyes" are personification.
Retelling the plot instead of analyzing how the author's language creates the effect. Always tie a specific word or device to a purpose.
Treating "Young Goodman Brown" as clearly a dream or clearly real; the story's power comes from the ambiguity.
Reading the pronoun or the speaker too quickly: check who is talking and who is being addressed (Roderick to the narrator; Rip to the villagers; Angela to Porphyro).
Using dictionary meanings instead of the meaning that fits the line. For vocabulary in context, test each choice back in the sentence.
Putting events in the wrong order. For chronology questions, run a quick timeline in your head for each story before choosing.
Choosing an interpretation that is true in general but not supported by the quote. Pick the answer the quote itself supports.
fms: Seven texts: Rip Van Winkle (Irving), Eve of St. Agnes (Keats), Fall of the House of Usher (Poe), Baker's Bluejay Yarn (Twain), Young Goodman Brown (Hawthorne), The Custom House (Hawthorne), Emerson handout.
Anthropomorphism = animals/living things with human traits; personification = objects.
Answer = claim + text evidence + how the words create the effect + purpose.
STEAL: Speech, Thoughts, Effect on others, Actions, Looks (indirect characterization).

flashcards.d: A framework for analyzing a text's rhetorical situation: Speaker, Occasion, Audience, Purpose, Subject, Tone.
The specific problem, need, or urgency that makes a piece of writing necessary at that moment.
What the writer wants the audience to think, feel, or do — always phrased as 'to ___.'
Limits on a writer, such as word count, audience expectations, or what's appropriate for the occasion.
An appeal to credibility and character — why the audience should trust the speaker.
An appeal to emotion, designed to make the audience feel something that moves them toward the writer's position.
An appeal to logic and reason, using facts, statistics, and clear chains of reasoning.
A logical fallacy that attacks the person making an argument instead of the argument itself.
A logical fallacy that misrepresents an opponent's argument as weaker than it really is, then attacks that weak version.
A logical fallacy presenting only two options when more actually exist.
Repetition of a word or phrase at the beginning of successive clauses or sentences.
Placing two contrasting ideas in a parallel grammatical structure.
Putting two things side by side for effect, such as Baker's earnest tone against a ridiculous tale.
A direct comparison between two unlike things, without using 'like' or 'as.'
A question asked for effect rather than to get a literal answer, leading the reader to a conclusion.
A word's literal, dictionary definition.
The emotional association attached to a word, beyond its literal meaning.
How a writer arranges words and constructs sentences — a rhetorical choice in itself.
The writer's attitude toward the subject, revealed through diction and syntax; it can shift within a passage.
An argument that something is good, bad, right, or wrong.
Analysis that explains WHY evidence matters and HOW it supports the argument — different from summary.
The logical thread connecting a thesis through each piece of evidence to a coherent overall argument.
A specific, arguable claim that someone could reasonably disagree with — the core of an essay's argument.
Acknowledging a valid point on the opposing side of an argument before pivoting back to your own position.
Directly refuting an opposing point by explaining why it's flawed or less compelling.
An essay that develops the writer's own argument using at least three provided sources as support.
Organizing a synthesis essay by summarizing each source in turn instead of by the writer's own claims — a major weakness.
An essay explaining HOW a writer builds their argument and its effect on the audience, not whether the reader agrees.
The core rhetorical analysis skill: identify a specific choice, then explain its effect on the audience.
An essay defending the writer's own position on an issue using the writer's own knowledge, with no provided sources.
Demonstrating nuance, qualification, or broader implications in an argument — beyond a simple thesis-evidence structure.
An error joining two independent clauses with only a comma; fix with a period, semicolon, or conjunction.
A group of words missing a subject, verb, or complete thought, unable to stand alone as a sentence.
Items in a list or series sharing the same grammatical form.
Independent clauses joined with no punctuation or connector at all.
The opportune moment: fitting the argument to the right time, audience, and circumstances.
The relationship among speaker (ethos), audience (pathos), and subject/message (logos).
Always a verb phrase: 'to convince [specific audience] that/to ___.'
Identifying the specific readers' values, assumptions, and knowledge so appeals can be aimed at them.
Appeals to the speaker's credibility, the audience's emotions, and logical reasoning, respectively.
Presenting only two options when more exist.
Assuming that because one event followed another, the first caused the second.
Drawing a broad conclusion from too little or unrepresentative evidence.
Citing an authority as support; a fallacy when the authority is irrelevant or offered as the sole proof.
Deductive: general principle to specific conclusion. Inductive: specific cases to a general (provisional) claim.
The character a writer projects through language, tone, and stance - not the same as the real author.
Repetition of a word or phrase at the end of successive clauses.
A reversal of grammatical structure in successive phrases ('ask not what... what you can do...').
Omitting conjunctions between items in a list, speeding the pace ('I came, I saw, I conquered').
Repeating conjunctions between items ('and... and... and'), slowing the pace and adding weight.
A metaphor states a comparison directly; a simile uses 'like' or 'as.'
A single comparison developed across multiple sentences or an entire passage.
A brief, indirect reference to a person, place, text or idea of historical, cultural, literary or political significance; relies on the reader's knowledge.
Understatement by negating the opposite ('not a small problem'), often for dry emphasis.
Saying the opposite of what is meant, expecting the audience to catch the gap; sarcasm is a pointed form.
A writer's word choice, including the connotations those words carry.
Denotation is the literal meaning; connotation is the emotional or cultural association.
A change in attitude within a text, often marked by 'but,' a paragraph break, or a change in sentence length; it signals a turn in the argument.
Withholds the main clause until the end, building suspense and emphasis.
States the main clause first, then adds modifying phrases and detail.
What a writer chooses to include or omit; itself a form of argument.
Language that appeals to the senses, making an abstraction vivid and felt.
Fact (is it true?), value (is it good?), and policy (what should we do?).
Summary restates what the evidence says; commentary explains HOW it supports the claim.
Narrowing a claim with words like 'often,' 'in most cases,' or a condition, so it fits the evidence.
Relevant evidence bears on the exact claim; sufficient evidence is enough, and varied enough, to be credible.
Specific and arguable; it previews a line of reasoning rather than stating an obvious truth.
Begin a sentence with familiar information and end with the new point, to create flow.
Grant an opposing point, then explain why it does not defeat the thesis ('While X is true, it does not follow that Y').
Words that must name the logical relationship between ideas (however, therefore, for instance), not just decorate.
Chronological, cause-effect, problem-solution, comparison-contrast, and climactic (order of importance).
The quality of prose that guides the reader from idea to idea without gaps; aided by repeated key terms and clear referents.
Build an argument using at least three of the provided sources as evidence, cited clearly.
Walking through sources one by one instead of organizing body paragraphs around your own claims.
A signal phrase names the source in the sentence ('Source B argues'); a parenthetical puts it at the end ((Source B)).
A clear, arguable, often qualified position that the sources can be used to support.
Use one source to complicate or answer another within a paragraph built on your claim.
Explain HOW a writer argues and to what effect - not whether you agree with the argument.
Weak: lists devices ('uses ethos, pathos, logos'). Strong: names what the writer does and to what end.
Naming a strategy and quoting a line without explaining its effect on the audience and purpose.
On a timed essay, analyze 2-3 strategies thoroughly rather than listing many.
The core structure of a body paragraph: identify a choice, quote the text, explain the effect.
Refutation directly answers an opposing argument and shows why it fails; concession grants it partial merit.
One or two well-developed, analyzed examples usually score higher than many shallow ones.
A colon follows a complete clause and introduces an explanation or list; a semicolon joins two independent clauses.
Usually reward the clearest and most concise option, not the longest or most formal.
'past history,' 'end result,' 'the reason ... is because,' 'in order to' when 'to' works.
Verify every answer choice against the exact wording and context of the passage.
Tuesday 10/6. Great American Short Stories, Literary Devices packet, nonfiction and handouts; only Hawthorne text is "Young Goodman Brown".
A movement reacting against Enlightenment rationalism that values emotion, imagination, nature, the individual, the past and the supernatural.
The order-and-reason outlook (rationalism, restraint, science) that Romanticism pushed against.
American Romantic author (1783-1859) of "Rip Van Winkle", first published in The Sketch Book under the pen name Geoffrey Crayon.
The fictional historian whose papers frame "Rip Van Winkle" (Irving's playful fake-history device).

flashcards.t: Rip Van Winkle: setting and time frame
flashcards.d: A Dutch village in the Catskills; Rip sleeps 20 years from British rule under George III into the new American republic.
Rip's wife, characterized as a shrewish "termagant"/"virago"; Irving's language invites sympathy for Rip.
Rip's dog and loyal companion, part of the sympathetic characterization of Rip as easygoing.

flashcards.t: What Irving comments on through Rip's sleep
flashcards.d: The changes from colony to independent nation: new flag, political arguing, and a village that no longer recognizes him.

flashcards.t: The Eve of St. Agnes: legend
flashcards.d: On St. Agnes' Eve (Jan 20), a young woman who follows the rituals may dream of her future husband.

flashcards.t: The Eve of St. Agnes: main characters
flashcards.d: Madeline (the dreamer), Porphyro (her lover from a hostile family), Angela (the old nurse), the Beadsman (opens and closes the poem).
Nine-line stanza rhymed ABABBCBCC, eight lines of iambic pentameter then a longer last line; used throughout Keats's poem.
English Romantic poet (1795-1821); wrote "The Eve of St. Agnes" in 1819 (published 1820).
American Gothic and Romantic writer (1809-1849); "The Fall of the House of Usher" (1839).
The ill, hypersensitive host whose nerves and mind mirror the decaying house.
Roderick's twin sister; entombed while appearing dead; her return precedes the collapse.
Both the physical mansion and the family line; the fissure and collapse show the family's end.
Poem inside Usher: a once-fair palace of Thought overrun by "evil things"; it mirrors Roderick's mind.
The romance the narrator reads to Roderick; sounds in it echo real noises, foreshadowing Madeline's return.
Poe's idea that every detail in a story should build one single emotional impact (in Usher, dread).
Genre with gloomy settings, decay, madness, death and the supernatural; strong mood.
Samuel Clemens (1835-1910); wrote "Baker's Bluejay Yarn" (1880), a humorous tall tale.
A tale, especially a long story of adventure or incredible happenings, often exaggerated.
A middle-aged, simple-hearted California miner who tells Twain that bluejays are the most human and best-talking animals.
Giving animate (living) beings human characteristics, like Baker's talking, swearing bluejays.
Giving inanimate (nonliving) objects human characteristics, like the house's "eye-like windows".

Baker's centerpiece: a jay drops acorns into a hole in a cabin roof that leads into an empty house; five thousand jays laugh when they see the acorns on the floor. Possible metaphor for foolish human effort.
Writing that captures a region or group's speech; builds Baker's characterization and humor.
American Dark Romantic (1804-1864); "Young Goodman Brown" (1835) is his only work on Unit 1.
Puritan Salem Village, Massachusetts; the story moves from town to the dark forest and back.
Brown's wife and the loss of his religious faith; the pink ribbons are her symbol of innocence.
A staff shaped like a black serpent; a Biblical allusion to the serpent in Eden, marking the traveler as the devil.
Hawthorne never confirms whether the forest meeting was a dream or real, leaving the theme of doubt and hypocrisy open.
Hints or clues about events that come later.
An object, person or action that stands for a larger idea, like Faith's pink ribbons.
A story in which characters, settings and events stand for moral, spiritual or political ideas.
Direct: the narrator states traits. Indirect: traits shown through actions, speech, thoughts, appearance and others' reactions.
Who tells the story (first person, third limited, omniscient); shapes what we know and trust.
Mood: the feeling created in the reader. Tone: the author's attitude toward the subject.
Leading Transcendentalist (1803-1882); the handout is from "The Transcendentalist".

Emerson excerpt: the materialist starts from the external world and respects society and social institutions; the idealist (transcendentalist) starts from consciousness and holds that "Mind is the only reality".

flashcards.t: James Truslow Adams and the American Dream
flashcards.d: Popularized the phrase in The Epic of America (1931): opportunity for each person according to ability, a fuller life for everyone, more than material wealth.
An open-ended, text-based question that prompts discussion, not a recall question. Start: To what extent, In what ways, For what reasons, How is/does and why is it significant?
Underline evidence, circle the key word, label the mood, and annotate how the words work together.
A violent, overbearing, quarrelsome woman; Irving's word for Dame Van Winkle.
A domineering, ill-tempered woman; another word Irving uses for Dame.
An impossible-to-overcome strong dislike; Rip's attitude toward profitable labor.
Obsequious: fawning, overly eager to please. Conciliating: trying to win over or calm.
Brisk, cheerful readiness or eagerness.
Ruddy; having a healthy reddish color.
A small group or faction, often political, that joins together in secret or for a shared aim.
Approval or praise.
With hands on hips and elbows turned out.
Inherited from one's father or ancestors.
Relating to marriage.
Noisy, boisterous revelers.
A man paid or bound to pray for others' souls; the cold, praying old man in Keats's poem.
Seraph: an angelic being of the highest order. Pinion: a wing or flight feather. Ramparts: protective earthen or stone walls of a fortress.
Discordant: harsh, disagreeing, out of tune. Throng: a large crowd.
Five methods of indirect characterization: Speech, Thoughts, Effect on others, Actions, Looks.
Static: does not change much in the story. Dynamic: changes in an important way because of the story's action.
Flat: one or two traits, one-dimensional. Round: complex, with many dimensions like real people.
Puritanism (1620-1770s), Neoclassic (1770s-early 1800s), Romanticism (early 1800s-1870s), Realism (1850s-early 1900s).
A 19th-century movement in the Romantic tradition holding that every individual can reach ultimate truths through spiritual intuition, which transcends reason and sensory experience.
Credited with founding Gothic fiction with The Castle of Otranto (1764), subtitled "A Gothic Story".
Wordsworth and Coleridge's 1790s collection that began English Romanticism; Wordsworth's Preface called poetry "the spontaneous overflow of powerful feelings".
Irving's first pen name (1802 letters) and the 1807 magazine that nicknamed New York "Gotham".
The Sketch Book of Geoffrey Crayon, Gent. (1819-20), the collection containing "Rip Van Winkle" and "The Legend of Sleepy Hollow".
Irving's home on the Hudson where he lived after returning from Spain; he is buried at Sleepy Hollow cemetery nearby.
The explorer whose crew, per the villagers, still haunt the Catskills and bowl ninepins, explaining the thunder.
Rip's grown daughter; Rip tells her he is her father, and she takes him in to live with her family.
The most ancient inhabitant, descended from a historian of the province, who recognizes Rip and corroborates the legend of Hendrick Hudson's crew.

flashcards.t: Union Hotel and the sign of General Washington
flashcards.d: The changed inn and sign in Rip's village show the switch from King George III to the new republic.
The question Rip is asked on his return; he does not understand the new political parties and answers as a loyal subject of the King.
The jay's exaggerated claim of how many acorns he dropped in the hole; hyperbole that fuels the yarn's humor.
The hole led into a cabin; the door is open and acorns are scattered on the floor, revealing the jay's absurd task.
The 1675-76 New England conflict alluded to when the traveler says Brown's father burned an Indian village.
The Puritan-era events behind Hawthorne's Salem setting; his ancestor John Hathorne was a judge.
Simple, clear writing stressing obedience to God; the main form of Puritan writers per the packet.
A word, phrase or line repeated for effect, like "round and round she goes" in Rubin's "The Widow's Walk".
An outrageously exaggerated, humorous story that is obviously unbelievable, like Baker's yarn.
Verbal: says one thing, means another. Situational: outcome differs from what is expected. Dramatic: the reader knows more than the character.
Deliberately suggesting two or more different, sometimes conflicting, meanings; on purpose it is a device, not vagueness.
Poe's story in the Philadelphia Saturday Courier (Jan 14, 1832) where he first used the single-effect technique on which the modern short story is built.
The technique of building every detail toward one preconceived impression, with the action focused on the climactic moment and the mood controlled from first to last.
Henry Seidel Canby's phrase for the moral or intellectual weight Hawthorne added to the American short story.
Poe's detective-style tale of reasoning, the parent of the detective story ("The Murders in the Rue Morgue").
Irving: an orderly tale of linked incidents in chronological order, graceful, humorous, urbane. Poe: a concentrated tale of a single, preconceived effect.
The Introduction says Usher and "Young Goodman Brown" both move from light into darkness and back into light; Poe's darkness is theatrical, Hawthorne's is the darkness of the soul.
Henry James's phrase for the probing story that Hawthorne began: less a complication resolved than an exposed situation.
The Introduction says Twain mastered the humorous frontier sketch and the fable; "Bluejay Yarn" is superb in its own kind and links to Uncle Remus and Thurber.
Writing that emphasizes a specific place's speech, customs and landscape; the Introduction credits Bret Harte's "The Luck of Roaring Camp" (1868) with popularizing the short story.
Pestilent: harmful, troublesome. Patrimonial: inherited from a father. Urchin: a mischievous small child (all describing Rip's farm and son).
Steady, careful diligence (Rip has plenty of it, but only for idle pursuits like fishing).
Confusing, hard-to-understand language; Rip cannot follow the election talk.
A state of inactivity or deep sleep; Irving's word for Rip's twenty-year sleep.
To confirm; Peter Vanderdonk corroborates Rip's story.
I pray thee; afraid; stay or wait (from Faith's plea in "Young Goodman Brown").
Scruples: moral doubts. Anathema: a formal curse or denunciation.
Benighted: in darkness, physical or moral. Wanton: immoral, reckless, unrestrained.
Wordiness; a crack; a small mountain lake; corpse-like paleness (Poe's Usher vocabulary).
Twain's term for stupid or thick-headed, describing the jays' opinions about the hole.
The silent landlord whose opinions control the idle bench-sitters at the inn; he has died eighteen years before Rip's return.
Per Peter Vanderdonk, the explorer and his crew keep a vigil in the Kaatskills every twenty years; the thunder is their ninepins.
Henpecked husbands wish for "a quieting draught out of Rip Van Winkle's flagon" (p. 51).
Respected Salem figures Brown sees in the forest; Cloyse taught him his catechism.
A woman at the forest ceremony who "received the devil's promise to be queen of hell"; her name is that of an actual Salem witch-trial defendant.
Brown's cry when the pink ribbon falls; followed by "There is no good on earth; and sin is but a name. Come, devil!"

flashcards.t: Quotation: "We have put her living in the tomb!"
flashcards.d: Roderick's confession to the narrator that he heard Madeline moving in the coffin (p. 90).
The jay's first delighted reaction to the knot-hole in the cabin roof (Baker's yarn).
The jay's boast of how many acorns he dropped; hyperbole in Baker's yarn.
Hawthorne claims The Scarlet Letter comes from a manuscript and a scarlet "A" left by former Surveyor Jonathan Pue, making the invented novel feel like a rediscovered true story.
A change in presidential administration replaces Hawthorne as Surveyor; he jokes he was "guillotined," but surviving it frees him to finally write the novel.
The idea that the modern short story is less a plot complication resolved than a situation uncovered, with the ending an illumination, not a trick.
A concentrated story built for one preconceived impression, with all the action aimed at the climax; first used in "Metzengerstein" (Jan. 14, 1832).
The Introduction's image for Hawthorne's story versus Poe's: Hawthorne's soul-darkness is far denser in specific gravity than Poe's theatrical Gothic.
Never wrote a good short story by the editors' standard; mastered the humorous frontier sketch and the fable. The Bluejay Yarn belongs to the beast-story tradition.

quiz.q: A politician gives a eulogy at a colleague's funeral. What is the OCCASION?
o: The politician’s long career and the party he represented in office
The colleague's death and the funeral service
The audience’s shared grief and the comfort they seek from the speaker
The political climate surrounding the colleague’s final months in office
quiz.e: Occasion is the event that prompts the writing — here, the death and funeral.

quiz.q: A textbook chapter and a passionate op-ed can share the same subject but differ in what?
o: Purpose and tone
Subject matter
Font size
Publication date only
quiz.e: Two texts can share a subject but differ completely in purpose and tone.

quiz.q: Identifying a speech's specific intended audience (rather than 'everyone') is important because:
o: Rhetorical choices are made for a general readership, so a narrow audience limits a writer’s persuasive range
The audience matters only in spoken texts, since written arguments are judged on their logic alone
Rhetorical choices are tailored to a specific audience's values and knowledge
A named audience limits the writer’s freedom, and strong rhetoric works best when it avoids any single group
quiz.e: Writers tailor their rhetorical choices to a specific audience, not a generic one.

quiz.q: A company's product recall letter is an example of what shaping the occasion?
o: A broad essay assignment that gives the writer wide freedom over the subject
A news story about an unrelated industry that has caught the writer’s attention
The writer’s personal preference to explain a policy before anyone has asked about it
A specific real-world event requiring a response
quiz.e: The recall itself is the event/occasion prompting the letter.

quiz.q: A CEO's shareholder letter written just after a scandal is shaped mostly by what exigence?
o: The company’s annual calendar, which sets the date by which the letter must reach investors
The need to respond to and address the scandal
A general trend in the industry that has little to do with the scandal itself
The CEO’s wish to reflect on the history of the company and the lessons of its founders
quiz.e: The scandal creates the urgent need (exigence) prompting this specific letter.

quiz.q: Which SOAPSTone element asks 'who is writing or speaking?'
o: Speaker
Subject
Purpose
Tone
quiz.e: Speaker identifies who is behind the text and what we know about them.

quiz.q: A formal court filing versus a casual text message about the same event differ mainly in what?
o: Subject matter, since a court filing must cover the facts in far more detail than a casual text
Register and constraints appropriate to the occasion
The event itself, which is described differently in a legal context than in a private one
The language used, since formal filings are written in a different language than private messages
quiz.e: The occasion and its constraints shape register/formality even when the underlying subject is the same.

quiz.q: Why is 'the audience is everyone' usually a weak rhetorical analysis claim?
o: Effective rhetoric is normally shaped for a specific, identifiable audience
Texts are normally written for a broad readership, so a specific audience limits their reach
A writer cannot reliably know who will read a text, so audience is best left out of the analysis
Naming an audience adds length to the analysis without improving the evidence for any claim
quiz.e: Strong analysis identifies a specific intended audience the rhetorical choices are shaped for.

quiz.q: A letter to the editor responding to a specific recent news event best illustrates:
o: Exigence driving the occasion for writing
A timeless, abstract meditation that could have been written in any year about anything
A text addressed to no one in particular and shaped by no specific reader’s concerns
A text written under no constraints, since the editor imposes no limit on a letter’s length or topic
quiz.e: The recent news event is the exigence prompting the letter.

quiz.q: Which best distinguishes SPEAKER from the actual author in some rhetorical texts (e.g., a persona)?
o: The speaker and the author are always the same person, so a persona is an error of analysis
The speaker is the voice/persona presented in the text, which may differ from the biographical author
Speaker refers only to the person who delivers an oral speech, as opposed to a written text
The speaker is the audience that the text addresses, while the author is the person who wrote it
quiz.e: In some texts a constructed persona speaks, distinct from the historical author.

quiz.q: Which SOAPSTone element would you use to analyze WHY a writer chose formal academic language?
o: Audience and occasion
Subject only
Tone only, unrelated to audience
None of these
quiz.e: Register often reflects choices shaped by both intended audience and occasion.

quiz.q: A graduation speech given right after a school tragedy would have its content most shaped by:
o: The conventional traditions of graduation speeches, which seldom change from year to year
The specific exigence of the tragedy
The weather and setting of the ceremony, which would dominate how the speaker chose to begin
The preferences of the school’s administration, who customarily approve each speech in advance
quiz.e: The tragedy is the driving exigence shaping the speech's content and tone.

quiz.q: Which correctly identifies constraints in an opinion column limited to 800 words for a general newspaper audience?
o: The writer’s personal beliefs and the strength with which she holds them, which limit what she can argue
Word count and audience expectations for the publication
The topic itself, which the editor has chosen and which sets the boundaries of the argument
The date of publication, which determines how much recent evidence the writer is able to use
quiz.e: Word limits and audience/publication norms are classic constraints.

quiz.q: A charity ad showing images of hungry children to evoke sympathy relies primarily on:
o: Pathos
Logos
Ethos
A straw man fallacy
quiz.e: Vivid, emotional imagery designed to evoke sympathy is a pathos appeal.

quiz.q: A doctor citing peer-reviewed studies to support a health claim uses primarily:
o: Pathos, supported by an appeal to the audience’s fear of illness and the stakes of ignoring medical advice
A slippery slope fallacy, which connects a minor choice to a catastrophic outcome without evidence
An appeal to tradition, since the doctor relies on accepted medical custom rather than new research
Logos, supported by ethos from expertise
quiz.e: Data/studies are logos; the doctor's expertise also lends ethos.

quiz.q: 'If we allow students one retake, soon no test will ever count' is an example of:
o: Slippery slope fallacy
Valid logical reasoning
Ethos appeal
Antithesis
quiz.e: This claims an extreme, unjustified chain reaction from one small step — a slippery slope.

quiz.q: 'My opponent wants to cut this program, so he clearly hates poor families' misrepresents the opponent's actual position. This is:
o: A straw man fallacy
A valid rebuttal
An example of logos
Antithesis
quiz.e: This exaggerates/distorts the opponent's real position to attack a weaker version — a straw man.

quiz.q: 'Either we ban the product entirely, or we do nothing at all' ignores middle-ground options. This is:
o: A false dilemma
A hasty generalization
Ethos
Pathos
quiz.e: Presenting only two extreme options when others exist is a false dilemma.

quiz.q: Attacking a scientist's argument by mocking their appearance instead of their data is:
o: Ad hominem
Logos
A valid ethos critique
Antithesis
quiz.e: Attacking the person rather than the argument is ad hominem.

quiz.q: 'I met three rude tourists from that city, so everyone from there must be rude' is a:
o: Hasty generalization
Slippery slope
False dilemma
Appeal to logos
quiz.e: Drawing a broad conclusion from too small a sample is a hasty generalization.

quiz.q: A speaker who fairly acknowledges the opposing view before responding builds:
o: Ethos, by appearing reasonable and fair
Pathos, by arousing sympathy for the opposing side and so softening the audience’s feelings
A logical fallacy, since conceding any point weakens the speaker’s own position in the debate
Authority by command, since the speaker shows that the opposing view has already been defeated
quiz.e: Fair acknowledgment of opposing views builds credibility/ethos.

quiz.q: Which is the best full analysis, not just labeling?
o: This sentence is an example of logos, because it uses a number to support the writer’s claim
Logos is used in this sentence, and it appears in the middle of the paragraph where the claim is made
The writer used numbers in this sentence, and the numbers are specific and easy for readers to follow
The statistic builds logos, making the argument feel objective and hard to dispute
quiz.e: Strong analysis explains the effect of the device, not just names it.

quiz.q: A veteran discussing the human cost of war through a personal story primarily appeals to:
o: Logos only, since the veteran presents events in order and lets the audience reach its own conclusion
A hasty generalization, since a single story is offered as proof about every soldier’s experience
Antithesis, since the story sets the soldier’s hopes against the harsh reality of the battlefield
Pathos, and secondarily ethos from firsthand experience
quiz.e: Personal storytelling evokes emotion (pathos) while firsthand experience also builds ethos.

quiz.q: Using vivid, charged language ('this catastrophe will devastate families') primarily builds:
o: Pathos
Only logos
Only ethos
No appeal
quiz.e: Emotionally charged language is designed to evoke feeling — pathos.

quiz.q: 'You can't trust her tax plan, she's not even an economist' dismisses her plan based only on her credentials rather than its content. This mixes:
o: A valid logos critique of the plan’s economics, since the speaker lacks the training to judge it
Antithesis, since the sentence sets her credentials against the contents of her tax plan
Parallelism, since the sentence repeats a grammatical form to emphasize the speaker’s authority
Ad hominem-style dismissal disguised as an ethos critique
quiz.e: Dismissing an argument based only on the person's background, without engaging the actual plan, echoes ad hominem reasoning.

quiz.q: Which best explains why using pathos is NOT automatically a logical fallacy?
o: All emotional appeals are inherently dishonest, so using pathos is always a fallacy in an argument
Only logos can ever make an argument valid, so a speaker should avoid emotion in a serious debate
Pathos always signals weak evidence, since writers use emotion only when they cannot find facts
Emotional appeals can be a legitimate, valid rhetorical strategy alongside logic
quiz.e: Pathos is a legitimate classical appeal; it becomes a fallacy only when it replaces valid reasoning deceptively.

quiz.q: 'Studies from three major universities all found the same result' primarily supports:
o: Logos, through convergent evidence
Pathos alone
A straw man
A false dilemma
quiz.e: Multiple corroborating studies is evidence-based reasoning — logos.

quiz.q: Identify the fallacy: 'We must ban video games entirely, or violence will completely destroy society.'
o: A valid appeal to logos, since the speaker states a cause and its likely effect in order
An ethos appeal that relies on the speaker’s authority to justify a total ban
Antithesis, since the sentence sets two outcomes against each other for rhetorical effect
False dilemma combined with slippery slope
quiz.e: This presents only two extremes (false dilemma) and an unjustified extreme chain (slippery slope).

quiz.q: On the exam, why is simply writing 'this is pathos' insufficient?
o: Pathos is rarely tested on the exam, so a student who names it gains nothing from doing so
It doesn't explain HOW the appeal functions or its effect on the audience
A label is always sufficient, since graders check only whether the correct term was used
Ethos is the only appeal that matters, so naming pathos adds nothing to the analysis
quiz.e: Analysis must connect the device to its specific effect, not just name it.

quiz.q: 'I have a dream... I have a dream... I have a dream' at the start of successive sentences is:
o: Anaphora
Epistrophe
Antithesis
Simile
quiz.e: Repetition at the BEGINNING of successive clauses is anaphora.

quiz.q: '...government of the people, by the people, for the people' repeats a phrase at the END of clauses. This is:
o: Epistrophe
Anaphora
Chiasmus
Hyperbole
quiz.e: Repetition at the END of successive clauses/phrases is epistrophe.

quiz.q: 'Ask not what your country can do for you—ask what you can do for your country' reverses grammatical structure. This is:
o: Chiasmus
Simile
Personification
Hyperbole
quiz.e: A reversal of grammatical structure across clauses is chiasmus.

quiz.q: 'The wind whispered through the trees' gives human qualities to wind. This is:
o: Personification
Simile
Antithesis
Epistrophe
quiz.e: Giving human qualities to something nonhuman is personification.

quiz.q: 'Do you really think that plan will work?' asked with no expectation of a literal answer is a:
o: Rhetorical question
Simile
Antithesis
Epistrophe
quiz.e: A question asked for effect, not a literal answer, is rhetorical.

quiz.q: Saying 'Great job' sarcastically after someone makes a mistake is an example of:
o: Verbal irony
Personification
Anaphora
A simile
quiz.e: Saying the opposite of what is meant, often to criticize, is verbal irony.

quiz.q: 'It was the best of times, it was the worst of times' places two contrasting ideas in parallel structure. This is:
o: Antithesis
Chiasmus
Personification
Understatement
quiz.e: Placing contrasting ideas in parallel grammatical structure is antithesis.

quiz.q: Placing a description of extreme wealth directly next to a description of extreme poverty to highlight the contrast is:
o: Juxtaposition
Anaphora
Hyperbole
Simile
quiz.e: Placing two things side by side to highlight contrast is juxtaposition.

quiz.q: Repeating the last word of one clause at the start of the next ('Fear leads to anger. Anger leads to hate.') is:
o: Anadiplosis
Chiasmus
Antithesis
Personification
quiz.e: Repeating the final word of one clause at the start of the next is anadiplosis.

quiz.q: A list of parallel infinitive phrases ('to run, to jump, to swim') used for rhythm and balance is:
o: Parallelism
Antithesis
Personification
Hyperbole
quiz.e: Repeating a grammatical structure across a series is parallelism.

quiz.q: Which distinguishes simile from metaphor?
o: They are identical devices, since both compare two unlike things for vivid effect in the same way
A metaphor always uses “as” to make its comparison, while a simile uses a stated verb
A simile never compares two things, whereas a metaphor always compares exactly two
Simile uses 'like' or 'as'; metaphor makes a direct comparison without them
quiz.e: The comparison word 'like'/'as' is present in a simile but absent in a metaphor.

quiz.q: Choosing elevated, precise vocabulary over casual everyday words reflects:
o: Formal diction
Colloquial diction
Syntax only
Tone shift
quiz.e: Elevated, precise word choice is formal diction.

quiz.q: A single long sentence with many clauses piling on top of each other can create a sense of:
o: Accumulation or breathless momentum
Simplicity and calm, since long sentences give each idea space and keep the reader at ease
Blunt emphasis, since each clause is stressed by the pause that follows it in the sentence
Silence and stillness, since the sentence slows the action so that nothing seems to happen
quiz.e: Long, complex sentences can build accumulation or momentum.

quiz.q: Mixing short and long sentences throughout a passage primarily controls:
o: Pacing and reader engagement
Grammar rules only
The essay's word count
The thesis statement
quiz.e: Sentence variety controls pacing and keeps the reader engaged.

quiz.q: A transition word like 'however' appearing mid-passage most likely signals:
o: A tone or idea shift
The end of the essay
A grammar error
A repeated claim
quiz.e: Contrast transitions often mark a shift in tone or idea.

quiz.q: The combination of a writer's characteristic diction, syntax, and tone is called their:
o: Style
Subject
Occasion
Constraint
quiz.e: Style is the recognizable combination of diction, syntax, and tone across a writer's work.

quiz.q: Concrete, sensory diction ('the acrid smell of smoke') mainly creates:
o: Vivid, specific imagery
Abstract analysis
Formal register only
No effect
quiz.e: Concrete, sensory words create vivid images for the reader.

quiz.q: Abstract diction ('justice,' 'freedom,' 'progress') tends to create a more:
o: Analytical or conceptual feel
Vivid sensory feel
Casual feel
Humorous feel
quiz.e: Abstract, conceptual words create a more analytical, less sensory tone.

quiz.q: How formal or informal language is, relative to the occasion, is called:
o: Register
Denotation
Anaphora
Exigence
quiz.e: Register describes the formality level of language relative to context.

quiz.q: Assuming short sentences always signal 'simple ideas' is a mistake because:
o: Short sentences are never used for emphasis, since a writer with weighty ideas needs long ones
Long sentences always signal simplicity, so the reverse is true of short sentences in most prose
Sentence length does not matter to a reader’s impression of the writer’s style or ideas
Short sentences are often used to emphasize complex or weighty ideas
quiz.e: Short sentences frequently emphasize complex or weighty points, not just simple ones.

quiz.q: 'The committee shall convene' vs. 'let's get together' differ mainly in:
o: Diction and register
Subject matter
Punctuation only
Length only
quiz.e: These phrases describe the same action with very different formal vs. casual diction/register.

quiz.q: An argument claiming something is TRUE or FALSE and can be verified is a claim of:
o: Fact
Value
Policy
Style
quiz.e: A claim of fact asserts something verifiable as true or false.

quiz.q: Citing a peer-reviewed study's data supports an argument primarily through:
o: Statistical evidence
Anecdotal evidence
Personification
Antithesis
quiz.e: Numerical/data-based evidence is statistical evidence.

quiz.q: Quoting a leading scientist's opinion on climate change borrows credibility through:
o: Expert testimony
Anecdotal evidence only
A logical fallacy
Antithesis
quiz.e: Citing an authority's opinion is expert testimony, which lends ethos.

quiz.q: A recommended ratio of evidence to commentary in a strong paragraph is roughly:
o: Five sentences of evidence to one of commentary, which lets the evidence carry the argument
One sentence of evidence to two or more of commentary
Only evidence and no commentary, since the evidence is meant to speak for itself
Only commentary and no evidence, since the writer’s own reasoning is what the reader wants
quiz.e: Strong paragraphs favor more commentary/analysis than raw evidence.

quiz.q: The logical thread connecting a thesis through evidence to a coherent argument is called the:
o: Line of reasoning
Rhetorical situation
Exigence
Register
quiz.e: This is the definition of a line of reasoning.

quiz.q: Evidence presented without ever connecting back to the thesis is a weakness because:
o: The reader shouldn't have to guess why the evidence was included
Evidence never needs to be justified, since a reader can supply the missing connection unaided
All evidence is self-explanatory, so the writer’s commentary only distracts from the quotation
Connections to the thesis are optional in a body paragraph if the topic sentence is clear
quiz.e: Every piece of evidence needs explicit commentary connecting it to the thesis.

quiz.q: A strong thesis usually combines which claim types?
o: Only claims of fact, since a thesis that takes a position on values cannot be proved
Only claims of policy, since an argument must always recommend an action to be persuasive
Elements of fact, value, and/or policy as needed for a specific position
No claim type at all, since a thesis is a summary of the topic and not an assertion
quiz.e: Strong theses often blend claim types into one specific, arguable position.

quiz.q: Which is the best example of commentary, not summary?
o: The study found a 40% increase in reported cases over the decade in the three cities examined
The article discusses pollution and its effects on the health of residents in the region
The data presented in the second source were collected by a team of three researchers
This statistic reveals how widespread the problem truly is, undermining the claim that it's rare
quiz.e: This explains the significance of the evidence rather than just restating it.

quiz.q: A paragraph that only restates evidence in different words, without analysis, is best described as:
o: Mostly summary
Strong commentary
A rebuttal
A synthesis
quiz.e: Restating evidence without analysis is summary, not commentary.

quiz.q: Why is repeating the same underlying point across multiple paragraphs a weakness?
o: It strengthens the thesis, since repetition makes the writer’s central claim seem more certain
It is required by AP graders, who look for the thesis to be restated in every paragraph
It always improves the essay’s organization because each paragraph then has a clear and identical purpose
It fails to build a genuine line of reasoning that advances the argument
quiz.e: Genuine line of reasoning requires each paragraph to add something new.

quiz.q: Which type of evidence draws a parallel to a past event to support a claim?
o: Historical evidence
Anecdotal evidence about the present
Statistical evidence
Ethos appeal only
quiz.e: Referencing a past event or precedent is historical evidence.

quiz.q: A claim asserting 'social media usage has tripled since 2015' is a claim of:
o: Fact
Value
Policy
Tone
quiz.e: This is a verifiable factual claim.

quiz.q: Which best shows a logical LINE OF REASONING across paragraphs?
o: All three paragraphs repeat the same statistic in different words to reinforce the writer’s claim
Paragraphs are ordered randomly so that the reader meets each idea in a fresh and unexpected way
Only the introduction contains a claim, and the following paragraphs supply a list of examples
Paragraph 1 establishes the problem's scope; paragraph 2 explains its cause; paragraph 3 proposes a solution
quiz.e: Each paragraph builds a distinct, connected part of the overall argument.

quiz.q: 'In this essay, I will discuss climate change' is a weak thesis because it:
o: Announces intent instead of taking an arguable position
It is too specific, since it limits the writer to a single claim about climate change
It is too controversial, since an arguable position cannot be supported with evidence
It uses too much evidence, since a thesis should contain none of the support it will later develop
quiz.e: This merely announces the topic rather than making a claim.

quiz.q: Acknowledging a valid point on the opposing side before returning to your own argument is called:
o: A concession
A rebuttal
A thesis
Anaphora
quiz.e: Acknowledging a fair opposing point is a concession.

quiz.q: 'Also' and 'another thing' are often weak transitions because they show:
o: Strong causal relationships, since each of these words marks the effect of the preceding sentence
A clear contrast between ideas, so that the reader expects a change of direction in the argument
Addition, but not the actual logical relationship between ideas
A concession to the opposing view, so that the reader knows the writer is about to qualify a claim
quiz.e: These words only signal addition, not deeper logical connections.

quiz.q: Introducing a completely new, unsupported argument in the conclusion is considered:
o: A structural weakness
A best practice
Required by convention
Irrelevant to essay quality
quiz.e: New unsupported arguments in a conclusion weaken structural coherence.

quiz.q: A body paragraph missing commentary that ties evidence back to the thesis is:
o: Structurally incomplete
Ideal
Required for high scores
Impossible to improve
quiz.e: Every body paragraph needs commentary linking evidence explicitly to the thesis.

quiz.q: Why should an introduction establish context briefly before the thesis?
o: It orients the reader without delaying the argument unnecessarily
It lets the writer survey the full history of the topic so that readers need no further background later
It delays the thesis long enough for the reader to feel the importance of the issue before the claim
It gives the thesis a stronger position by placing it at the end of a long and detailed opening paragraph
quiz.e: Brief context orients the reader efficiently before the thesis arrives.

quiz.q: A thesis that simply restates a factual prompt statement is weak because it:
o: Is too controversial, since a thesis that restates a prompt will be rejected by most readers
Uses evidence effectively, but only because it quotes the prompt and leaves no room for the writer’s claim
Is too specific, since it names the details of the prompt and gives the essay no room to develop
Isn't arguable — no one could reasonably disagree with a plain fact
quiz.e: A thesis must be arguable; a bare fact restatement isn't.

quiz.q: Which paragraph structure element ties the evidence back to the paragraph's claim?
