o: The topic sentence alone, since it announces the claim that the paragraph is meant to support
The transition at the paragraph’s opening, since it links the evidence to the previous paragraph’s claim
The quotation itself, since a well-chosen piece of evidence makes its own connection to the claim
Commentary at the paragraph's close
quiz.e: Closing commentary should tie the evidence explicitly back to the thesis/claim.

quiz.q: Which best represents a genuine counterargument being engaged, not dismissed?
o: Explaining the opposing view's strongest form, then explaining specifically why it falls short
Mentioning the opposing view in one dismissive sentence and moving on to the writer’s strongest evidence
Ignoring the opposing view entirely so that the essay’s line of reasoning is not interrupted by objections
Restating your own thesis in place of the counterargument, so that the reader remembers the main claim
quiz.e: Genuine engagement requires presenting the opposing view fairly before rebutting it.

quiz.q: Which best distinguishes a concession from a rebuttal?
o: A concession acknowledges a valid opposing point; a rebuttal explains why a point is flawed
They are the same move, since each acknowledges the opposing view before returning to the writer’s thesis
A rebuttal always comes before a concession, since the writer must refute a point before granting any part of it
A concession is never followed by a rebuttal, since granting a point ends the discussion of that objection
quiz.e: Concession = acknowledge; rebuttal = refute — they are distinct, often paired, moves.

quiz.q: A conclusion that only repeats the thesis word-for-word is considered:
o: The strongest possible conclusion, since a repeated thesis reminds the reader of the central claim
A requirement for a passing score, since the rubric asks the writer to restate the thesis at the end
A missed opportunity to extend the argument's significance
A conclusion that cannot be improved, since the thesis has already been stated in its best possible form
quiz.e: Strong conclusions go beyond simple restatement to broaden significance.

quiz.q: The synthesis essay primarily requires the writer to:
o: Summarize every source in the order given, with a brief comment on each source’s main point
Develop their own argument, supported by at least three provided sources
Argue against all of the sources provided, in order to show independent thinking and original judgment
Avoid citing any sources directly, since the essay is meant to rest on the writer’s own knowledge
quiz.e: The synthesis essay is the writer's own argument, using sources as support.

quiz.q: What is the minimum number of sources that must be cited in the synthesis essay?
o: Three
One
All provided sources
Zero
quiz.e: At least three of the provided sources must be cited.

quiz.q: Organizing a synthesis essay strictly source-by-source ('Source A says... Source B says...') is:
o: A common weakness — it becomes a summary rather than an argument
The strongest possible structure, since it shows that the writer has read every source with equal care
Required by the prompt, which asks the writer to discuss each source in the order that it is printed
Impossible to avoid, since the sources are presented in a sequence that the essay must follow
quiz.e: Source-by-source organization tends to become summary instead of a genuine argument.

quiz.q: A 'qualified' thesis on the synthesis prompt (agreeing with conditions/nuance) is:
o: Never acceptable, since the synthesis prompt asks the writer to take one clear position and no other
Acceptable only for the argument essay, where nuance is welcome but the synthesis task requires a firm stance
Automatically a weak thesis, since conditions and exceptions show that the writer has not decided
Completely acceptable and often stronger than an all-or-nothing stance
quiz.e: A specific, qualified position is a legitimate and often strong approach.

quiz.q: A vague thesis that doesn't commit to any real position on the synthesis prompt is:
o: The safest and strongest option, since a claim that commits to nothing can never be shown to be wrong
A weakness — it isn't defensible or specific
Required by the rubric, which asks the writer to avoid taking a position on contested questions
Impossible to avoid when the sources disagree, since any position will be open to objection
quiz.e: Vague, noncommittal theses fail to take a defensible position.

quiz.q: Citing a source and then explaining how it supports your specific claim demonstrates:
o: Improper use of sources, since a quotation should speak for itself without any explanation from the writer
Proper integration of evidence with commentary
A rhetorical fallacy in which the writer’s commentary substitutes for the source’s own evidence and reasoning
Nothing useful, since graders look only at the number of sources rather than at how they are used
quiz.e: Sources need commentary connecting them to the writer's own argument.

quiz.q: Citing sources by their letter (e.g., 'Source B') or clear paraphrase, rather than quoting at length, is generally:
o: Preferred, when paired with analysis
Never acceptable, since graders credit only direct quotations that appear in the printed source
Required to be verbatim, since a paraphrase risks misrepresenting the source and costing the writer credit
Irrelevant to scoring, since graders look only at whether the essay’s claim is clearly stated
quiz.e: Concise citation paired with analysis is generally more effective than long unanalyzed quotes.

quiz.q: A synthesis essay that could be outlined using ONLY the writer's own claims (sources filling in support) is:
o: A sign of strong, argument-driven organization
A sign of a weak essay, since the writer relies on the sources too little to show careful reading
Impossible to achieve, since a synthesis essay cannot be written without presenting each source in turn
Relevant only to rhetorical analysis, in which the writer’s own claims drive each paragraph
quiz.e: This shows the essay is organized by argument, not merely summarizing sources.

quiz.q: Anticipating the strongest counterargument to your synthesis position and addressing it with a source is:
o: A strong strategic move
Prohibited by the prompt
Irrelevant to the essay's score
Only for extended-response history essays
quiz.e: Addressing the strongest counterargument, supported by a source, strengthens the essay.

quiz.q: Which best distinguishes synthesis from summary?
o: They are identical tasks, since both ask the writer to restate the ideas found in the sources
Summary requires more sources than synthesis, since it must include each one in the writer’s account
Synthesis never uses sources directly, since it relies only on the writer’s own knowledge and judgment
Synthesis develops the writer's OWN argument; summary just restates sources' content
quiz.e: Synthesis is argument-driven; summary is restatement without a governing claim.

quiz.q: Why is using FEWER than three sources a problem on the synthesis essay?
o: Fewer sources are always preferred, since a focused essay is easier to organize and to defend
It fails to meet the minimum sourcing requirement of the task
There is no source requirement, and a writer may use as many or as few as the argument demands
Fewer sources improve organization, since the writer has less material to fit into a single line of reasoning
quiz.e: At least three sources must be cited to meet the task's requirements.

quiz.q: A synthesis essay thesis that says 'Some believe X, others believe Y' without taking a position is:
o: Too noncommittal to be defensible
An ideal thesis
Required by the rubric
The safest possible choice
quiz.e: A thesis must commit to a specific, defensible position, not just describe both sides.

quiz.q: Which best represents strategic sourcing to acknowledge a counterargument?
o: “Source C says cost is a concern, and Source A says the plan has long-term benefits for the town.”
'While Source C raises a valid concern about cost, the long-term benefits described in Source A outweigh it.'
Leaving out Source C altogether so that the essay’s argument appears to face no serious objection
Quoting Source C at full length with no commentary, so that the reader can judge its force directly
quiz.e: This acknowledges the counterpoint, then explains why the writer's position still holds — using sources purposefully.

quiz.q: Why might a writer use a source they don't fully agree with in a synthesis essay?
o: Sources the writer disagrees with can never be cited, since they would weaken the writer’s own argument
To increase the word count so that the essay appears to be as long and thorough as the task requires
Because the prompt requires the writer to use every source with equal weight and in the order given
To acknowledge and then rebut it as part of the argument
quiz.e: Sources can be used to represent and then rebut opposing views.

quiz.q: A synthesis essay entirely organized as 'Source A, then Source B, then Source C' with no unifying claim across paragraphs is:
o: An ideal structure, since it ensures that each source receives careful attention in turn
Required by the College Board, whose scoring guide asks writers to treat the sources in order
The best way to cite sources, because it prevents the writer from confusing them with one another
A structural weakness resembling a summary, not an argument
quiz.e: This organization pattern fails to build a genuine, unified argument.

quiz.q: Which best reflects a synthesis essay's core goal?
o: Reporting what each source states in order, so that the reader can see how closely it has been read
Disproving every source provided in order to show that the writer’s judgment is independent
Using sources as evidence to support the writer's own defensible claim
Avoiding any position at all, so that the essay appears fair to every source and every point of view
quiz.e: The synthesis essay's core goal is the writer's argument, supported by sources.

quiz.q: The rhetorical analysis essay primarily asks the writer to:
o: Argue for or against the passage’s topic, using the passage’s evidence as support for the writer’s own view
Summarize the passage’s content in order and comment on its overall tone and its apparent purpose
Explain HOW a writer builds their argument and its effect on the audience
List every device in the passage with its definition, so that the grader can see the writer knows the terms
quiz.e: Rhetorical analysis focuses on HOW the argument is built, not whether the reader agrees with it.

quiz.q: The single most common error in rhetorical analysis essays is:
o: Using too many quotations, so that the writer’s own analysis is crowded out of each paragraph
Citing too few devices, so that the essay does not cover the passage’s rhetorical strategies
Being too concise, so that each paragraph’s claim is stated without enough support from the passage
Arguing for or against the passage's topic instead of analyzing the writer's choices
quiz.e: Students often mistakenly argue the topic itself instead of analyzing HOW the writer argues.

quiz.q: A strong rhetorical analysis thesis should:
o: Restate the passage’s topic and summarize its argument so that the grader sees the writer understood it
Identify the writer's purpose and preview the strategies to be analyzed
Avoid mentioning the writer’s purpose, which belongs in the conclusion rather than in the thesis
List every device in the passage in order, so that the thesis shows the full range of the writer’s skill
quiz.e: An effective thesis names purpose and previews the specific strategies discussed.

quiz.q: How many rhetorical strategies should a strong essay typically focus on?
o: 2–3, discussed in real depth
10 or more, briefly mentioned
Exactly one, in extreme depth
None — just summarize
quiz.e: A few well-developed strategies are stronger than many shallow ones.

quiz.q: Choosing strategies you can trace across MULTIPLE parts of a passage, rather than a single isolated line, is important because:
o: Isolated examples are always stronger, since a single well-chosen line can be analyzed in great depth
It supports a more developed, well-evidenced analysis
The exam requires only one example per device, so a pattern across the passage adds nothing
Multiple examples are never useful, since they distract the reader from the writer’s central claim
quiz.e: Tracing a strategy across the passage allows for deeper, more convincing analysis.

quiz.q: Why should a rhetorical analysis essay start by identifying the rhetorical situation?
o: It grounds the analysis in speaker, audience, purpose, and occasion
It is unnecessary busywork, since the grader already knows the passage and its occasion
Rhetorical situation matters only for synthesis essays, in which several sources must be compared
It replaces the need for a thesis, since the situation already tells the reader what the essay will claim
quiz.e: Establishing the rhetorical situation grounds the entire analysis that follows.

quiz.q: A rhetorical analysis essay that spends a whole paragraph arguing the topic is wrong (e.g., disagreeing with the writer's stance) is:
o: The correct approach, since an analysis must first show that the writer’s stance is wrong
Required for a high score, since graders reward writers who take a clear position on the topic
Off-task — this isn't what rhetorical analysis asks for
Optional but encouraged, since it shows the writer’s independence and willingness to take a position
quiz.e: Arguing the topic itself, rather than analyzing the writer's rhetoric, is off-task.

quiz.q: Explaining WHY a specific word was chosen over an alternative demonstrates:
o: Irrelevant nitpicking, since graders care about the writer’s main claim and not about individual words
A logical fallacy, since the writer cannot know why the author chose one word over another
Strong, precise rhetorical analysis
Weak analysis, since a single word cannot carry enough meaning to support a claim about purpose
quiz.e: Explaining specific word choices over alternatives shows precise, strong analysis.

quiz.q: Which best completes a device-to-effect analysis: 'The anaphora of "we must"...'?
o: “…is used three times in the second paragraph, in the first sentence of each section.”
“…is a rhetorical device in which a phrase is repeated at the beginning of successive clauses.”
“…appears in the second paragraph of the speech, where the speaker first mentions the audience.”
'...builds a mounting sense of urgency, compelling the audience toward collective action.'
quiz.e: This explains the specific effect on the audience, completing the device-to-effect move.

quiz.q: Analyzing a persuasive speech, a student instead explains why they personally disagree with the speaker's cause. This essay:
o: Correctly fulfills the task, since the student has shown a clear and personal engagement with the topic
Fails to fulfill the rhetorical analysis task
Is the strongest possible approach, since a personal view is the most direct form of analysis
Does not need a thesis, since a personal response to the speaker’s cause serves in its place
quiz.e: This confuses rhetorical analysis with an argument essay about the topic itself.

quiz.q: A rhetorical analysis thesis that only restates the passage's topic, without naming strategies or purpose, is:
o: Underdeveloped for this essay type
Ideal for rhetorical analysis
Required by the rubric
Impossible to improve
quiz.e: A strong thesis must go beyond topic restatement to name purpose and strategies.

quiz.q: Which is a valid organizational approach for rhetorical analysis?
o: Only a strategy-based structure is ever acceptable, since a chronological one reduces the analysis to summary
Only a chronological structure is ever acceptable, since a strategy-based one ignores the passage’s order
Either strategy-based or chronological structure, if reasoning is clear
No structure is required, since graders read for the quality of each sentence and not the plan of the essay
quiz.e: Both structures are valid as long as the essay's reasoning is clear and well-organized.

quiz.q: Discussing 5+ rhetorical devices shallowly, with one sentence each, compared to 2-3 devices in depth, is generally:
o: A stronger approach, since covering many devices shows the grader the breadth of the writer’s knowledge
A weaker approach than fewer, well-developed strategies
Required by the exam, which scores essays by the number of devices that the writer correctly identifies
Irrelevant to the essay’s quality, since graders count only whether each device was identified correctly
quiz.e: A few well-developed strategies produce stronger analysis than many shallow ones.

quiz.q: Which is considered valid evidence in an argument essay?
o: Only statistics from an official source, since a claim must rest on figures that readers can check
Nothing, since the essay must be built from opinion and the writer’s own reasoning about the claim
Historical examples, current events, literature, or personal experience
Only quotations from famous authors, since an authority’s words carry more weight than the writer’s own
quiz.e: A wide range of evidence types are valid, as long as they're specific and relevant.

quiz.q: A 'qualified' thesis ('X is true, except when...') in an argument essay often demonstrates:
o: Weak, indecisive reasoning, since a thesis with an exception shows that the writer is unsure
A violation of the task, since the prompt asks the writer to agree or disagree and not to qualify
More sophisticated thinking than an absolute, all-or-nothing claim
Nothing about sophistication, since the grader looks only at whether a position was clearly taken
quiz.e: Nuanced, qualified positions often show more sophisticated thinking than absolute claims.

quiz.q: Addressing a counterargument in the argument essay, then explaining why your position still holds, primarily demonstrates:
o: Awareness of the issue's complexity
A logical fallacy, since raising an objection gives the reader a reason to doubt the thesis
Weakness in your position, since the writer has shown that a reasonable person could disagree
An unnecessary structural step, since the thesis has already been supported by the earlier paragraphs
quiz.e: Engaging counterarguments shows awareness of complexity and strengthens the essay.

quiz.q: Explaining the broader implications or stakes of an argument is one way to demonstrate:
o: Sophistication of thought
Weak reasoning
A logical fallacy
Poor organization
quiz.e: Broader implications/stakes are a recognized marker of sophisticated argumentation.

quiz.q: Vivid, effective writing style alone (without complex reasoning) is:
o: Sufficient by itself for sophistication credit, since a graceful style shows mastery of the topic
Not equivalent to sophistication — reasoning must also be genuinely complex
Irrelevant to the essay entirely, since graders look only at the reasoning and not at the writing
Required for a passing thesis, since a thesis must be written in an elevated and polished style
quiz.e: Sophistication requires substantive complexity of reasoning, not just polished prose.

quiz.q: Making nuanced distinctions ('this is true in some contexts but not others') shows:
o: A weak and indecisive argument, since the writer has not committed to a clear position
A logical fallacy, since a claim that is true in one context cannot be false in another
Sophistication over an all-or-nothing stance
Poor thesis construction, since a claim with conditions is not defensible in a short timed essay
quiz.e: Nuanced context-dependent claims demonstrate sophisticated thinking.

quiz.q: Ignoring the counterargument entirely in an argument essay tends to make the essay seem:
o: More persuasive and complete, since the essay does not distract the reader from the writer’s own case
Incomplete or naive in its reasoning
Required by the rubric, which asks the writer to avoid giving any space to the other side
Impossible to improve, since the writer has no obligation to consider any viewpoint but her own
quiz.e: Ignoring counterarguments weakens the perceived completeness of the reasoning.

quiz.q: Which best shows specific, well-developed evidence rather than a vague generality?
o: Detailing the 1969 moon landing's effect on public trust in science, with specifics
“Space exploration has helped society in many ways, and the benefits have reached most countries.”
“Science is generally good for people, and its benefits have made life better for everyone.”
“History shows that progress happens, and the world has become better over the last century.”
quiz.e: The specific, detailed example is far stronger than the vague general statements.

quiz.q: An argument essay may take which kind of position on the given claim?
o: Only fully agree with the claim, since a qualified position is not defensible on a timed exam
Only fully disagree with the claim, since the prompt is written to invite a rebuttal of the claim
Agree, disagree, or agree with qualifications — any defensible position
No position is allowed, since the prompt asks only for a balanced discussion of both sides
quiz.e: Any well-supported, defensible position is acceptable.

quiz.q: Why must argument-essay evidence be 'verifiably true or at least reasonably plausible'?
o: Invented 'facts' undermine the writer's credibility
Fabricated evidence is always more persuasive
Verifiability doesn't matter for essays
Only statistics need to be true
quiz.e: Invented or implausible 'facts' damage the writer's ethos/credibility.

quiz.q: A basic thesis-evidence-conclusion structure without further nuance is generally scored as:
o: Always the highest-scoring approach, since its clear structure lets graders find every element easily
Impossible to score, since the rubric requires evidence of more complex reasoning than a plain structure shows
Competent but not necessarily the most sophisticated approach
Automatically a failing response, since a thesis without nuance cannot earn the point for a defensible claim
quiz.e: Basic structure can be competent, but sophistication requires going beyond it with nuance.

quiz.q: Which best reflects addressing complexity in an argument essay?
o: “This policy is always correct in every case, because the evidence supports it without exception.”
'While exceptions exist in emergency situations, the general policy remains sound because...'
Ignoring any possible exceptions so that the reader’s attention stays on the writer’s main line of reasoning
Repeating the thesis in different words at the start of each paragraph so that it remains clear
quiz.e: Acknowledging exceptions while still defending the general position shows nuanced, complex thinking.

quiz.q: Which best distinguishes the argument essay from the synthesis essay?
o: They are functionally identical tasks, since both ask the writer to support a claim with outside sources
Argument essays require three sources, just like synthesis, though the sources are chosen by the writer
The argument essay uses the writer's own evidence; synthesis requires citing provided sources
Synthesis essays never require a thesis, since the writer’s task is to report what the sources contain
quiz.e: This is the defining structural difference between the two essay types.

quiz.q: 'Running quickly to the store.' with no subject or complete thought is a:
o: Sentence fragment
Comma splice
Run-on sentence
Correct sentence
quiz.e: This lacks a complete subject-verb thought and cannot stand alone — a fragment.

quiz.q: 'I went to the store I bought milk' with no punctuation at all connecting the clauses is a:
o: Run-on sentence
Sentence fragment
Correct sentence
Parallel structure
quiz.e: Independent clauses joined with no punctuation or connector at all form a run-on.

quiz.q: Which correctly demonstrates subject-verb agreement despite intervening words?
o: 'The box of old books is heavy.'
'The box of old books are heavy.'
'The boxes of old book is heavy.'
'The box of old book are heavy.'
quiz.e: 'Box' (singular) is the true subject, so it takes 'is,' regardless of the intervening 'of old books.'

quiz.q: A multiple-choice reading question asking for a passage's main claim tests:
o: Close reading of the passage's overall argument
Grammar and punctuation, since the main claim is identified by the way each sentence is constructed
The reader’s personal opinion, which should be set out clearly and need not match the passage’s claim
Vocabulary memorization, since the claim is usually found by defining the key words in the first paragraph
quiz.e: Main-claim questions test comprehension of the passage's overall argument.

quiz.q: A writing multiple-choice question asking for the 'best transition' tests:
o: Spelling and word choice, since a transition is correct when each word in it has been spelled properly
Historical facts about the subject, since the best transition depends on what happened earlier in the passage
Vocabulary definitions, since the right transition is the one whose literal meaning is closest to the previous sentence
Revision skill — choosing language that fits the passage's logic
quiz.e: Writing questions test a student's ability to revise for clarity, logic, and fit.

quiz.q: A question asking 'which choice best maintains the established tone' requires:
o: Ignoring the rest of the passage, since tone is determined by the sentence containing the blank
Choosing the most formal option automatically, since formal language is safe in any context
Checking the surrounding sentences' tone, not just grammar
Choosing the shortest option automatically, since concision always fits the established tone of a passage
quiz.e: Tone-matching questions require attention to the surrounding passage's tone.

quiz.q: A question asking which choice would be 'LEAST effective' requires:
o: Choosing the best-written answer as usual, since the stem does not change the task
Ignoring the question’s direction, since the answer is judged by the same standard in every question
Picking the first option automatically, since the worst answer is generally the one that appears first
Reading the question stem carefully — the correct answer is the WORST option
quiz.e: Some questions invert the usual logic and ask for the least effective/worst choice.

quiz.q: 'Everyone must bring their own laptop' mixing a singular antecedent ('everyone') with a plural pronoun ('their') is an example (in the strict formal usage tested) of:
o: A comma splice, in which two independent clauses are joined by a comma without a conjunction
A run-on sentence, in which two independent clauses run together without any punctuation
A pronoun-antecedent agreement issue
Correct parallel structure, since both parts of the sentence use the same grammatical pattern
quiz.e: 'Everyone' is singular, so strict formal usage pairs it with a singular pronoun form.

quiz.q: Fixing a comma splice by just deleting the comma with nothing else added typically creates:
o: A grammatically correct sentence, since two independent clauses may be placed side by side
A sentence fragment, since one clause no longer has a verb of its own after the comma is gone
Correct parallel structure, since each clause now follows the same grammatical pattern as the other
A run-on sentence instead of a correct one
quiz.e: Removing only the comma, with no replacement punctuation, creates a run-on.

quiz.q: A question asking where to best place a sentence within a paragraph tests:
o: Organizational logic and flow
Only spelling accuracy
Only vocabulary knowledge
Only the essay's thesis
quiz.e: Placement questions test understanding of a paragraph's logical organization.

quiz.q: Why is it important to read the multiple-choice question stem carefully before answering?
o: All questions ask for the best option, so the stem need only be read after the choices
Some questions ask for the least effective option or a deletion, reversing the usual logic
Question stems are purely decorative, since the choices themselves show what is being asked
Stems matter only on the reading section, since writing questions are always the same type
quiz.e: Careful reading prevents missing inverted questions (e.g., 'least effective,' 'should be deleted').

quiz.q: A speaker who cites their own years of firsthand field experience is primarily building:
o: Ethos
Pathos
A slippery slope fallacy
Antithesis
quiz.e: Firsthand experience/credentials build credibility — ethos.

quiz.q: 'The negotiations collapsed. Talks failed. Trust was gone.' uses short syntax primarily to create:
o: A blunt, emphatic sense of finality
A relaxed, meandering tone
Confusion about the sequence of events
No rhetorical effect
quiz.e: The clipped, short sentences create emphasis and a sense of blunt finality.

quiz.q: Which best shows a synthesis essay citation properly paired with commentary?
o: “Source A discusses wait times in the emergency department and the effect they have on care.”
“According to Source A, patients wait longer than they used to, and the delay is a problem.”
“Source A’s full paragraph on wait times is reproduced here, and readers can judge it for themselves.”
'Source A's data on wait times shows the current system is failing patients most in need.'
quiz.e: This pairs the citation with commentary explaining its significance to the argument.

quiz.q: Which best reflects analyzing a shift in strategy across a passage's structure?
o: The essay opens with logos-heavy statistics before pivoting to pathos-driven anecdotes in the closing paragraphs
Only discussing the opening paragraph in depth, since it sets the argument that the rest will follow
Ignoring how the passage changes over its length, since the strategies are the same throughout
Treating the whole passage as using one unchanging strategy that the writer repeats in each paragraph
quiz.e: Tracking how strategies shift across the passage shows sophisticated structural analysis.

quiz.q: Which best demonstrates addressing the 'stakes' of an argument for sophistication credit?
o: Simply restating the thesis a second time at the end, using stronger language than at the beginning
Explaining what could go wrong for real communities if the policy is NOT adopted
Ignoring consequences entirely so that the essay’s argument appears focused on a single question
Listing more unrelated examples from history, so that the claim appears supported by a wider range of cases
quiz.e: Explaining real-world stakes/implications is a recognized way to show sophistication.

quiz.q: 'Neither the teacher nor the students was ready' should actually use which verb to agree with the nearer subject?
o: 'were,' agreeing with the nearer plural subject 'students'
“was” is already correct, since the verb agrees with the singular subject “teacher” that comes first
“is,” regardless of context, since “neither” is always a singular pronoun in formal writing
“be,” regardless of context, since the sentence expresses a condition that has not yet occurred
quiz.e: With 'neither...nor,' the verb agrees with the subject closer to it — 'students' (plural) takes 'were.'

quiz.q: In the SOAPSTone framework, the 'S' that refers to the argument's central idea or message is:
o: Subject
Speaker
Syntax
Setting
quiz.e: SOAPSTone: Speaker, Occasion, Audience, Purpose, Subject, Tone.

quiz.q: A speech delivered the day after a natural disaster, urging immediate aid, is a strong example of using:
o: kairos
hyperbole
anaphora
litotes
quiz.e: Kairos is choosing the opportune moment and fitting the message to it.

quiz.q: 'Constraints' in a rhetorical situation refers to:
o: the limit on the length of the essay that the writer is given and the time allowed to write it
factors that limit how the writer can respond (beliefs, conventions, prior events)
the rules of grammar and punctuation that the writer must follow in the formal parts of the text
the word choices a writer makes that restrict the range of tones available to the audience
quiz.e: Constraints shape and restrict the available means of persuasion.

quiz.q: A well-reasoned op-ed published years after the relevant debate has ended most clearly fails at:
o: kairos
logos
organization
citation
quiz.e: It may be logically sound but misses the opportune moment and audience.

quiz.q: Which question best begins an audience analysis?
o: How long is the passage, and how many paragraphs does it contain about the writer’s main topic?
What does this audience already believe, and what would it take to move them?
What devices does the writer use, and in which paragraphs do they appear most often?
When was the text published, and how did readers at that time respond to the writer’s ideas?
quiz.e: Effective analysis starts from the audience's assumptions, values, and needs.

quiz.q: An appeal based on the speaker's character, expertise, and trustworthiness is:
o: ethos
pathos
logos
kairos
quiz.e: Ethos is the appeal to credibility.

quiz.q: 'You can't trust her argument about the budget; she failed a math class in college' is an example of:
o: ad hominem
straw man
false dilemma
slippery slope
quiz.e: Ad hominem attacks the person rather than the argument.

quiz.q: Misrepresenting an opponent's position to make it easier to attack is:
o: a straw man
begging the question
an appeal to authority
post hoc
quiz.e: The straw man refutes a distorted version of the argument.

quiz.q: Reasoning that moves from specific observations to a general conclusion is:
o: inductive
deductive
circular
analogical
quiz.e: Induction builds a general claim from particular cases and is always provisional.

quiz.q: Which best completes strong rhetorical analysis of an emotional appeal?
o: state that the author uses pathos, and then quote the sentence in which the appeal is most evident
quote a particularly sad sentence from the passage and note that it is emotional
name the words used, then explain the feeling they create and its effect on the audience
list three emotions that the passage seems to arouse, and then move to the next paragraph
quiz.e: Always connect the specific language to the effect on the reader and the writer's purpose.

quiz.q: 'This policy must work; the senator who wrote it is very experienced' relies on:
o: an appeal to authority (which is weak if the authority is not relevant or is the only support)
logos, since the senator’s experience is a reason that the policy’s success is likely
a concession to the opposition, since the speaker grants that the policy might fail
an analogy between the senator’s experience and the policy’s likelihood of succeeding in practice
quiz.e: Authority can support a claim, but it is a fallacy when the authority is irrelevant or offered as sole proof.

quiz.q: A writer who admits a personal mistake early in an essay is most likely trying to:
o: strengthen ethos by appearing honest
weaken the argument by drawing attention to the writer’s own failings before the thesis is stated
introduce a fallacy by shifting the reader’s attention from the argument to the writer’s character
establish kairos by linking the admission to the moment in which the essay appears
quiz.e: Acknowledging limits can build trust with the audience.

quiz.q: Repetition of a word or phrase at the beginning of successive clauses is:
o: anaphora
epistrophe
chiasmus
asyndeton
quiz.e: Anaphora repeats at the START of clauses; epistrophe repeats at the end.

quiz.q: Deliberately omitting conjunctions from a list ('I came, I saw, I conquered') is:
o: asyndeton
polysyndeton
parallelism
anaphora
quiz.e: Asyndeton speeds a list and can create urgency or breathlessness.

quiz.q: An extended metaphor is best described as:
o: a metaphor used once in a sentence, with each of its terms stated in a single phrase
a comparison using “like” or “as,” developed through more than one sentence in the passage
two metaphors placed in the same sentence so that the second reinforces the meaning of the first
a single comparison developed across several sentences or a whole passage
quiz.e: It structures a stretch of text around one governing comparison.

quiz.q: Verbal irony occurs when a writer:
o: describes a sensory image so vividly that the reader can feel what the writer is describing
repeats a phrase at the beginning of successive clauses to emphasize the writer’s central claim
says the opposite of what is meant, expecting the audience to catch the gap
uses a formal citation in order to give the argument the authority of a recognized source
quiz.e: Sarcasm is a common, pointed form of verbal irony.

quiz.q: After identifying anaphora in a passage, the next step in analysis is to:
o: name two more devices in the passage and move to the next paragraph in order to cover the whole text
explain the emphasis or momentum it builds and how that serves the purpose
quote the whole paragraph that contains the anaphora so that the grader can see its context
identify the audience of the passage and then summarize how it would have responded to the writer
quiz.e: Analysis must move from naming the device to explaining its effect.

quiz.q: A sudden shift from long, complex sentences to a short, blunt one usually functions to:
o: create emphasis by contrast
confuse the reader
signal a citation
establish the audience
quiz.e: The abrupt change in rhythm draws attention to the short sentence's content.

quiz.q: Which sentence is commentary rather than summary?
o: The author states that 40 percent of families in the study could not afford basic medical care.
The passage includes several statistics, which are drawn from the survey of families in the region.
The author cites a government report in the second paragraph in order to support the main claim.
This statistic matters because it shows the policy affects the very group it claims to help.
quiz.e: Commentary interprets the evidence's significance for the argument.

quiz.q: 'Concede-then-counter' means:
o: ignoring opposing points so that the argument seems unanswerable in the reader’s eyes
granting an opposing point, then explaining why it does not defeat the thesis
agreeing with the opposition and changing the thesis to match the opposing position
restating the opposing view sympathetically and leaving the reader to judge which side is stronger
quiz.e: It shows fairness, then limits the concession's force.

quiz.q: Repeating a key term across paragraphs, rather than always finding synonyms, helps:
o: pad the word count so that the essay reaches the length that graders seem to expect
keep the argument's thread visible to the reader
avoid plagiarism by ensuring that each term in the essay is used exactly as it appears in the sources
establish a formal tone by repeating the words that are used most often in academic prose
quiz.e: Consistent key terms aid coherence more than 'elegant variation'.

quiz.q: The AP synthesis essay requires the writer to:
o: summarize each source in turn, noting the main point and any evidence in each of the sources provided
compare the sources to one another, showing which are more reliable and which are less so
choose the single best source and analyze it in depth, using the others only for brief contrast
develop an argument that uses at least three of the provided sources as support
quiz.e: Sources are evidence for the writer's own position, cited (at least three).

quiz.q: The 'summary trap' in a synthesis essay is:
o: using too many quotations, so that the writer’s own claims are crowded out of each paragraph
citing fewer than three sources, so that the essay fails to meet the task’s minimum requirement
writing an essay that is too short to develop the writer’s own argument beyond a brief statement
walking through the sources one by one instead of organizing by your own claims
quiz.e: Body paragraphs should be built around sub-claims, drawing in sources as needed.

quiz.q: A 'defensible' thesis for a synthesis prompt is one that:
o: restates the prompt in different words so that the grader can see that the writer understood it
agrees with every source provided so that the essay shows that the writer has read each one
avoids taking a side so that the essay can be defended against any reasonable objection
takes a clear, arguable position that the sources can be used to support
quiz.e: It should be specific and possible to argue against.

quiz.q: In a synthesis essay, a quotation should generally be:
o: dropped in without framing so that the source’s own words make the point without help from the writer
the majority of each paragraph, since graders reward writers who show close reading of the sources
avoided entirely, since paraphrase demonstrates better understanding than the use of the source’s words
introduced and then explained, used only when the exact wording matters
quiz.e: Frame quotations and keep them short; paraphrase when wording is not the point.

quiz.q: Organizing a synthesis essay 'by your claims' means:
o: each body paragraph advances one of your sub-points, supported by whatever sources fit
each paragraph covers one source in the order given, with the writer’s view added at the end
paragraphs alternate between sources that support the claim and sources that oppose it
the essay follows the order in which the sources are printed in the packet that is provided
quiz.e: Your argument, not the source list, provides the structure.

quiz.q: A qualified synthesis thesis (e.g. 'Public financing helps in local races but less in national ones') is preferable because it:
o: is more precise and defensible than a sweeping claim
is longer and therefore gives the grader more evidence of the writer’s control of the topic
cites more sources than a plain thesis, which raises the score on the evidence row of the rubric
avoids a position so that it can be defended against objections from every side of the debate
quiz.e: Nuance that the sources can support tends to score higher.

quiz.q: For a timed rhetorical analysis, the best approach to strategies is usually:
o: analyze 2-3 strategies in depth
list 5 or more strategies briefly
focus on one device only
summarize the passage first
quiz.e: Depth of analysis beats breadth of identification.

quiz.q: A defensible rhetorical analysis thesis should be:
o: a statement of fact that everyone accepts, so that the writer’s analysis can build on common ground
a summary of the passage that identifies each of its main points and the order in which they appear
arguable - a reasonable reader could interpret the choices differently
a personal opinion about the topic that the writer supports with evidence from the passage
quiz.e: It makes a claim about the writer's choices that requires support.

quiz.q: A strong body paragraph in a rhetorical analysis essay:
o: identifies a choice, provides textual evidence, and explains the effect on the argument
only quotes the passage at length so that the grader can see the evidence on which the claim rests
only names the devices that the writer uses and defines each one in the paragraph’s opening
restates the thesis in the first and last sentences and includes one example in between
quiz.e: Claim-evidence-analysis is the core structure.

quiz.q: 'Sophistication' on the AP argument rubric can be earned by:
o: situating the argument in a broader context or acknowledging complexity
using longer words and more complex sentences so that the essay reads as the work of a skilled writer
writing a longer essay with more paragraphs than the task requires in order to show command of the topic
citing more examples than the task requires, so that the claim is supported by every relevant case
quiz.e: Nuance, tension, and a compelling style signal sophisticated thought.

quiz.q: A nuanced thesis such as 'Curfews reduce some crimes but at a civic cost' is preferable to a flat one because it:
o: reflects the complexity of the issue and is easier to defend well
is safer because it avoids a position and cannot be shown to be false by any single example
uses more sophisticated vocabulary, which graders reward in the sophistication row of the rubric
is longer, and so allows the writer to show more of the thinking behind the claim
quiz.e: Qualified, specific claims tend to support stronger reasoning.

quiz.q: A colon is correctly used when:
o: the clause before it is complete and it introduces an explanation, list, or appositive
it joins two independent clauses in a casual way where a writer wants a less formal effect
it replaces a comma in a series so that the items in the list stand out more clearly
it ends a question that the writer has asked for the purpose of introducing the next paragraph
quiz.e: 'She had one goal: to finish.' The clause before the colon stands alone.

quiz.q: On a multiple-choice 'writing' revision question, the best answer is usually the one that is:
o: clearest and most concise
longest and most formal
most varied in vocabulary
most detailed
quiz.e: AP MC writing items reward economy and precision.

quiz.q: A principal writes to parents: "I know many of you worry that a later bell means later practices and later dinners. Consider instead what the sleep research says about your teenager's grades and safety on the road." Which choice best describes how the writer responds to the rhetorical situation?
o: He establishes authority by citing his credentials as a sleep researcher before offering any advice
He appeals to the audience’s fear of change by describing the dangers of early school start times
He anticipates the audience's likely objection and redirects it toward a concern the audience already shares
He shifts from a personal tone to an impersonal one in order to give his claim greater objectivity
quiz.e: The first sentence names the objection; the second recasts the issue around grades and safety, which parents care about. The excerpt cites no credentials and never frames change itself as the threat.

quiz.q: A writer composing a newsletter article for retired teachers about a new pension rule chooses to explain the rule through two short anecdotes about retirees instead of quoting the statute. The writer's choice is best explained by:
o: The need to demonstrate expertise in pension law, since the readers expect the writer to cite the statute
The exigence of a rule most readers cannot easily interpret, combined with an audience who values personal stories
The constraint of a strict word limit that rules out any long explanation of how the new rule works
A purpose of entertaining readers rather than informing them, since the audience prefers a lighter tone
quiz.e: Choosing anecdotes over statute language responds to audience (retirees, not lawyers) and the need to make a complex rule understandable. A word limit is not mentioned, and the purpose is to inform.

quiz.q: Which pairing correctly distinguishes a writer's subject from the text's exigence?
o: Subject: to persuade the council to keep the branch open; Exigence: a city’s budget for libraries
Subject: the council; Exigence: a persuasive essay that the author has written to influence its members
Subject: library budgets; Exigence: the author’s own opinion that libraries should receive more funding
Subject: a city's plan to close a library branch; Exigence: the vote scheduled for next week that could end the plan
quiz.e: Exigence is the particular pressing occasion that makes writing necessary (an imminent vote), while the subject is what the text is about. Persuading the council describes purpose, not subject.

quiz.q: A speech by a mayor after a flood begins, "Tonight I am not speaking to you as a politician; I am speaking as someone who also lost a basement." What is the primary rhetorical effect of this opening?
o: It undermines the speaker’s authority by admitting that he has suffered the same losses as the audience
It aligns the speaker with the audience's experience to create common ground before making requests
It signals that the speech will be primarily a technical report on the causes and costs of the flood
It shifts blame for the flood away from the speaker’s office and toward the weather and the residents
quiz.e: Identification with the audience builds trust. The admission does not cost authority; it adds credibility through shared experience.

quiz.q: A student's argument essay about school cafeteria policy is intended for the school board. Which revision best reflects awareness of the actual audience?
o: Replacing slang and complaints with specific budget figures and a proposal the board could vote on
Adding more emotional stories about hungry children so that board members feel the cost of the current policy
Addressing the essay to “all students” so that the writer’s argument reaches the largest possible readership
Using a humorous tone throughout to keep the board’s attention and to make the proposal seem less threatening
quiz.e: A decision-making audience needs evidence and a feasible proposal. Emotion alone, an altered addressee, or humor would not meet the board's needs as a deliberative audience.

quiz.q: A writer notes that a magazine's readers are suspicious of corporate claims. Which strategy would best account for this audience in an article defending a company's new safety program?
o: Opening with the company’s mission statement and a list of the awards its safety record has received
Conceding a past failure candidly before presenting independent audits of the new program
Quoting the company’s CEO at length about her personal commitment to protecting the people who work there
Avoiding any mention of past problems so that readers’ attention stays on the program’s present results
quiz.e: For a skeptical audience, concession and independent evidence build credibility. Corporate statements and silence about problems reinforce suspicion.

quiz.q: In an editorial, the sentence "We have debated this for years; the next meeting is the last chance" most directly establishes which element of the rhetorical situation?
o: Audience
Subject
Genre
Exigence
quiz.e: The urgency of a final meeting is the occasion that demands a response. It signals timing and necessity, not who the readers are or what the topic is.

quiz.q: Which description best identifies the difference between a text's purpose and its message?
o: Purpose is what the writer wants the text to accomplish with the audience; the message is the idea the text conveys
They are the same thing, since a writer’s purpose is simply the message that the text delivers
Purpose is the writer’s emotion at the moment of writing; message is the audience’s reaction to the text
Purpose concerns the text’s style and word choice; message concerns the structure of its paragraphs
quiz.e: Purpose concerns the writer's intended effect (inform, persuade, inspire); message is the content of the claim or idea.

quiz.q: A nonprofit's fundraising letter and its annual report cover the same project but differ greatly in diction and structure. This difference is best attributed to:
o: A change in the project’s subject between the two documents and in the people it concerns
Differences in genre, audience and purpose
Random stylistic choices by the writers, which do not reflect the way each document is meant to be used
The tone alone, since the two documents might otherwise be identical in structure and in diction
quiz.e: Genres carry conventions shaped by their audience and purpose, so the same subject is presented differently.

quiz.q: A writer says, "I will not pretend that this policy is perfect." Which statement most accurately describes the likely rhetorical function?
o: It abandons the writer’s position by admitting that the policy has flaws that cannot be defended
It weakens the writer’s logos by suggesting that the evidence for the policy is incomplete or unreliable
It builds ethos through honesty and prepares the audience to accept qualified support
It is an appeal to pity that asks the audience to sympathize with the difficulties of the policy’s authors
quiz.e: Admitting imperfection can increase credibility and make a measured argument appear more reasonable.

quiz.q: "If we allow students to retake one exam, soon they will demand to retake every assignment, and the school will lose all standards." Which fallacy does this sentence most clearly commit?
o: Slippery slope
Ad hominem
Straw man
Circular reasoning
quiz.e: The sentence claims a small step will inevitably cause an extreme chain of consequences without showing the links.

quiz.q: A candidate says, "My opponent wants to cut the parks budget, so clearly he hates children." The most precise label for the flaw is:
o: An appeal to authority that relies on the opponent’s office in order to prove the claim about children
A bandwagon appeal that suggests everyone agrees with the speaker and so the opponent must be wrong
Circular reasoning that assumes the conclusion is true and then offers it again as the evidence
A straw man that exaggerates a position and then attacks the exaggeration
quiz.e: The claim misrepresents a budget position as hatred of children and attacks that distorted version.

quiz.q: "Everyone in my neighborhood supports the new stadium, so it must be a good idea." The reasoning depends on which flaw?
o: Bandwagon appeal, assuming popularity proves correctness
Post hoc reasoning, which assumes that an earlier event caused the later support for the stadium
A false dilemma, which presents the stadium as the only possible choice for the neighborhood
A red herring, which distracts the reader from the stadium’s cost by raising a related subject
quiz.e: The claim substitutes popularity for evidence that the stadium is a good idea.

quiz.q: A writer argues, "Ever since the new highway opened, crime has risen, so the highway caused the increase." Which statement best evaluates the reasoning?
o: It correctly uses deductive logic by moving from a general rule about highways to a specific conclusion
It uses an emotional appeal by describing the effect of crime on families in the writer’s neighborhood
It commits a post hoc fallacy by treating sequence as proof of cause
It is an ad hominem attack on the officials who approved the highway before it opened to traffic
quiz.e: Two events occurring in sequence does not establish that one caused the other; other factors might explain the rise.

quiz.q: A speaker begins a speech to nurses with a story of a night shift, then cites staffing data, and ends with an appeal to professional pride. Which sequence of appeals does this reflect?
o: Pathos, logos, ethos
Logos, ethos, pathos
Ethos, pathos, logos
Pathos, ethos, logos
quiz.e: The story is an emotional appeal, the data is logical, and the appeal to professional pride speaks to shared identity and values (ethos-based).

quiz.q: Which of the following is the best example of a writer using logos?
o: Describing a student’s tears on the first day of the program in a way that makes readers share her fear
Citing the writer’s twenty years of experience as a teacher in the district in order to establish authority
Presenting a comparison of test scores before and after a program, with the sample sizes
Using a metaphor of a ship sinking to suggest the danger to the school’s budget if nothing changes
quiz.e: Logos appeals to reason through evidence and logical structure; the others use pathos, ethos or figurative language.

quiz.q: "You can either support this tax or you can watch the city fall apart." What is the primary flaw?
o: A hasty generalization that draws a broad conclusion from a few examples of cities that raised taxes
An appeal to tradition that assumes the tax is justified because earlier councils had approved similar ones
False dilemma that presents only two extreme options
Circular reasoning that assumes the tax is necessary and then offers its necessity as the evidence
quiz.e: The sentence ignores alternatives between the extremes.

quiz.q: A pharmaceutical advertisement features a famous athlete praising a medicine. Which fallacy might the ad rely on?
o: Hasty generalization
Appeal to inappropriate authority
Slippery slope
Equivocation
quiz.e: The athlete's fame does not make them an expert on medicine.

quiz.q: "The senator is wrong about education policy because she dropped out of college." Which statement best identifies the error?
o: A slippery slope that predicts a series of consequences from the senator’s decision to leave college
An equivocation that shifts the meaning of “education” between the senator’s experience and her policy
Ad hominem, because it attacks personal history rather than the argument
An appeal to emotion that asks the audience to feel contempt for the senator’s failure to graduate
quiz.e: The claim attacks the person instead of addressing the policy's merits.

quiz.q: "It's a good law because it is the law." This argument is best described as:
o: Red herring
False dilemma
Post hoc
Circular reasoning
quiz.e: The conclusion simply restates the premise.

quiz.q: "Our schools do not need more money; our schools do not need more slogans; our schools need more teachers." Which pair of devices is most clearly at work?
o: Anaphora and parallelism building to a climactic claim
Antithesis and hyperbole that set opposing needs against each other and exaggerate the schools’ plight
Oxymoron and paradox that join contradictory terms to make a statement that seems true on reflection
Allusion and irony that refer to a well-known work and say the opposite of what the speaker means
quiz.e: The repeated 'our schools do not need' is anaphora in parallel clauses that culminate in the claim.

quiz.q: The sentence "The report was long on promises and short on proof" depends primarily on which device?
o: Personification that treats the report as a person who makes promises and then fails to keep them
Synecdoche that uses a part of the report to represent the whole of the document and its findings
Onomatopoeia that imitates the sound of a long document being read aloud to a restless audience
Antithesis within a parallel structure
quiz.e: It balances contrasting terms (long/short, promises/proof) in parallel construction.

quiz.q: A writer describes a city council as "a committee of the willing, appointed by the unprepared." The phrase most strongly employs:
o: Simile
Irony and parallel structure
Apostrophe
Understatement
quiz.e: The reversal of expected terms is ironic and delivered in a balanced form.

quiz.q: In "The White House issued a statement," the use of 'White House' for the president's staff is an example of:
o: Metonymy
Synecdoche
Hyperbole
Euphemism
quiz.e: A related object stands in for the thing it represents; synecdoche would use a part of the whole.

quiz.q: "All hands on deck" used to request help from workers is an example of:
o: Metonymy
Simile
Oxymoron
Synecdoche
quiz.e: 'Hands' is a part representing the whole person.

quiz.q: Which sentence best exemplifies understatement for rhetorical effect?
o: “The flood destroyed everything in the world,” in an essay that describes a single ruined house
"The flood caused some inconvenience for the town's residents," in an essay describing destroyed homes
“The river wept as it rose,” in a passage that gives human feelings to the water
“The flood was like a monster,” in a paragraph that compares the water to a destructive beast
quiz.e: Understatement deliberately minimizes a serious matter to produce irony or emphasis.

quiz.q: A writer says a rival's plan is "a masterpiece of confusion." The phrase is best characterized as:
o: Ironic and an oxymoron-like reversal of praise
Literal praise of a plan that the writer regards as admirably complicated and sophisticated
An allusion to a famous work of art that the writer expects the audience to recognize
An understatement that minimizes the plan’s faults in order to make the criticism sound milder
quiz.e: Praising the plan for confusion turns the praise sarcastic.

quiz.q: "We shall not be moved by fear, nor shaken by threats, nor turned by flattery" is notable for:
o: Parallel structure that accumulates force through repetition
Alliteration only, in which the repetition of initial sounds makes the sentence easy to remember
A single extended metaphor in which fear, threats and flattery are compared to physical forces
The use of dialect, which gives the speaker’s words a regional and conversational flavor
quiz.e: The repeated grammatical pattern builds momentum and emphasizes resolve.

quiz.q: Which statement best explains why a writer might choose a euphemism?
o: To increase the harshness of a statement so that the reader cannot avoid its meaning
To soften or avoid a harsh reality, which can also obscure the truth
To imitate spoken dialect, which gives the passage the sound of an actual conversation
To create a rhyme that makes the sentence easier to remember and more pleasant to hear
quiz.e: Euphemisms mask unpleasant realities, sometimes for tact and sometimes for evasion.

quiz.q: "I've told you a million times to knock" most clearly contains:
o: Understatement
Metonymy
Hyperbole
Antithesis
quiz.e: The exaggeration is not meant literally.

quiz.q: A writer follows several long, flowing sentences with the sentence "Then nothing." The most likely effect of this contrast in syntax is to:
o: Make the passage easier to read by relieving the reader after a sequence of complex clauses
Create abrupt emphasis and a sense of sudden finality
Introduce a new subject that the writer will take up in the following paragraph
Express the writer’s uncertainty about whether anything remains to be said on the matter
quiz.e: A short sentence after long ones produces emphasis through contrast.

quiz.q: Which description best captures the connotative difference between "thrifty" and "stingy"?
o: They have different denotations, since “thrifty” refers to saving and “stingy” to refusing to spend
“Stingy” is the more formal word, while “thrifty” belongs to everyday speech and so sounds casual
"Thrifty" carries a positive judgment while "stingy" carries a negative one, though both denote spending little
They are interchangeable, since both words describe a person who spends very little money
quiz.e: The words refer to similar behavior but suggest opposite attitudes.

quiz.q: A passage uses long periodic sentences that withhold the main clause until the end. The most likely effect is:
o: Creating a casual, conversational tone in which the writer seems to speak directly to the reader
Making the argument seem hasty, since the reader waits for the point and may lose the thread
Reducing complexity, since the main idea is placed in the sentence’s last clause for clarity
Building suspense or emphasis for the final idea
quiz.e: Delaying the main idea creates anticipation.

quiz.q: A writer opens an essay with technical jargon and then shifts to plain language. The most likely purpose is to:
o: Confuse the audience so that readers accept the writer’s claims without examining them
Show disrespect for the audience by suggesting that its members are unable to follow the argument
Create a humorous tone by contrasting the difficult opening with the simple language that follows
Demonstrate expertise before making the ideas accessible
quiz.e: The shift establishes credibility and then clarifies for readers.

quiz.q: Which phrase most strongly suggests a sarcastic tone?
o: "Oh, what a wonderfully efficient system, requiring only three hours of waiting"
“The system requires three hours of waiting before an applicant can be seen by a clerk”
“The wait is three hours, though it is sometimes shorter when the office is not crowded”
“Waiting takes time, and the system’s users should plan their visits with that in mind”
quiz.e: The praise contrasts with the described inefficiency, signaling sarcasm.

quiz.q: A writer repeatedly uses first-person plural pronouns like 'we' and 'our' in an argument. This choice most likely:
o: Creates a sense of shared responsibility and solidarity
Distances the writer from the audience by presenting the argument as a formal and impersonal report
Shows scientific objectivity by removing the writer’s own voice from the account of the evidence
Indicates uncertainty, since the writer shares the responsibility for the claim with other people
quiz.e: Inclusive pronouns unite the speaker and audience.

quiz.q: A passage shifts from formal diction ("proceeded to commence") to blunt monosyllables ("it broke"). The shift most likely functions to:
o: Make the passage more formal by moving from simple words to those that are more elevated
Create ironic contrast between pomp and reality
Express the writer’s confusion about how the event is to be described in a single sentence
Provide historical context by showing how the vocabulary of the period differed from ours
quiz.e: The deflation from elevated to blunt language undercuts the pretension.

quiz.q: Which sentence most clearly uses a conversational tone?
o: “The aforementioned procedures shall be implemented in accordance with the guidelines issued earlier.”
"Look, nobody likes paying more, but here's the thing: the old way wasn't working."
“It is incumbent upon the committee to deliberate with care before it renders any decision.”
“Pursuant to the statute, the fee has been adjusted to reflect the cost of administration.”
quiz.e: Contractions, direct address and informal phrasing mark conversational tone.

quiz.q: A writer lists seven examples in rapid succession with commas and no conjunction (asyndeton). The most likely effect is:
o: Slow, formal pacing in which each example receives the same weight and the reader is invited to dwell on it
Ambiguity about how the items are related, since no conjunction tells the reader how to connect them
A reduction in emphasis, since a long list makes each of its items seem less important
Rapid pacing and a sense of accumulation or urgency
quiz.e: Omitting conjunctions speeds the list and can suggest overwhelming quantity.

quiz.q: Which of the following best explains the effect of an imperative sentence such as "Imagine a town without a school"?
o: It states a fact that the audience is expected to accept without examining the evidence
It reports an event that the writer has witnessed and describes it in the order that it occurred
It qualifies a claim that the writer made earlier and suggests that it is not true in every case
It directly engages the reader and invites participation in a hypothetical
quiz.e: Commands pull the audience into the writer's scenario.

quiz.q: Which thesis is most defensible and specific enough for a rhetorical analysis?
o: “Lopez uses many rhetorical devices, including metaphor, statistics and a personal anecdote, to make her case.”
"By pairing a personal anecdote with comparative statistics, Lopez persuades skeptical readers that the policy has worked in other cities."
“The essay is about a policy that Lopez describes, and it appeals to both logic and emotion.”
“Lopez is a good writer who presents her ideas clearly, and readers will find her essay persuasive.”
quiz.e: A strong thesis identifies specific choices and their effect on a particular audience for a purpose.

quiz.q: In an argument essay a student writes: "Social media harms teenagers. A survey found that students who spend more than four hours a day online report lower sleep." What is the best revision to strengthen the commentary?
o: Add another survey statistic about teenagers’ sleep without comment, so that the evidence appears more complete
Replace the claim with a question so that the reader is invited to consider whether social media is harmful
Remove the survey and rely on the writer’s own experience of social media to support the claim
Explain how lower sleep connects to the claim of harm and acknowledge the survey shows correlation rather than cause
quiz.e: Commentary connects evidence to the claim and handles limits of the evidence.

quiz.q: Which sentence best qualifies a claim for accuracy?
o: "In most large districts, later start times have been associated with modest gains in attendance."
“Later start times always fix attendance in every school that has tried them.”
“Nobody can deny that later start times work in any district that has adopted them.”
“Start times never matter to students’ attendance, whatever the community’s circumstances may be.”
quiz.e: Qualifiers like 'most' and 'associated with modest' acknowledge limits.

quiz.q: A student's body paragraph states a claim, quotes a source, and moves on. Which element is missing?
o: Commentary explaining how the evidence supports the claim
A topic sentence that tells the reader what the paragraph will argue before the quotation appears
A transition linking the paragraph to the one before it so that the argument moves in a clear line
A concluding sentence for the entire essay that restates the thesis and its significance
quiz.e: Evidence must be followed by explanation tying it to the argument.

quiz.q: Which source would be most credible for a claim about the economic effects of minimum-wage increases?
o: An anonymous blog post that summarizes the debate and cites several news articles in its footnotes
A politician’s campaign speech that cites recent figures from her state’s department of labor
A viral social media post that reports an economist’s opinion in a short and confident message
A peer-reviewed study by labor economists with a clear method
quiz.e: Credibility depends on expertise, method and transparency.

quiz.q: A writer cites a statistic: "Seventy percent of surveyed students support the policy." Which question would best test the evidence's reliability?
o: How long is the sentence, and does it follow the conventions for presenting a statistic in a formal essay?
Who was surveyed and how were they selected?
What color is the chart, and is it easy to read for someone who is color-blind?
When was the paper printed, and did the publisher have a good reputation at the time?
quiz.e: Sampling method determines whether results can be generalized.

quiz.q: Which of the following is an example of commentary rather than evidence?
o: “Test scores rose 8 percent over the three years in which the program was in operation.”
“The study followed 1,200 students in six districts from the fall of 2019 until the spring of 2022.”
“The mayor said that the plan would help families in the neighborhoods most affected by the closure.”
"This pattern suggests the program's benefits are strongest where funding is steady."
quiz.e: Commentary interprets and links evidence to the argument.

quiz.q: A writer concedes that a policy has costs and then argues the benefits outweigh them. This strategy primarily:
o: Strengthens credibility by acknowledging a counterpoint before refuting it
Weakens the claim by drawing the reader’s attention to costs the writer cannot completely refute
Changes the topic so that the reader’s attention moves from the policy’s costs to its benefits
Shows a lack of conviction, since a writer who admits a cost is unsure that the policy is right
quiz.e: Concession and rebuttal show fairness and strengthen the argument.

quiz.q: Which claim would be most appropriate for an argument essay that needs a defensible position?
o: “Year-round calendars exist in several states, and some of them are used by large school districts.”
“Many schools have calendars that divide the year into terms of various lengths and breaks of different sizes.”
“Summer is a season in which many students are away from school, and some of them travel with their families.”
"Schools should adopt year-round calendars because they reduce learning loss over the summer."
quiz.e: A defensible claim takes a position that reasonable people could dispute and signals reasons.

quiz.q: A writer uses a hypothetical example to illustrate an abstract idea. Which assessment is most accurate?
o: A hypothetical is the strongest form of evidence, since it can be designed to fit the claim exactly
A hypothetical is irrelevant to an argument, since graders credit only examples that have really occurred
A hypothetical is a kind of statistic, since it represents what would happen in a typical case
A hypothetical can clarify an idea but cannot serve as proof of how the world actually is
quiz.e: Illustrations aid understanding; they do not substitute for empirical evidence.

quiz.q: An essay on school uniforms opens with a vivid scene of a student turned away at the door, then states a claim, then concedes the strongest opposing point before refuting it. Which sequence correctly identifies the structure?
o: Anecdotal introduction, claim, concession, refutation
Claim, anecdote, refutation, conclusion
Concession, anecdote, claim, call to action
Narration, definition, comparison, summary
quiz.e: The anecdote opens, the thesis follows, and the writer then concedes and refutes in the standard concession-and-rebuttal pattern.

quiz.q: A writer ends a paragraph with, "Critics are right that the program is costly; they are wrong that it is wasteful." This sentence primarily:
o: Changes the topic from the cost of the program to its waste, so that the reader considers a new issue
Provides a statistic about the program’s cost that the reader can compare with the claim in the next paragraph
Concedes a point and then distinguishes it from the claim the writer rejects
Introduces a new thesis that the writer will defend in the second half of the essay
quiz.e: It accepts the criticism of cost while separating it from waste, which the writer denies.

quiz.q: Which transition best signals that the next paragraph will complicate the previous argument?
o: “For example, consider the following case, which shows how the principle works in practice.”
“In addition, the evidence shows that the policy has also been effective in other communities.”
“Similarly, the same is true of the other cases that the writer has considered in the essay.”
"Yet this account overlooks an important complication."
quiz.e: 'Yet' and 'overlooks' announce a complication; the others extend or illustrate.

quiz.q: A writer organizes an essay by identifying a problem, explaining its causes, proposing a solution, and anticipating objections. This pattern is best described as:
o: Chronological
Problem-solution
Compare-contrast
Cause-effect only
quiz.e: The organization moves from problem to a proposed remedy and addresses objections.

quiz.q: Which of the following would most effectively place a counterargument in an essay?
o: Never, since counterarguments weaken essays by giving readers reasons to doubt the writer’s thesis
After the main claim, where the writer acknowledges and then answers a serious objection
In the introduction only, where the writer states the objection but does not respond to it later
At the end of the essay with no rebuttal, so that the reader is left to weigh the two sides
quiz.e: A good counterargument is acknowledged and answered, strengthening the thesis.

quiz.q: A paragraph moves from a general principle to a specific example and then to a conclusion about the claim. Which reasoning pattern does it follow?
o: Inductive reasoning from many examples
Analogy
Causal chain
Deductive reasoning
quiz.e: Beginning with a general principle and applying it to a case is deductive.

quiz.q: A writer examines five cases of town councils that reduced speed limits and concludes that lower limits reduce accidents. The most important limitation of this reasoning is that:
o: Five cases may not be representative enough to support a general claim
Inductive reasoning is never valid, since a general claim cannot be proved by observing particular cases
Town councils do not matter, since speed limits are set by state agencies and not by local officials
Speed limits cannot change driver behavior, since most accidents are caused by carelessness and not by speed
quiz.e: Inductive conclusions are only as strong as the sample's size and representativeness.

quiz.q: A conclusion that merely repeats the introduction word for word is least effective because it:
o: Is too long for a final paragraph, since a conclusion should be brief and should not resemble the introduction
Fails to show how the argument developed or why it matters
Uses a quotation from the sources, which turns the writer’s last words into another writer’s argument
Introduces a new claim that the essay has not defended, so that the reader finishes with a loose end
quiz.e: A strong conclusion synthesizes and extends the argument.

quiz.q: A writer uses an extended analogy between a school and a ship to explain leadership. Which weakness is most associated with arguing by analogy?
o: The analogy may not hold in all relevant respects
Analogies are always fallacies, since two different things can never be compared in a valid argument
Analogies cannot be persuasive, since readers regard them as ornamental and not as reasons
Analogies require statistics, since a comparison is convincing only when it is supported by numbers
quiz.e: Analogies are persuasive only to the extent the compared cases are alike in relevant ways.

quiz.q: Which revision most improves coherence between two body paragraphs?
o: Adding an unrelated quotation that gives the reader a break between the two paragraphs and renews interest
Deleting the second paragraph’s topic sentence so that its idea seems to flow directly from the first
Repeating the introduction at the start of the second paragraph so that the thesis stays in view
Adding a sentence that links the previous paragraph's idea to the next paragraph's claim
quiz.e: Transitions that connect ideas maintain the line of reasoning.

quiz.q: A student writes: "Source A says later start times help sleep. Source B says they cost money. Source C says they improve grades." What is the main weakness?
o: It summarizes sources in sequence without using them to develop an argument
It uses too many sources for a short essay, so that none of them is examined in any depth
It cites its sources incorrectly, since each of them should be introduced with the author’s full name
It states a position in the opening sentence before the evidence has been presented in order
quiz.e: Synthesis requires the writer's argument to organize the sources, not the other way around.

quiz.q: Which sentence best integrates evidence from a source into a synthesis argument?
o: "As Rivera's study of three districts shows, the benefits of later bells appear within a year, which counters Chen's worry about long adjustment periods."
“Rivera has a study of three school districts, and Chen has a different study, which is mentioned later.”
“Rivera and Chen disagree about when the effects of later bell times can be observed in schools.”
“The study says that later start times have effects on students, and these effects are listed above.”
quiz.e: It uses the source for a purpose in the argument and links it to a second source, creating dialogue between them.

quiz.q: A synthesis prompt provides six sources. Which approach best meets the expectation to synthesize?
o: Quoting every source at length so that the grader can see that each of them has been read with care
Using at least three sources in service of the writer's own position and showing how they relate to each other
Using one source for the entire essay, since a single strong source can support a defensible position
Summarizing each source in a separate paragraph, with a brief remark on how it supports the thesis
quiz.e: Synthesis integrates multiple sources into the writer's own argument.

quiz.q: A student cites a source by writing, "According to the source, the policy works." What is the best revision for credible attribution?
o: "According to economist Maria Lopez in a 2021 report, the policy raised participation by 12 percent."
“Some people say the policy works, and the evidence of their experience is persuasive to many readers.”
“Experts agree that the policy works, and their view is shared by most of the people who study it.”
