“The source says it works, and the source’s evidence is strong enough to support the writer’s claim.”
quiz.e: Strong attribution identifies the source and gives a specific claim.

quiz.q: Two sources reach opposite conclusions about a policy. Which response best reflects sophisticated synthesis?
o: Explaining why the sources differ, such as differences in sample or context, and taking a position
Ignoring the source that disagrees with the writer so that the essay appears to rest on a consensus
Choosing the shorter source, since a concise source is easier to integrate into a brief essay
Summarizing each source without comment and leaving the reader to decide which of them is right
quiz.e: Evaluating the reasons for disagreement shows analysis.

quiz.q: A writer uses a source's statistic to support a claim but the source's data come from a very different context. What is the most significant concern?
o: The statistic is too specific, since a precise figure suggests a certainty that the data cannot support
The source is too short, since a brief document cannot give the context that a statistic requires
The evidence may not apply to the writer's claim
The statistic is cited, which shows the writer has not done any independent reasoning about the claim
quiz.e: Evidence must be relevant to the claim being supported.

quiz.q: Which thesis for a synthesis essay on public libraries is best?
o: “Libraries are important to their communities, and the sources show how many people rely on them.”
“The sources discuss libraries, and this essay will explain what each of them says about the topic.”
“Many people use libraries, and the number of visitors has grown over the last several years.”
"Although digital resources reduce some demand for books, libraries remain essential community spaces because they provide access, programming and a refuge that online alternatives do not."
quiz.e: A strong thesis takes a position, acknowledges complexity and previews reasoning.

quiz.q: A student's synthesis essay includes quotations that are longer than the student's own commentary. What is the most likely consequence?
o: The essay may read as a patchwork of sources rather than the student's argument
The essay will receive higher credit, since the quotations show the writer’s command of the sources
The essay will sound more objective, since the writer’s own voice is limited by the quotations
The essay will have a clearer thesis, since the quotations state the central claims directly
quiz.e: The writer's analysis should dominate.

quiz.q: In synthesis, what is the best use of a source that opposes your position?
o: Avoid it, since mentioning an opposing source gives the reader grounds to doubt the writer’s claim
Acknowledge it and respond with evidence or reasoning
Quote it without comment, so that the reader can see that the writer has represented it fairly
Use it as your own claim, since the opposing source states a position that the essay can adopt
quiz.e: Engaging opposing evidence strengthens credibility.

quiz.q: A student cites Source D to show that the problem is urgent and Source B to show that the proposed solution is feasible. This best demonstrates:
o: Over-reliance on sources, since the essay appears to be built from other writers’ ideas
Using different sources for distinct purposes in an argument
Plagiarism, since the writer has used the sources’ ideas without developing independent reasoning
A weak thesis, since the writer’s claim depends on the sources more than on the writer’s own thinking
quiz.e: Each source supports a different part of the reasoning.

quiz.q: A passage's author, writing to a hostile audience, begins by praising the audience's commitment to safety before criticizing a policy. Which analysis best explains the strategy?
o: The praise is an example of hyperbole that wins the audience’s sympathy by exaggerating its virtues
The praise is a distraction that keeps the audience from seeing the criticism until it is too late
The praise establishes common ground so the criticism seems a shared concern rather than an attack
The author is changing the subject so that the audience will not notice that the policy is flawed
quiz.e: Opening with shared values lowers resistance, positioning the criticism as consistent with the audience's own commitments.

quiz.q: Which topic sentence for a rhetorical analysis body paragraph is strongest?
o: “Kim uses statistics and an anecdote in the second paragraph, and both help to support her main point.”
“Kim’s essay is persuasive because it uses strong evidence and a clear structure to defend its claim.”
“The second paragraph is about an anecdote, and the anecdote is drawn from Kim’s own experience.”
"By shifting from statistics to a personal anecdote in the second paragraph, Kim humanizes the issue and encourages empathy from a general audience."
quiz.e: It names a specific choice, explains the effect and links it to the audience.

quiz.q: A student writes, "The author uses a metaphor, which makes the essay better." What is the primary weakness?
o: It identifies a device and so shows that the student can recognize rhetorical strategies in the passage
It does not explain how the metaphor works or its effect on the audience
It uses too much evidence, so that the writer’s own commentary is lost among the quotations
It states a claim, but the claim is too broad to be supported by any single piece of evidence
quiz.e: Naming a device is not analysis; the student must explain the effect.

quiz.q: Which of the following best describes the difference between summary and analysis in a rhetorical analysis essay?
o: Summary reports what the text says; analysis explains how and why the writer's choices produce an effect
They are the same, since both explain what the passage says in the writer’s own words
Analysis is longer than summary, and graders reward essays that spend most of their time on analysis
Summary identifies the tone of the passage, while analysis identifies the devices that create it
quiz.e: Rhetorical analysis explains the relationship between choices and effects.

quiz.q: A writer opens a speech with a long list of historical wrongs and then asks the audience to act now. Which assessment best explains the structure's effect?
o: It confuses the audience, since a long list makes the speaker’s point difficult to follow
It undermines the speaker’s purpose, since a list of past wrongs seems to excuse inaction now
The accumulation builds urgency so the call to action seems the natural response
It establishes a neutral tone, since the list presents the facts without any evident emotion
quiz.e: The list generates momentum that the appeal then channels.

quiz.q: A student argues that an author uses ethos by mentioning her twenty years as a nurse. Which addition would most deepen the analysis?
o: Counting the number of years mentioned and comparing it with the experience of other authors
Quoting the sentence again so that the grader can see the exact wording of the writer’s claim
Explaining how the experience makes her claims about staffing more credible to readers who distrust administrators
Defining ethos as an appeal to the credibility of the writer and giving two other examples
quiz.e: The analysis should connect the choice to its effect on the audience in context.

quiz.q: A rhetorical analysis essay discusses an author's tone as 'passionate.' How could the student improve this?
o: Specify the tone more precisely, such as 'indignant but controlled,' and show how diction creates it
Replace it with “good,” which is a simpler word and describes the writer’s attitude toward the topic
Remove the discussion of tone, since the essay should concentrate on the passage’s evidence
State it again in the conclusion so that the reader is certain to remember the writer’s point
quiz.e: Precise tone words supported by textual evidence show insight.

quiz.q: Which sentence best shows a line of reasoning that connects evidence to the thesis?
o: “The writer uses second person in the third paragraph, which is the first appearance of the pronoun.”
“Second person is used often in the passage, and it appears in nearly every paragraph of the text.”
"The writer's use of second-person address invites readers to imagine themselves in the scene, making the abstract policy feel personally consequential."
“Readers like the second person, since it makes the passage seem friendlier and easier to follow.”
quiz.e: It explains how the device works and its effect on readers.

quiz.q: A student's analysis claims the author is 'trying to persuade the audience' without describing how. This is most accurately characterized as:
o: A sophisticated analysis that places the passage in its larger social and historical context
A thesis that identifies the writer’s purpose and previews the strategies that the essay will examine
A summary of the conclusion that reports what the writer says in the passage’s last paragraph
A general statement that does not analyze specific choices
quiz.e: Analysis requires attention to specific rhetorical choices and effects.

quiz.q: A writer shifts abruptly from formal diction to colloquial language. What is the best way to analyze this shift?
o: Ignore it, since a change of diction is a matter of style and not a rhetorical choice
Identify the shift, describe its effect on tone and relate it to the writer's relationship with the audience
Say that it is a mistake, since a writer who shifts diction has lost control of the passage’s tone
Say that it is a metaphor, since the shift compares the formal and the casual registers
quiz.e: Shifts in diction signal changes in attitude or relationship worth analyzing.

quiz.q: Given the prompt "Is it more important to preserve tradition or embrace change?", which thesis best reflects the sophistication expected in an argument essay?
o: “Tradition is important to every society, and its value has been recognized by thinkers in many different periods.”
“Change is good for any society, and a community that resists it will eventually be left behind.”

"While tradition provides continuity, a community that refuses change risks becoming irrelevant, so the healthiest societies preserve traditions that serve their values and revise those that no longer do."
“There are many opinions about tradition and change, and each of them contains a measure of truth.”
quiz.e: A nuanced thesis acknowledges complexity and makes a defensible, reasoned claim.

quiz.q: A student's essay argues that homework should be limited and supports this with only personal anecdotes. How could the essay best be improved?
o: Add varied evidence, such as research and examples from other schools, and explain how they support the claim
Add more personal anecdotes, so that the writer’s view is supported by a larger number of cases
Remove the claim, since a thesis supported by anecdote alone cannot be defended in a timed essay
Change the topic to one on which the writer has access to more reliable statistical evidence
quiz.e: Strong arguments use multiple kinds of evidence and commentary.

quiz.q: A writer concedes that 'online classes are convenient' and then argues that 'convenience is not the same as learning.' This move best demonstrates:
o: Circular reasoning, in which the writer assumes the claim and then offers it as the evidence
A fallacy of false dilemma, in which the writer presents convenience and learning as the only options
A summary of the opposing view, in which the writer reports it without commenting on its force
Qualification and refutation of an opposing idea
quiz.e: Granting a point and then limiting its force is a sophisticated argumentative move.

quiz.q: Which of the following best illustrates the use of specific, relevant evidence in an argument about public transportation?
o: A claim that “everyone knows” transit is good for cities, followed by a statement of its popularity
A quotation about trains from a novel that describes the pleasure of traveling across the countryside
A comparison of commute times and costs in two cities with different transit investment
A statement that transit exists in most cities and that many people use it in their daily lives
quiz.e: Specific and relevant evidence supports a particular claim.

quiz.q: A student argues that a school should extend the library's hours, but the essay never addresses cost. Which revision would best strengthen the argument?
o: Remove all evidence so that the essay is focused on the writer’s claim and not on the support
Add emotional appeals only, so that the reader feels the importance of the library to students
Anticipate the objection about cost and respond with an estimate or an alternative funding approach
Say that cost does not matter, since the value of extended hours is greater than any expense
quiz.e: Addressing a likely objection strengthens the argument.

quiz.q: Which sentence from an argument essay most effectively uses commentary?
o: “The policy has benefits that are shown in the data, and these benefits are available to many students.”
“Many students are affected by the policy, and the effects are described in the sources the writer cites.”
"This difference matters because it shows the policy's benefits reach the students who are least likely to be reached by existing programs."
“There are students who attend the schools where the policy has been tried, and they number in the thousands.”
quiz.e: Commentary explains the significance of evidence.

quiz.q: A writer begins an argument with a definition of a key term and then uses that definition throughout. What is the strategic purpose?
o: To confuse the audience so that readers accept the writer’s claim without noticing how it is defined
To fill space in an essay that has too little material to reach the length that is expected
To establish a precise meaning on which the argument depends
To add humor to a serious argument so that the reader’s attention is held through the middle of the essay
quiz.e: Defining terms prevents misunderstanding.

quiz.q: Which of the following would most weaken an argument essay's credibility?
o: Acknowledging the complexity of the issue, since a writer who admits difficulty seems indecisive
Using precise language, since a writer who is exact seems to be more concerned with words than with ideas
Relying on an exaggerated claim without evidence
Citing a credible source, since an argument that depends on others’ authority seems to lack original thought
quiz.e: Overstated claims erode trust.

quiz.q: An essay argues that the voting age should be lowered to 16 and supports this by noting that 16-year-olds can work and pay taxes. What is the best way to deepen the reasoning?
o: Explain the principle behind the claim, such as taxation implying representation, and address differences between work and voting
Repeat the claim in stronger language so that the reader is convinced of the writer’s certainty
Add a statistic about the average age at which students begin to work and pay taxes
Remove the example, since an argument that relies on work and taxes is too narrow to be persuasive
quiz.e: Reasoning should state the principle that connects the evidence to the claim.

quiz.q: A student writes: "Some might say technology isolates us, but it also connects us." What does this sentence do?
o: Develops a full rebuttal of the counterclaim, with evidence for each part of the writer’s response
Acknowledges a counterclaim and responds, though it needs development to be persuasive
Provides evidence that technology connects people, in the form of a study of social networks
Concludes the essay by summarizing its argument and restating the thesis for the reader
quiz.e: It begins a concession-rebuttal but remains thin without evidence.

quiz.q: Which choice correctly punctuates the sentence? "The mayor, who had promised reform _ lost the election."
o: The mayor, who had promised reform, lost the election.
The mayor who had promised reform, lost the election.
The mayor, who had promised reform lost the election.
The mayor who had promised reform; lost the election.
quiz.e: A nonrestrictive clause set off with a comma at the start requires a closing comma after it.

quiz.q: Which sentence contains a misplaced modifier?
o: Walking down the street, Maria thought the trees looked beautiful.
Maria walked down the street and admired the trees.
As Maria walked down the street, the trees looked beautiful.
Walking down the street, the trees looked beautiful to Maria.
quiz.e: 'Walking down the street' appears to modify 'the trees' rather than Maria.

quiz.q: Which choice correctly completes the sentence? "Neither the principal nor the teachers _ aware of the change."
o: was
is
were
has been
quiz.e: With 'neither ... nor' the verb agrees with the nearer subject, 'teachers,' which is plural.

quiz.q: Which sentence uses a semicolon correctly?
o: The committee reviewed; the proposal and approved it.
The committee reviewed the proposal; it decided to approve it.
The committee reviewed the proposal; and approved it.
The committee; reviewed the proposal.
quiz.e: A semicolon joins two independent clauses.

quiz.q: In the sentence "Between you and me, the plan is flawed," the pronoun 'me' is correct because:
o: It is the subject of the sentence, since it names the person who is described as being between
It is a possessive pronoun, since it refers to something that belongs to the speaker
It is a reflexive pronoun, since it refers back to the speaker who is making the statement
It is the object of the preposition 'between'
quiz.e: Prepositions take object-case pronouns.

quiz.q: Which of the following best corrects the faulty parallelism? "The coach praised their dedication, speed, and that they never gave up."
o: The coach praised their dedication, speed, and they never gave up.
The coach praised their dedication, being fast, and perseverance.
The coach praised dedication, speed and that they persevere.
The coach praised their dedication, speed, and perseverance.
quiz.e: Items in a series should share the same grammatical form.

quiz.q: On a multiple-choice question asking for the best way to combine two sentences, which strategy is most effective?
o: Choose the longest option, since it is most likely to include every detail from the original sentences
Choose the first option, since it is usually the one that preserves the original word order
Identify the relationship between the ideas and choose the option that expresses it concisely and correctly
Choose the option with the most commas, since punctuation shows that the ideas are properly joined
quiz.e: Look for logical relationship and economy of expression.

quiz.q: Which sentence uses 'its' or 'it's' correctly?
o: The committee issued it's report, and its clear the results are mixed.
The committee issued its report, and it's clear the results are mixed.
The committee issued its' report, and its' clear.
The committee issued it's report and it's clear.
quiz.e: 'Its' is possessive; 'it's' means 'it is.'

quiz.q: A multiple-choice question asks which revision improves the logical flow between two sentences. Which strategy is best?
o: Choose any transition that sounds formal, since the exam rewards a polished and academic tone
Choose the shortest transition, since concise wording is always preferred in a revision question
Choose “however” whenever it appears, since it is the transition most often used by good writers
Determine what relationship (contrast, cause, example) the second sentence has to the first and pick the transition that matches
quiz.e: The correct transition expresses the actual logical relationship.

quiz.q: Which sentence has correct comma use with a coordinating conjunction?
o: The speech was long but, the audience stayed.
The speech was long but the audience, stayed.
The speech was long, but, the audience stayed.
The speech was long, but the audience stayed.
quiz.e: A comma precedes the conjunction joining two independent clauses.

quiz.q: Irving frames "Rip Van Winkle" as papers left behind by the fictional historian Diedrich Knickerbocker, and appends a postscript in which Knickerbocker vouches for the tale. The most significant effect of this frame is to:
o: Convince readers that the events actually occurred in the Hudson Valley by appealing to a respected historian’s sworn statement
Provide the biographical background of Rip’s family, so that readers can understand why he behaves as he does in the village
Shift the narrative to the first person so that a participant can describe the events and so persuade readers that they happened
Establish a tragic tone that the comic events of the story will later contradict, so that the ending gains an ironic force
Lend a mock-scholarly authority to a fanciful legend, which gently satirizes the claims of historical writing
Introduce a second plot, concerning the historian’s own life, that is resolved by the revelation of Rip’s long sleep
quiz.e: The pedantic, sworn-to-be-true frame is itself humorous; it parodies historical authority while giving a folk legend an air of credibility. It does not seriously try to convince readers the events happened.

quiz.q: Irving writes that the changes of states and empires "made but little impression on him," but "there was one species of despotism under which he had long groaned, and that was—petticoat government." The effect of this sentence is primarily to:
o: Condemn the American Revolution as a form of tyranny that has ruined Rip’s village and destroyed the peace he enjoyed before it began
Reveal that Rip was secretly a political revolutionary who disguised his views by playing the part of a lazy and ignorant man
Mock Rip's narrow priorities by treating a domestic grievance as equal to a political revolution
Praise Dame Van Winkle for the strength of character that allows her to manage the household while her husband neglects his duties
Suggest that Rip understands politics better than his neighbors, since he has recognized the tyranny that exists in his own home
Establish the story’s setting in the years before the Revolution, so that the reader will understand why Rip does not mind the king
quiz.e: The mock-heroic comparison elevates a household squabble to the level of political despotism, and the narrator's gentle irony reveals Rip's self-centered point of view.

quiz.q: Rip is described as willing to do any amount of work for his neighbors but unwilling to do the work of his own farm. The best interpretation of this contrast is that:
o: Rip is secretly wealthy and therefore does not need to farm, so his idleness is a pleasure that he can well afford
Irving distinguishes between work that offers social companionship and work that offers only obligation, making Rip's idleness a matter of temperament and not simple laziness
Irving believes that neighborly work is more valuable than farming, and so Rip’s choices are admirable and worth imitating
The narrator disapproves of Rip’s neighbors for taking advantage of him, which he treats as a defect in the village’s character
Irving intends to show that Rip is a hypocrite who values the approval of others more than the welfare of his own family
Rip’s farm is too far from the village to be worked efficiently, and so his neglect of it has a practical cause
quiz.e: Rip happily helps neighbors but avoids his own labor; the contrast characterizes him as sociable and easygoing, not merely lazy, which makes him sympathetic.

quiz.q: The narrator remarks that a tart temper "never mellows with age, and a sharp tongue is the only edged tool that grows keener with constant use." The second clause is notable chiefly for:
o: Its use of dialect to reveal the narrator’s social class and so to distance him from the Dutch villagers he describes with such amusement
Its use of understatement to minimize the seriousness of Rip’s problem, so that his wife’s temper appears a trifling inconvenience
Its use of a metaphor that turns a proverb-like generalization into a witty comment on Dame Van Winkle
Its use of apostrophe to address the reader directly and so to ask for sympathy with Rip in his unhappy domestic situation
Its use of allusion to a historical figure whom the reader is expected to recognize as a model of a sharp-tongued woman
Its use of personification of the tongue as a living creature, which gives the sentence a violent and almost frightening tone
quiz.e: The tongue as an 'edged tool' that sharpens with use is a metaphor delivered as a witty aphorism; humor, not dialect or apostrophe, drives the line.

quiz.q: Which statement best explains the significance of the sign at the village inn changing from a portrait of King George III to one of General Washington?
o: It shows that Rip has awakened in a different country, since the portrait of Washington is the emblem of a new nation across the ocean
It proves that Rip has been asleep for exactly twenty years, since the sign was painted on the day that he fell asleep
It suggests that the villagers are loyal to the British crown, since they have retained a portrait of a leader in the inn
It dramatizes how thoroughly the Revolution has changed the world Rip wakes into, without requiring the narrator to explain the change
It indicates that the owner of the inn has become wealthy, since he can afford to repaint the sign with a new portrait
It warns Rip that he is in danger from the village authorities, who have replaced the king’s portrait to frighten any visitor
quiz.e: The altered sign is a concrete, nearly wordless way to show political transformation; Irving relies on a symbol rather than exposition.

quiz.q: When Rip declares himself "a poor quiet man, a native of the place, and a loyal subject of the King, God bless him!", the crowd reacts with hostility. The irony of the moment is that:
o: Rip is actually a spy for the British, and the crowd’s suspicion is justified by words that he has spoken without any knowledge of its effect
Rip is deliberately provoking the villagers by declaring his loyalty, for he wishes to test whether the people have changed in his absence
The villagers misunderstand Rip because he speaks Dutch, and the crowd takes his words for a threat that he has not intended
The king mentioned is a character in the story whom the villagers have known, and they resent Rip’s calling him a good ruler
Rip speaks with innocent sincerity in a language of loyalty that has become dangerous without his knowing it
Rip is being sarcastic about the Revolution, and the crowd’s hostility is the natural reaction to a joke made at its expense
quiz.e: His speech would have been unremarkable twenty years earlier; now it marks him as a Tory. The irony arises from the gap between his intention and the way it is received.

quiz.q: When Rip says "I'm not myself—I'm somebody else," which interpretation is most consistent with the rest of the passage?
o: It is an attempt to deceive the crowd by giving a false name, in the hope that the villagers will let him alone and go away
It reveals that Rip has lost his memory of his earlier life, and so he is unable to say who he is or where he belongs
It is a joke aimed at the villagers, intended to ease the tension of the moment by making light of his own confusion
It expresses his genuine bewilderment at a world in which both his surroundings and his identity have been displaced
It shows that Rip has become suspicious of his dog, which no longer seems to him the animal that he knew before
It proves that someone else has taken Rip’s place in the village, and that the stranger he meets is in fact himself
quiz.e: Every familiar marker of identity (people, houses, politics, even his appearance) has changed, so Rip's confusion is literal and comic and underscores the theme of time and change.

quiz.q: Which of the following best describes how Irving uses the character Peter Vanderdonk, the village historian, near the end of the story?
o: He challenges Rip’s account and exposes him as a fraud, since no one in the village can recall the legend that Rip describes
He becomes Rip’s main antagonist, for he resents the attention that Rip’s story has attracted from the village’s inhabitants
He represents the new American government, which regards Rip’s story as dangerous and wishes to prevent its being spread
He interprets Rip’s dream through philosophy, and shows that the long sleep is a symbol of the colony’s age under the king
He becomes Rip’s business partner, and together they use the legend to attract visitors to the inn and the village
He confirms Rip's story by appealing to legend, which helps resolve the plot while keeping the tone playful
quiz.e: Vanderdonk ties Rip's story to the local legend of Hendrick Hudson's crew, giving the tale a folkloric resolution.

quiz.q: Rip's final position as a village patriarch who tells his story to visitors mainly suggests that:
o: Rip has become an important political leader, whose stories about his sleep persuade the villagers to adopt the new government
The Revolution had little effect on the village, since the same people live there and the same customs are observed
Rip has become wealthy through the sale of his story, and he enjoys the comforts that his years of idleness had denied him
Irving believes that storytelling is a form of work, and that Rip has at last found an occupation worthy of his talents
The old, comfortable order can survive in memory and storytelling even after historical change
Rip has accepted the new government enthusiastically, and he now regards the Revolution as the best event of his lifetime
quiz.e: Rip becomes a living link to the pre-Revolutionary past, valued for his stories, which reflects the story's gentle nostalgia.

quiz.q: Compared with Dame Van Winkle, the narrator's treatment of Rip's idleness is best characterized as:
o: Harshly critical, since the narrator regards Rip’s neglect of his farm as a serious fault that has brought ruin on his family
Neutral and clinical, since the narrator reports the facts of Rip’s idleness without any attempt to judge or to excuse them
Admiring and heroic, since the narrator presents Rip’s refusal to work as a principled stand against the demands of society
Ironically disapproving of Rip’s neighbors, since the narrator suggests that they are the ones who ought to be blamed
Entirely uncritical, since the narrator never mentions any flaw in Rip’s character and lets his conduct appear faultless
Indulgent and affectionate, even while it acknowledges Rip's faults
quiz.e: The narrator forgives Rip's faults with humor, while Dame's temper is the object of satire; tone is indulgent, not clinical.

quiz.q: The description of the strange men playing ninepins in the mountains, whose faces and silence seem unnatural, primarily serves to:
o: Show that Rip has been drinking too much, so that the strange scene is understood as a drunken fancy and not as a real event
Demonstrate that Rip has joined the Revolution, since the men are soldiers whose silence and odd dress are military discipline
Provide comic relief that contradicts the rest of the story’s serious tone, and so lets the reader laugh at Rip’s credulity
Reveal that the men are villagers in disguise, who have staged the scene in order to play a joke on Rip while he is asleep
Establish a realistic setting for the plot, in which the men are ordinary travelers who have stopped to rest in the mountains
Create a supernatural, eerie atmosphere that makes Rip's long sleep plausible within the world of the legend
quiz.e: The silence, odd costumes and thunder-like rolling of the balls create a folkloric, uncanny mood.

quiz.q: The principal irony in Rip's twenty-year sleep is that:
o: He becomes famous during his absence, since the villagers talk of his disappearance and add to the legend that they tell
He sleeps through a battle in which he had fought, and so misses the one event that would have given his life a meaning
The great historical events of his time pass him by while he is absent for a nap, and he returns with no sense of loss
He returns to find that his farm has prospered in his absence, so his idleness has proved more useful than industry
He wakes up as a different person, who has been changed by the long sleep and now wishes to atone for his earlier neglect
He sleeps through only a single night, though the villagers insist that he has been absent for twenty years and more
quiz.e: He misses the entire Revolution and returns relatively unscathed; the humor lies in the contrast between historical magnitude and Rip's obliviousness.

quiz.q: Irving's narrator describes the inn's "rubicund portrait of His Majesty George the Third" as faded and weatherworn by the time Rip returns. If the portrait is treated as a symbol, it most plausibly represents:
o: Rip's affection for the king
The wealth of the innkeeper
The author's disapproval of kings
The beauty of the Catskill landscape
The passage of a single season
The fading of the old colonial order
quiz.e: A symbol of royal authority that has been replaced highlights the transition between regimes.

quiz.q: Which sentence best captures the story's attitude toward change?
o: It portrays change as a catastrophe to be resisted, and so it encourages the reader to hold fast to old customs and loyalties
It celebrates revolution as the end of all injustice, and presents Rip’s sleep as a missed opportunity to take part in it
It portrays change as an illusion, since the village in the end seems no different from the one that Rip had left
It condemns Rip for ignoring change, and shows that his idleness has cost him the chance to take part in the nation’s history
It presents change as a punishment for idleness, since Rip’s sleep is the penalty for his neglect of the farm and the family
It treats change with humor and wistfulness, as something that comes whether or not one is paying attention
quiz.e: Irving's tone is amused and a little nostalgic rather than angry or triumphant.

quiz.q: In the village's political argument that greets Rip, the crowd shouts questions such as whether he is "Federal or Democrat." Rip's baffled reaction primarily emphasizes that:
o: Rip has strong opinions about both parties, though his long absence has made it difficult for him to explain what they are
Rip had secretly voted before his sleep, and so the question touches a private matter that he would rather not discuss
The villagers are mocking him, since they know that a man who has been absent so long cannot answer the question
Rip does not understand English, and so he is unable to follow the questions that the crowd is shouting at him
The language of politics has changed in his absence so that even simple loyalty questions seem foreign
Rip is a lifelong Democrat, and his hesitation reflects only his surprise at the fact that the crowd should ask the question
quiz.e: The unfamiliar party vocabulary shows the gap between his world and the new republic.

quiz.q: The narrator's habit of using mock-formal diction to describe homely matters is best exemplified by:
o: Describing Rip’s dog as a dignified courtier who is skilled in the arts of the royal court and the etiquette of its ceremonies
Using dialect for Rip’s speech so that the reader hears the accent of the Dutch settlers and recognizes his place in the village
Reporting dialogue in short sentences, which gives the narration the swift movement of a play and the sharpness of conversation
Using one-word paragraphs to mark the story’s turning points, so that the reader’s attention is directed to each important event
Describing a household dispute in terms of despotism and government
Omitting description of the setting, so that the reader’s attention remains fixed on the characters and on their speech
quiz.e: Elevated diction applied to trivial subjects produces mock-heroic humor.

quiz.q: Dame Van Winkle's death is reported near the end of the story in a way that most clearly:
o: Elicits deep sympathy for Dame Van Winkle, whose death is described in language that stresses her suffering and the family’s loss
Suggests that Rip caused her death by his neglect, and so makes the narrator’s later affection for him seem questionable
Treats her as a figure of comic menace whose absence relieves Rip, without the narrator expressing sorrow
Shows that Rip is cruel, since he does not mourn for his wife but seems pleased that she is no longer there to scold him
Makes the ending tragic, since the wife’s death comes at a moment when Rip might have been reconciled with her
Implies that she has secretly been a good wife, since the narrator mentions her death in a tone of regret and respect
quiz.e: Her death is reported briefly and without lament; the tone aligns with Rip's relief.

quiz.q: Which feature of "Rip Van Winkle" most strongly marks it as a tale of the American literary tradition rather than a purely European folktale?
o: Its use of magic, since folktales of the old world were full of enchanted sleepers and supernatural beings of every kind
Its use of a frame narrator, since European tales had long been presented as the work of an invented and learned compiler
Its use of a comic tone, since the humor of the story is drawn from a tradition of German and Dutch folklore
Its focus on a husband and wife, since the quarrel between a henpecked man and his wife is a common figure of European comedy
Its use of a mountain setting, since the enchanted mountain is a familiar feature of the folktales of northern Europe
Its blending of an old-world legend with the specific history of the Hudson Valley and the American Revolution
quiz.e: Irving adapted a European folktale type to a distinctly American setting and political history.

quiz.q: Why might Irving have chosen to make Rip's reaction to the Revolution one of mild confusion rather than strong opinion?
o: It shows Rip to be a coward, who fears the consequences of expressing an opinion in a village that has been divided by war
It is the only way to maintain realism, since a man who had slept for twenty years could have no opinion about politics
It reveals that Irving opposed the Revolution, and wished to suggest that its changes were of little real importance to the people
It allows the narrator to treat the historical upheaval with gentle humor, emphasizing the continuity of ordinary life
It makes the story a tragedy, since a man who cannot understand the change in his world is shown to be helpless
It shows that Rip is secretly wise, since he has seen that politics is less important than a quiet and contented life
quiz.e: A bewildered, apolitical protagonist lets Irving examine historical change through a comic, human lens.

quiz.q: The narrator's description of Dame Van Winkle's household, with the wife's loud "curtain lecture" at night, primarily functions to:
o: Introduce a subplot about the village’s opinion of Rip’s marriage, which the narrator will resolve by describing the neighbors’ views
Establish the domestic conflict that motivates Rip's flight to the mountains
Show that the family is wealthy, since the wife’s long lectures are those of a woman with servants and a large household
Foreshadow Rip’s death, since the scene suggests that he will not long survive in a house governed by such a temper
Provide a contrast with Rip’s daughter, whose gentle manner is set against the harsh temper of her mother in the household
Introduce the story’s frame, in which the narrator explains how the tale came to be written down and preserved
quiz.e: Rip's retreat to the woods is motivated by his wife's scolding, setting up the central event.

quiz.q: In a rhetorical analysis of the story, which statement most accurately describes the narrator's persona?
o: Naive and unreliable, since the narrator accepts the legend without question and reports it in good faith to the readers
Hostile to the characters, since he portrays the village and its inhabitants in an unflattering and often contemptuous manner
Detached and scientific, since he records the facts of Rip’s story as an observer who has no feeling about them
Knowing and amused, adopting the pose of an antiquarian historian while slyly undercutting that pose
Mournful and nostalgic only, since the narrator’s chief concern is to lament the loss of the village’s earlier customs
Argumentative and didactic, since he uses the story of Rip to teach the reader a lesson about industry and thrift
quiz.e: The Knickerbocker persona is a comic, self-aware antiquarian.

quiz.q: The sentence "A tart temper never mellows with age" is most closely related to which of these generalized aims of the story?
o: Teaching a moral lesson about hard work, since the sentence shows what comes to a woman who is unwilling to hold her tongue
Describing historical events in the language of a chronicle, so that the reader may place the story in its period
Providing a realistic portrait of marriage in the colonial period, based on the narrator’s observation of village households
Foreshadowing the Revolution, since the sentence compares a domestic quarrel with the strife between the colonies and the crown
Offering gentle satire of human types through proverb-like observation
Explaining Rip’s drinking, since a man who lived with so sharp a tongue might be expected to seek relief in liquor
quiz.e: Aphoristic generalizations about human nature are part of the satiric voice.

quiz.q: Rip's dog Wolf is said to be as much afraid of Dame Van Winkle as Rip is. The detail is most useful for:
o: Showing that Wolf is a poorly trained dog, whose timidity makes him a poor companion for a hunter and a source of embarrassment
Foreshadowing Wolf’s disappearance, since the dog is described in a way that suggests he will not be seen again
Showing that Wolf is brave, since he alone dares to stay in the house when Dame Van Winkle’s anger is at its height
Suggesting that Dame is secretly kind, since the dog’s attachment to the household indicates that she treats animals gently
Extending the comic portrait of Dame Van Winkle's domestic power to the household animals
Describing the setting of the farm, so that the reader may picture the yard and outbuildings of the Van Winkle property
quiz.e: The shared fear unites man and dog against the wife and builds the comedy.

quiz.q: Which of the following would be the strongest evidence that Irving's story is more concerned with how people experience historical change than with the change itself?
o: Rip's personal bewilderment and the focus on his small-scale experiences rather than battles or leaders
The presence of a historian character, Peter Vanderdonk, who records the events that Rip describes and verifies them for the village
The mention of Washington, whose portrait appears on the inn’s sign and whose name is known to everyone in the village
The setting in the Catskills, whose mountains and valleys give the story its distinctive atmosphere and its air of legend
The description of Dutch customs, which shows the village’s way of life before the Revolution and after it had ended
The inclusion of a frame narrator, who introduces the story and assures the reader in a postscript that it is true
quiz.e: The story keeps the Revolution offstage and follows an ordinary man's reaction.

quiz.q: What function does the long first-person-like introduction describing the Catskill Mountains play?
o: It contains the story’s central conflict, since the mountains are described as the source of the troubles that Rip later suffers
It reveals the narrator’s identity, so that the reader may judge his reliability before the story of Rip begins
It establishes a mythic, atmospheric setting that makes the legend feel timeless
It introduces Rip’s wife, whose temper is compared with the changing weather that the narrator describes among the hills
It argues for the independence of the colonies, since the mountains are presented as a symbol of the land’s freedom
It explains the plot of the story in advance, so that the reader will know what to expect from the events that follow
quiz.e: The romantic description of the mountains sets up the folkloric tone.

quiz.q: Twain introduces the bluejay tale by having Jim Baker claim that jays have a command of slang and grammar. This claim is best understood as:
o: A scientific observation, which Twain includes to show that the narrator has studied the habits of birds with real care
Comic exaggeration that anthropomorphizes the birds and establishes the tall-tale mode
A serious argument about language, which Twain makes in order to claim that animals possess a form of speech like ours
A literal description of bird behavior, which Baker offers as evidence that jays can communicate more fully than other creatures
An attack on human grammar, since Baker suggests that people use their own language less skillfully than the birds do
A sign that Baker is unreliable in all respects, so that the reader must doubt every other statement that he makes
quiz.e: The absurd praise of jay language is a tall-tale exaggeration, not a literal claim.

quiz.q: The simile that the jay's smile "faded gradually out of his countenance like breath off'n a razor" is effective because it:
o: Combines a precise, unexpected visual comparison with dialect, which conveys both the jay's embarrassment and Baker's voice
Uses formal diction to contrast with the humor, so that the elevated language makes the jay’s embarrassment seem more absurd
Relies on abstract imagery, which leaves the reader to supply the details and so to share in the speaker’s humor
Appeals to patriotic feeling, since the razor is a familiar emblem of the frontier’s spirit of independence and self-reliance
Is a literal description of the jay’s expression, which Baker has observed and which he reports with a naturalist’s precision
Foreshadows the jay’s death, since a razor suggests the danger that awaits the bird in the final scene of the tale
quiz.e: A fogging razor surface fading is a vivid comparison phrased in Baker's dialect ("off'n").

quiz.q: Twain presents the story as told by Jim Baker rather than directly by the narrator. The most important effect of this frame is:
o: It makes the story more scientific, since a miner who has lived among jays is an authority on their conduct
It reduces the humor, since Baker’s plain manner is less lively than the narrator’s own style would have been
It allows Twain to avoid the use of dialect, since a character’s speech may be reported in standard English
It lets a character with a distinctive voice deliver the exaggerations, adding humor and a sense of oral tradition
It removes the narrator’s opinions, so that the story is presented as a plain account of what Baker has seen
It changes the genre to tragedy, since the character’s earnest manner gives the jay’s labor a serious and moving tone
quiz.e: The tale gains authority and comedy from Baker's deadpan, dialect-rich storytelling.

quiz.q: Baker's repeated pronouncement that the jay is better than a human in some respects (using "human" traits) functions mainly as:
o: A scientific hypothesis, which Baker proposes in order to explain why the jay’s behavior is so much like that of a person
A moral lesson on kindness to animals, which Baker hopes the narrator will remember when he next meets a jay
A criticism of Baker himself, whose own foolish habits are the real subject of the comparison with the bird
A claim about literary style, in which Baker suggests that jays are better storytellers than most human writers
A symbol of the Old West, in which the jay’s self-reliance and independence represent the spirit of the frontier
Satire of human behavior through animal comparison
quiz.e: By giving birds human foibles, the story mocks human pride and behavior.

quiz.q: The central comic situation in the story arises because:
o: A jay learns to speak and begins to bargain with Baker over the price of the acorns that he has carried to the cabin
Baker captures a jay and then keeps it in the cabin, where the other birds come to look at it and to laugh
A jay's determined effort to fill a hole fails in a way that grows more absurd as more jays arrive
The jays steal a miner’s gold from the cabin and carry it up to the hole, where it is later discovered by Baker
The cabin collapses under the weight of the acorns that the jay has dropped, and the jays flee in confusion
A jay defeats an owl in a contest of strength, and the jays gather to celebrate his victory in front of Baker
quiz.e: The acorns keep falling through the hole into an empty cabin, and the jay's persistence and the others' amusement drive the humor.

quiz.q: The phrase "sweating like an ice-pitcher" is best classified as:
o: A formal metaphor that compares a person to a pitcher, so that the phrase suggests dignity and a cool temper
An allusion to a well-known story about a pitcher, which the original audience would have recognized at once
A pun that depends on two meanings of “pitcher,” one a container and the other a thrower of a ball
A colloquial simile built on a paradoxical image
Personification of the pitcher, which is made to perspire like a person who has been working in the heat
Hyperbole only, since the phrase exaggerates the amount of sweat without comparing it to any other object
quiz.e: It compares the bird to a pitcher whose cold surface beads with water, in a homespun idiom.

quiz.q: Which of these best describes Twain's tone in the bluejay passage?
o: Deadpan humor that treats an absurd story as sober fact
Bitter satire of miners and their ways, which the narrator uses to show his contempt for the people of the West
Elevated and solemn, in the manner of a heroic tale in which the jay’s labor is treated with great respect
Nostalgic and sentimental, since the narrator recalls the pleasures of life in a mining camp and mourns their passing
Fearful and suspenseful, since the story depends on the narrator’s uncertainty about what the jays may do next
Didactic and instructive, since the narrator presents the story as a lesson in patience and in the value of labor
quiz.e: The humor depends on the straight-faced delivery.

quiz.q: The detail that the jays gather in large numbers to look at the hole and laugh primarily serves to:
o: Provide the setting, by showing that the cabin stands in a region where jays are numerous and the winters are mild
Show that the jays are cruel to their companion, since they enjoy his failure and take pleasure in his distress
Illustrate predation, since the jays gather to feed on the acorns that have fallen around the cabin and in its yard
Prove that the hole is real, since a large number of witnesses is able to confirm its existence to Baker
Intensify the humor by giving the gathering a social, human-like quality
Foreshadow an attack, since the gathering of so many jays suggests that they mean to do harm to the miner
quiz.e: The crowd of jays behaving like jeering spectators emphasizes the comedy and anthropomorphism.

quiz.q: Which statement best explains the effect of Baker's dialect (for example, "off'n") on the reader?
o: It confuses the plot, since the reader must work to understand each sentence and so loses the thread of the story
It makes the story less funny, since the humor depends on language that is more formal and precise than Baker’s
It establishes a folksy, authentic oral voice that supports the tall-tale conventions
It suggests that Baker is a well-educated man, whose speech is a deliberate imitation of the frontier’s dialect
It sets a tragic tone, since the speech of the working classes is associated with suffering and hardship
It tells readers that the setting is the East Coast, since the dialect belongs to the working people of that region
quiz.e: Dialect creates character and local color in a frame narrative.

quiz.q: The jay's attempt to fill a hole that cannot be filled can be read as a comic image of:
o: The success of hard work, since the jay persists until at last he accomplishes what he has set out to do
The destruction of nature by human settlement, since the cabin and the hole are signs of the miners’ presence
Human futility and stubborn effort in the face of obvious failure
The cruelty of owls, which prey upon smaller birds and have caused the jay to labor so hard at his task
The rhythm of nature, in which creatures perform the same tasks again and again according to the seasons
The cycle of life, in which the work of one generation is taken up and completed by that which comes after it
quiz.e: The jay's labor, observed with comic detachment, is a parody of human persistence.

quiz.q: Hawthorne names the protagonist's wife Faith and has Brown say, "With Heaven above and Faith below, I will stand firm against the devil." The most significant effect of this naming is that:
o: It identifies Faith as the story’s villain, since her name suggests that she has misled Brown into leaving his home
It proves that the story takes place in a dream, since the name is so exactly suited to the theme that it cannot be real
It allows the story to operate on two levels, so Brown's loss of trust in his wife also reads as a loss of religious faith
It establishes that Faith is a spiritual guide, whose advice Brown ought to follow whenever he is in doubt
It shows that Brown is a religious hypocrite, since he speaks of Heaven while he is about to go and meet the devil
It suggests that Faith will lead Brown to the forest meeting, where he will see that she is the devil’s servant
quiz.e: The allegorical name makes the personal and spiritual losses inseparable; the reader cannot easily tell which one Brown is describing.

quiz.q: As Brown leaves, Faith's pink ribbons are mentioned in the first paragraph and a pink ribbon later flutters down in the forest. The ribbon functions primarily as:
o: A clue that Faith has secretly followed him into the forest, so that the reader suspects that she is part of the plot
A sign that Brown has found his way out of the forest, since the ribbon marks the path that leads him back to the village
A symbol of the devil’s power over the village, since the ribbon is left by the traveler as a mark of his triumph
Evidence that the events were a dream, since a ribbon could not remain in the air after Brown had seen it
A concrete symbol that Brown interprets as proof of Faith's corruption, though its meaning remains open to question
A decoration with no thematic importance, which Hawthorne mentions only to give the scene an air of realistic detail
quiz.e: The ribbon sets off Brown's conclusion that Faith is lost, but the story never confirms it, which preserves ambiguity.

quiz.q: The traveler Brown meets in the forest carries a staff "which bore the likeness of a great black snake, so curiously wrought that it might almost be seen to twist and wriggle itself like a living serpent." The description most directly suggests:
o: That the traveler is a hunter, whose staff is carved to resemble the animals that he pursues in the forest
A comic detail that lightens the story’s mood, since the staff’s behavior is more amusing than frightening to the reader
An allusion to the serpent of Eden that identifies the traveler with the devil and connects the story to the theme of temptation
A literal threat of violence, since the snake is real and the traveler means to use it against Brown
That the traveler is lame, since he needs the staff for support and has carved it in a form that interests him
That the forest contains dangerous animals, and that Brown ought to be on his guard as he continues on his way
quiz.e: The twisting snake-staff echoes the Garden of Eden and signals the traveler's identity.

quiz.q: The traveler claims to have helped Brown's father and grandfather in acts of cruelty in Puritan history. The purpose of this claim in the story is to:
o: Prove that Brown’s ancestors were innocent, since the traveler’s claim is shown to be false by the village’s records
Provide historical detail about Salem, so that the reader will understand the events of the period in which the story is set
Undermine Brown's confidence in the moral purity of his community and ancestors
Show that the traveler is a historian, who knows the village’s past better than any of the people who live in it
Reassure Brown that the journey is safe, since the traveler has been the friend of his family for several generations
Introduce a subplot about Brown’s father, which the author will develop in the later pages of the story
quiz.e: By linking Brown's forebears to violence, the traveler erodes the idea that Puritan society is purely good, pushing Brown toward doubt.

quiz.q: When Brown sees Goody Cloyse, who taught him his catechism, in the forest, he reacts by hiding. The moment is important because:
o: It shows that Brown is brave, since he hides in order to observe what the old woman means to do in the forest
It proves that Goody Cloyse is a witch in fact, since she is seen to speak with the traveler as an intimate friend
It shows the traveler’s kindness to the old woman, whom he helps to travel faster by giving her his staff
It is the climax of the story, since Brown’s discovery of the old woman is the event that decides his later actions
It introduces Faith to the reader, since the old woman speaks of her in the conversation with the traveler
It begins a series of discoveries that the most pious figures in his life are also present at the devil's meeting, intensifying his doubt
quiz.e: Each respected figure Brown sees compounds his fear that virtue is universally false.

quiz.q: Brown cries, "My Faith is gone! ... There is no good on earth; and sin is but a name. Come, devil! for to thee is this world given." The passage most clearly demonstrates:
o: His resolution to resist evil, which he expresses in the language of a man who has overcome his doubt
His decision to return to Faith, which he announces in the hope that she will forgive him for having left her
A sincere conversion to the devil’s cause as a matter of conviction, which he accepts with calm and with resolve
A sudden swing from rigid belief to total cynicism, revealing that his faith was fragile
A comic exaggeration of the despair of a man who has seen very little, and has been frightened by a dream
That Brown is dreaming, since the extravagance of the speech is the mark of a man who is not awake
quiz.e: The absolute swing from piety to despair indicates the shallowness of his faith, which depended on assuming everyone else's goodness.

quiz.q: The devil's address to the converts, "Evil is the nature of mankind," is most useful as a window into the story's theme because it:
o: Proves the story is a sermon, since the devil’s words state a doctrine that the author wishes his readers to accept
States the doctrine of universal human depravity that Brown, and perhaps the Puritan community, has been trying to deny
Shows that the devil is truthful, and so that everything he has told Brown about the village is certainly true
Is Hawthorne’s own statement of belief, which he gives to the devil so that it will be better remembered by the reader
Gives the story a happy ending, since the converts accept the devil’s teaching and are reconciled to one another
Proves that Brown is guilty of the sins that the devil describes, and that he deserves to be counted among the converts
quiz.e: The devil voices the Calvinist idea of innate sinfulness; the story explores the effect of this knowledge, not necessarily its truth.

quiz.q: Hawthorne never confirms whether Brown dreamed the forest meeting. Which reading best explains the effect of this ambiguity?
o: It reveals that Hawthorne could not decide on an ending, and so left the reader to choose between two possibilities
It proves that the events were real, since a dream would have been described as one by a careful narrator
It makes the effect of the experience on Brown more important than whether the events were literally real
It shows that Brown is lying about what he saw in the forest, in order to cover his own wrongdoing
It proves that Faith is guilty, since a narrator who denies the dream must regard the vision as true
It turns the story into a mystery to be solved, so that the reader’s task is to find out what really happened
quiz.e: The consequence for Brown's life is the same either way; the ambiguity shifts attention to the psychological and moral effect.

quiz.q: In the closing paragraphs Brown is described as "a stern, a sad, a darkly meditative, if not a distrustful, soul." The stacking of adjectives with the qualifier "if not" is best described as:
o: A neutral list of traits that the narrator reports without commenting on their effect on Brown’s later life
An escalating series whose final qualification points to the extent of his lasting damage
A comic exaggeration of Brown’s change, which the narrator offers in order to make fun of the village’s gloomy mood
An indirect compliment to Brown, since the adjectives describe qualities that the Puritan community held in high regard
An example of understatement only, since the narrator’s words are weaker than the facts that they are meant to describe
A shift to first-person narration, in which the narrator voices his own judgment of Brown’s character
quiz.e: The sequence intensifies, and "if not a distrustful" suggests a more severe condition than the earlier words.

quiz.q: After the night in the forest, Brown shrinks from the minister's blessing and snatches a child away from Goody Cloyse. These actions primarily show that:
o: He has become a devoted churchgoer, who attends each service with a new seriousness and listens with pleasure to the sermons
His suspicion has isolated him from the community he once trusted
The minister is a harmful man, whose blessing carries a curse that Brown has recognized from his experience in the forest
He has forgiven everyone, and his withdrawal from the villagers is a sign of his humility and his wish to be alone
He has become a leader of the village, and his authority leads him to protect the children from the old woman
He is rewarding the child, whom he regards as the only innocent member of the community he has known
quiz.e: His distrust turns ordinary gestures of piety into occasions of fear, which isolates him.

quiz.q: The statement that "they carved no hopeful verse upon his tombstone, for his dying hour was gloom" contributes to the story's effect by:
o: Providing a happy ending, since the villagers’ choice of an inscription shows how highly they regarded his piety
Revealing that Brown is a hero, whose death is remembered by the village as that of a man of great courage
Establishing that Brown died young, since the absence of a hopeful verse suggests that his life was cut short
Contradicting the rest of the story, since the villagers’ treatment of Brown shows that they never doubted him
Showing that the doubt is lifelong and that the community, though unaware of the cause, perceives it
Providing a comic tone, since the villagers’ refusal to carve a verse is a joke at the expense of a gloomy man
quiz.e: The grim epitaph confirms that his night in the forest shaped his entire life.

quiz.q: The setting of Salem village during the era of witch accusations is most important to the story because:
o: It provides a happy contrast with the forest, so that the reader is made to feel the safety and warmth of the village
It makes the story a documentary of the trials, since the events are drawn from the records of the period
It names the villain, whose identity is revealed by the historical setting and by the details of the time
It explains Faith’s name, since it was common among Puritan women of the period to be called after virtues
It limits the story’s relevance to the past, since the fears it describes belong to a world that has disappeared
It evokes a historical atmosphere of suspicion and hidden guilt that parallels Brown's internal crisis
quiz.e: The Puritan background of fear of secret sin amplifies the story's psychological themes.

quiz.q: Hawthorne's description of the forest path as dark and narrow, with trees closing in, functions chiefly to:
o: Provide a realistic map of the village and the forest, so that the reader can follow Brown on his journey
Show that Brown is lost, since he has strayed from the path and cannot find his way back to the village
Foreshadow rain, which falls in the later part of the story and adds to the gloom of the setting
Externalize Brown's moral wilderness and his growing fear and isolation
Contrast with the light of the village, whose brightness is the symbol of the safety that Brown has left
Introduce a monster, which waits for Brown in the forest and attacks him as he makes his way along the path
quiz.e: The setting reflects the inner state of the character, a hallmark of allegory.

quiz.q: Faith's last words to Brown in the forest scene are "Look up to Heaven, and resist the Wicked One." Which interpretation is best supported?
o: They prove she is a witch, since a woman who speaks in the forest at night must be one of the devil’s servants
Her appeal suggests she may remain faithful at the crucial moment, a possibility that the story deliberately leaves unresolved
They are spoken by Brown, who cries out in the hope that Faith will hear and will come to him
They show that Faith has been taken by the devil, and that her words are a plea for her husband’s help
They prove that the events were real, since a voice in a dream would not be so clearly heard
They mean that Brown has been forgiven for his sins, and that the devil’s power over him has ended
quiz.e: Her last-minute resistance is undercut or confirmed by Brown's morning doubt; Hawthorne leaves it unsettled.

quiz.q: An analysis of the story's structure would most reasonably note that:
o: The story is a series of unrelated incidents, each of which presents a different aspect of the village’s character
The journey into the woods and return to the village forms a descent-and-return pattern in which the hero is not restored
It is told in reverse order, beginning with Brown’s old age and returning step by step to the evening of his departure
It follows a standard romance structure, in which the hero is tested and in the end restored to his place
It begins with the resolution, in which Brown’s doubts are settled, and then turns back to explain how they arose
It is an epistolary story, told through letters that Brown wrote to his wife on the night that he went away
quiz.e: Brown returns, but changed and unable to rejoin the community's trust.

quiz.q: The traveler's remark, "Faith kept me back a while," when Brown explains his lateness, is ironic because:
o: The traveler is surprised by Brown’s lateness, since he had expected Brown to arrive before the time they had agreed
Faith is the traveler’s name, and Brown has used it to show that he knows the identity of the man he is meeting
Brown is lying about the cause of his delay, since the real reason is that he is afraid of the journey
It reveals that Faith is present in the forest, and that she has prevented Brown from keeping his appointment
Brown means his wife's name, while the phrase also suggests that his faith is what delays his entering into evil
It is a clear statement of the story’s theme, which the traveler is able to understand and to explain to Brown
quiz.e: The double meaning of 'Faith' (wife and belief) is a central pun.

quiz.q: Hawthorne's narrator describes the congregation in the forest as including both the respectable and the notorious. This detail most directly emphasizes:
o: That Salem is a pleasant town, whose citizens are respected by their neighbors and live in peace with one another
That Brown is the only good man in the village, who has been invited to the meeting because he is innocent
That the devil is powerless over the righteous, since the congregation has been gathered by force and not by choice
That the ceremony is a trial of the village’s sins, at which the congregation is judged by the devil and the converts
The idea that sin is universal and not limited to obvious sinners
That the community is united in virtue, since respectable and notorious persons stand together in the forest at the meeting
quiz.e: The mixture shows evil as common to all, challenging the notion of a moral dividing line.

quiz.q: Which of the following best describes the role of the minister and Deacon Gookin in the story?
o: They are villains who have planned to lead Brown astray, and who use their reputations for piety to deceive him
They represent the community's respected moral authorities, whose apparent presence at the devil's gathering shakes Brown's trust
They are heroes who attend the meeting in order to discover the devil’s plans and to protect the village
They are comic figures, whose behavior in the forest is meant to amuse the reader and to relieve the story’s gloom
They are narrators, whose reports of the meeting give the reader a second account of what Brown saw in the forest
They are imaginary characters that Brown invents in his dream, and that have no counterpart among the villagers
quiz.e: Their presence turns the symbols of religious authority into symbols of hypocrisy.

quiz.q: In what way does the story's ending most strongly critique Brown's response to what he saw?
o: It shows that he was right about the village, since the people whom he had trusted were found to be hypocrites
It shows that evil is not real, since the forest’s events are only a dream and have no effect on the village
It implies that his rigid assumption of others' perfection made him unable to live with human imperfection
It praises his skepticism, since a man who doubts his neighbors is more careful than one who accepts them
It shows that he was a hero, who had the courage to face the devil and the wisdom to withdraw
It rewards him with wisdom, since the night in the forest taught him a truth that others in the village had not learned
quiz.e: Brown's inability to reconcile belief with human flaws is the story's implied criticism.

quiz.q: The devil is described as bearing a resemblance to Brown himself. This detail most plausibly suggests that:
o: The traveler is Brown’s father, who has returned from the grave to lead his son to the meeting in the forest
The traveler is a relative of Brown’s who has lived in another part of the colony and who has come to visit
Brown is the devil, and the story’s events are an account of what he does under another name in the forest
The evil he confronts is not wholly external but connected to his own nature
Brown is lying about the traveler, whom he has invented to excuse his own conduct in the forest at night
The story is a comedy, since a traveler who looks like Brown is a humorous device and not a serious one
quiz.e: Resemblance hints that temptation is internal; Brown is complicit in the evil he sees.

quiz.q: The narrator confesses that on seeing the house he felt "a sense of insufferable gloom" that he could not explain. This admission is significant because:
o: It establishes the narrator as an emotionally impressionable, possibly unreliable, interpreter of events, shaping how readers view what follows
It proves that the house is haunted, since a feeling of gloom that cannot be explained is the sign of a ghost
It is an objective account of the house’s appearance, which the narrator gives in order to inform the reader accurately
It shows that he is a skeptic, who is able to resist the house’s effect and to judge it with a clear mind
It reveals the house’s owner, whose identity the narrator guesses from the feeling that the building produces in him
It resolves the plot by explaining the cause of the gloom, so that the reader need not wonder what lies behind it
quiz.e: The narrator's subjective reaction colors the entire account and invites readers to question his perception.

quiz.q: Poe describes the house's "vacant eye-like windows" and a barely visible fissure running from roof to foundation. Together these details most likely:
o: Personify the house and foreshadow its collapse while linking it to the Usher family's decay
Provide a realistic description of a ruined house, so that the reader will have an accurate picture of the building’s condition
Contrast with the interior, which is bright and welcoming and so makes the narrator’s first impression seem unfounded
Introduce a comic note, since the house’s appearance is so odd that the narrator is unable to take it seriously
Show that the house is new, since a fissure of such a kind is found in buildings that have recently been constructed
Represent the narrator’s wealth, since only a rich man could have taken such a house for his visit to his friend
quiz.e: The house is figured as a living face and its fissure presages its destruction, mirroring the family's end.

quiz.q: The title's phrase "House of Usher" refers both to a building and to a family line. This double meaning is important because:
o: It is a pun intended to be comic, since the name suits both the house and the family in an unexpected way
It is a mistake that Poe corrects later in the story, when he explains that the family and house are distinct
It means the family is wealthy and respected, since the house bears its name in the manner of a noble line
It suggests that the physical house and the family's bloodline decay together and share a fate
It shows that the house is a hotel, in which the Usher family has lived for several generations
It refers only to the building, since the family has all died and no one remains to bear the name of Usher
quiz.e: The collapse of the house and the extinction of the family are simultaneous.

quiz.q: Roderick Usher's belief in the "sentience of all vegetable things" and the house's stones primarily serves to:
o: Deepen the atmosphere of morbid superstition and suggest the house exerts an influence over its inhabitants
Prove the supernatural is real, since a man who believes that stones can feel must have seen evidence of it
Introduce a scientific theory that Poe took from the writers of his own time and presents without comment
Show that Usher is a botanist, whose studies have led him to believe that plants have feelings like those of animals
Establish a comic tone, since a belief of this kind is absurd and the narrator reports it with amusement
Reveal the narrator’s beliefs, since he shares Usher’s opinion and is persuaded by what he has seen at the house
quiz.e: Usher's belief in the house's life underlines his obsession and fear.

quiz.q: In the poem "The Haunted Palace," the splendid palace is overrun by a "hideous throng." In context, the poem is best read as:
o: A description of Usher’s real home, whose towers and windows the narrator has seen and recognizes in the poem
A comic song that Usher composed to amuse his guest, and whose gloomy imagery is meant to be taken as a joke
A historical ballad that tells how an ancient king lost his palace and his throne to an invading army
A hymn that praises the house and its family, which Usher sings in a moment of pride in his ancestry
An unrelated interlude that gives the narrator a rest from the story’s tension before the climax approaches
An allegory of Usher's mind descending from sanity into madness
quiz.e: The palace corresponds to a head and mind, and the ruin to the loss of reason.

quiz.q: Poe withholds the narrator's name and gives little background about him. The most reasonable effect of this choice is to:
o: Make the narrator a villain, whose silence about himself conceals his part in the disaster that overtakes the house
Focus attention on the atmosphere and on Usher's decline while making the narrator a vehicle for the reader's perceptions
Conceal the plot, so that the reader cannot guess the ending until the narrator has fled from the house
Make the story a comedy, in which an anonymous visitor is the victim of a series of mishaps and misreadings
Suggest that the narrator is dead, and that the account is that of a ghost who recalls his last visit
Replace the narrator with Usher, whose personality is the story’s only real subject and the focus of every scene
quiz.e: An anonymous observer allows readers to experience the unfolding horror directly.

quiz.q: Madeline's illness, described as cataleptic, plays a key role in the plot because:
o: It shows that she is an ordinary invalid, whose weakness is of no importance to the plot or to the story’s theme
It is a comic detail that relieves the story’s gloom, since the narrator regards her condition as a joke
It proves she is a ghost, since a woman who appears to die and then returns cannot be a living person
It symbolizes her wealth, since only a rich family could afford the doctors who attend her in her illness
It makes plausible her premature burial and her eventual return, which brings about the story's climax
It is a symbol of Roderick’s recovery, since her illness grows worse as his own condition becomes better
quiz.e: The catalepsy provides the mechanism for a living burial and return.

quiz.q: When the narrator reads aloud from the romance "Mad Trist," the sounds described in the story are heard from within the house. The narrator's use of this device most directly:
o: Provides comic relief, since the coincidence of the noises in the story and in the house is absurd and amusing
Shows that the narrator has been dreaming, since the sounds he hears are the product of his own half-sleeping mind
Proves that the house is a stage, on which the events of the romance are acted out for the narrator’s benefit
Blurs the boundary between fiction and reality, heightening suspense as the unseen events draw nearer
Resolves the mystery of the house by revealing that the noises are made by a servant who wishes to alarm Usher
Shows that Usher invented the sounds, in order to make the narrator believe that his sister has come back
quiz.e: The synchronous noises make the story-within-the-story appear to enter the narrative, intensifying dread.

quiz.q: Madeline's appearance at the door, bloody and trembling, causing Roderick's death by terror, is an example of:
o: A gothic climax in which long-suppressed fear and guilt finally materialize
A comic reversal, in which the figure of a woman believed dead appears unexpectedly and frightens a man who has been mourning her
A realistic scene, which the narrator describes with the accuracy of a physician who has observed the death of a patient
An anticlimax, in which the story’s tension is released in a quiet moment that brings the narrative to a close
A flashback to an earlier time in the family’s history, which explains the cause of Usher’s fear of his sister
A parody of romance, since the scene imitates the events of the “Mad Trist” in a manner meant to be funny
quiz.e: The scene fulfills the story's atmosphere of terror and guilt.

quiz.q: In the final image, the house splits along the fissure and the tarn closes "over the fragments of the 'House of Usher.'" This conclusion most strongly emphasizes:
o: The narrator’s rescue from the collapsing house, which he escapes in time to see its fall and to tell the story
The simultaneous destruction of the family and its home, closing the story's pattern of decay with finality
The restoration of order after the catastrophe, since the tarn closes over the house and its troubles are ended
The beauty of the tarn, whose dark and still waters reflect the house and give the scene its final image
A comic punishment of the Usher family, whose pride has led them to neglect the building that bears their name
Roderick’s survival, since the narrator sees him escape from the house before the walls fall into the water
quiz.e: The collapse unites symbol and plot, as the House of Usher ends in both senses.

quiz.q: Poe's emphasis on a single, unified emotional effect in the story is best illustrated by:
