o: The consistent use of gloomy setting, diction and imagery from the opening to the final line
The use of multiple narrators, each of whom adds a different view of the house and its inhabitants to the account
A sudden shift to comedy in the middle of the story, which relieves the tension before the climax is reached
A twist ending that is unrelated to the rest of the story and leaves the reader with a final surprise
A variety of settings, which the narrator describes in turn as he travels between the house and the countryside
The use of dialect, which gives the characters’ speech a regional flavor and makes the story seem more realistic
quiz.e: Every detail contributes to a pervasive mood of dread.

quiz.q: The narrator's first-person account of Roderick's behavior most likely invites readers to question:
o: Whether Roderick exists, since the narrator is the only person who has seen him and the house is empty of others
Whether the house exists, since the narrator’s description of it seems more like a dream than a real building
Whether the story is true to history, since the details of the house and family do not match any known record
Whether the tarn is real, since the narrator says that it is black and still and has no visible source
How much of the horror is in Roderick and the narrator's minds rather than in the supernatural
Whether Madeline is a ghost, since the narrator does not see her again after she has been placed in the vault
quiz.e: Subjective narration leaves open the distinction between psychological and supernatural horror.

quiz.q: Which of the following best explains why Usher's artwork and improvised music are described in the story?
o: They show that he is a celebrity in his community, whose paintings and songs are admired by the people of the region
They reveal his extreme sensitivity and nervous temperament, deepening the portrait of his mental state
They are a diversion that Poe includes to relieve the monotony of the narrator’s long stay at the house
They prove the house is haunted, since the pictures and the music are produced by spirits that live within it
They serve as comic relief, since the pictures are strange and the music is so odd that it amuses the narrator
They are used to solve a puzzle, since the narrator finds in them a clue to the cause of Madeline’s illness
quiz.e: His morbid art and music reflect his fragile psyche.

quiz.q: The comparison of the house's appearance to a decayed structure whose "minute fungi overspread the whole exterior" suggests:
o: That the house was recently built, since fungus appears on new timber before it has been seasoned and painted
That the house is clean and well kept, since the narrator notices no sign of damage when he first looks at it
That nature is benevolent, since the fungi spread over the house like a covering and protect its walls from the weather
That the house is a hospital, since the narrator compares its condition to that of a building where sick people stay
That the narrator is wealthy, since he is able to observe the house’s condition without being troubled by its cost
That outward appearance hides slow internal rot, paralleling the family's condition
quiz.e: Surface integrity masks deep decay, a motif in the story.

quiz.q: Keats opens the poem with the bitter cold, the owl and the hare, and the Beadsman's numb fingers and frosted breath. This opening most plausibly serves to:
o: Introduce a comic subplot about the Beadsman, whose cold hands and breath amuse the reader before the main story begins
Describe the poem’s climax, in which the lovers escape from the castle into the cold of the winter night
Establish a setting of austere cold and piety that will contrast with the warmth and sensuous richness of Madeline's chamber
Introduce Porphyro, whose journey through the cold to the castle is the subject of the stanzas that open the poem
Demonstrate Keats’s disdain for religion, since the Beadsman’s devotion is shown to be cold and useless to him
Provide a realistic weather report, so that the reader will know the season and the conditions at the time of the poem
quiz.e: The chilly, ascetic opening sets up a contrast with the warm, sensuous interior that follows.

quiz.q: The Spenserian stanza that Keats uses has nine lines, with eight iambic pentameter lines followed by a longer final line. The effect of the longer last line is most likely to:
o: Create a sense of closure and a slower, weightier cadence at the end of each stanza
Introduce a comic note at the end of each stanza, so that the poem’s serious subjects are relieved by a touch of wit
Break the pattern of rhyme, so that the reader is made to notice the final line as an exception to the rest
Create the impression of speech, since the last line is longer and so more like the rhythm of a person talking
Make the poem seem unfinished, since the extra length of the line leaves the stanza without a firm conclusion
Reduce the stanza’s musicality, since a longer line is harder to read aloud and breaks the rhythm of the verse
quiz.e: The extended final line (an alexandrine) provides a concluding sweep.

quiz.q: In the lines describing the Beadsman's frosted breath, "Like pious incense from a censer old, / Seem'd taking flight for heaven," the simile achieves which of the following?
o: It uses the visible breath to merge the physical cold with the religious ritual, elevating a mundane detail
It insults the Beadsman by comparing his breath to smoke, and so suggests that his prayers are empty and false
It describes a literal fire that the Beadsman has lit in the chapel, and by whose light he is able to pray
It anticipates the lovers’ escape, since the breath that seems to fly toward heaven foretells their flight
It is a comic exaggeration, since the Beadsman’s breath cannot be compared with the smoke of incense in any serious way
It serves as a transition to Madeline, since the incense moves toward the castle and the room where she lies
quiz.e: The breath becomes incense, joining sensory observation with spiritual imagery.

quiz.q: The legend of St. Agnes' Eve, in which a maiden who performs certain rituals will dream of her lover, matters to the poem's plot because:
o: It is mentioned only in passing, and has no real connection with the plot or the characters’ later behavior
It makes the poem a religious poem, whose chief purpose is to celebrate the saint and the rites of her festival
It condemns Madeline for her superstition, and the poem suggests that her faith in the legend has led her astray
It motivates Madeline's actions and makes possible Porphyro's plan to enter her chamber
It describes Porphyro’s origin, since he is a descendant of the family that first established the festival
It explains the family feud, since the legend tells how the two houses came to be enemies in earlier times
quiz.e: Madeline's belief in the ritual keeps her from seeing Porphyro as real, enabling the plot.

quiz.q: Porphyro's preparing a lavish feast of delicacies beside Madeline's bed is described in rich sensory detail. The most likely purpose of this lavish description is:
o: To satirize luxury, since the feast is an excess that Keats presents as foolish and unsuited to the lovers’ situation
To provide recipe details that will interest the reader, who may wish to prepare the dishes that are described
To introduce a villain, since the preparation of so large a feast suggests that Porphyro has plans to deceive her
To heighten the poem's sensuous, romantic atmosphere and contrast the warmth of love with the cold outside
To show that Porphyro is wealthy, since the quantity and variety of the food are signs of his rank and his means
To advance a legal argument, since the feast is offered as evidence that Porphyro has the right to enter the room
quiz.e: Keats's sensuous imagery is central to the poem's Romantic mood.

quiz.q: Which of the following best describes the relationship between the lovers' families in the poem?
o: A close alliance, in which the two families have been united for many years and their children are expected to marry
An arranged marriage, which has been planned by the lovers’ parents and which the lovers have accepted without objection
Madeline’s family is unknown to Porphyro, who has never met her relatives and has no knowledge of their wishes
Porphyro is Madeline’s brother, and the secrecy of his visit is due to the nature of their family’s history
They are rivals in business, and their quarrel concerns the rights of trade rather than any difference of feeling
A feud that makes their love dangerous and requires secrecy
quiz.e: The family hostility raises the stakes of Porphyro's presence.

quiz.q: The poem ends with the lovers fleeing into a storm and then returns to the Beadsman and Angela, both of whom die. What is the likely effect of returning to them at the end?
o: It provides a comic coda, in which the deaths of the two old people are treated as a joke after the lovers’ flight
It shows that Madeline has died, since the poem’s last lines announce the end of her life and of her story
It reintroduces the cold, ascetic world of the opening, framing the lovers' escape in a contrast of youth and age, warmth and death
It reveals that Porphyro is the Beadsman’s son, who has come back to the castle after many years of absence
It suggests that the poem is a dream, since the return to the first scene shows that the story has ended
It introduces new characters, whose arrival at the castle prepares the reader for a sequel to the lovers’ story
quiz.e: The frame returns to the opening's cold piety, reinforcing contrast and transience.

quiz.q: In the poem, Madeline's reaction on waking to find Porphyro present, is best described as:
o: Anger at Porphyro, whom she accuses of having entered her room without permission and of having broken her sleep
Indifference, since she regards the visit as a part of her dream and takes no notice of what he says
Terror and flight, since she is alarmed by a stranger’s presence and runs from the chamber in order to call for help
Recognition and rejection, since she knows him as the enemy of her family and will not accept his love
A mixture of confusion and tenderness, in which she compares the real lover to the dream
Amusement at his scheme, which she finds so absurd that she cannot take it seriously or respond with any feeling
quiz.e: She is dismayed that the dream has faded but accepts the real Porphyro.

quiz.q: Which poetic device is most responsible for the poem's sense of richness and sensuous warmth?
o: Vivid sensory imagery appealing to sight, taste, smell and touch
Satire, which exposes the faults of the characters and shows the reader how the poem’s society ought to be reformed
Irony, in which the speaker says one thing and means another in order to show how the lovers’ plan has failed
Understatement, in which the speaker’s restraint allows the reader to feel the scene’s emotion without being told of it
Colloquial diction, which brings the speech of ordinary people into the poem and gives it a natural and easy flow
A repeated refrain, which returns at the end of each stanza and gives the poem its rhythm and its mood
quiz.e: Keats's imagery is lush and sensory throughout.

quiz.q: As a Romantic poem, "The Eve of St. Agnes" most clearly reflects which of the following Romantic values?
o: Strict adherence to reason, which governs the lovers’ conduct and ensures that their plan is carried out with prudence
Emotion, imagination and the intensity of individual experience
Public duty, which the lovers place above their private feelings and which leads them to leave the castle
Satire of social customs, since the poem exposes the follies of a society that has made the lovers enemies
Simplicity of diction only, since Romantic poets avoided ornament and used the plain language of ordinary speech
Faith in industrial progress, since the poem celebrates the new age and its power to improve human life
quiz.e: Romanticism privileges feeling and imagination.

quiz.q: Both Hawthorne's "Young Goodman Brown" and Poe's "The Fall of the House of Usher" leave readers uncertain about whether the horror is supernatural or psychological. Which statement best explains how each author achieves this ambiguity?
o: Both authors state outright that the events were imaginary, and each uses the dream to explain what has happened
Both use omniscient narrators who explain the events, so that the reader knows exactly what has occurred in each story
Both rely on comic exaggeration, so that the horror in each tale is softened and the reader is not frightened
Both resolve the uncertainty in the final paragraph, where a character explains that the cause was natural
Hawthorne never confirms the forest events were real, while Poe filters events through a narrator whose perceptions are colored by dread
Neither author uses symbolism, since the stories’ effects depend on plain narration and on the order of the events
quiz.e: Hawthorne's open question ("Had Goodman Brown fallen asleep...?") and Poe's subjective first-person narrator each preserve the ambiguity by different means.

quiz.q: Which pairing best contrasts the narrative frames of "Rip Van Winkle" and "Baker's Bluejay Yarn"?
o: Both are told in the third person by Rip and the miner, who describe the events they have seen in plain speech
Irving’s frame is a letter and Twain’s is a diary, and each of them is presented as the writer’s private record
Irving's frame is a mock-scholarly historian's papers, while Twain's is a character's oral tale told in dialect
Both stories are narrated by their main characters, who describe what happened to them in a manner that is meant to amuse
Irving’s narrator is Rip himself, and Twain’s is a jay who recounts the events in the speech of the frontier
Neither story uses a frame, since each begins directly with the events and ends with the end of the action
quiz.e: Both stories use storytellers, but Irving's persona is a pedantic historian and Twain's is Jim Baker, a talker in dialect.

quiz.q: Which of the following texts relies most heavily on dialect to establish the voice and characterization of its narrator?
o: "The Eve of St. Agnes"
"The Fall of the House of Usher"
"Baker's Bluejay Yarn"
"Young Goodman Brown"
"Rip Van Winkle" in its frame narration
The Haunted Palace
quiz.e: Twain's Jim Baker speaks in a Western dialect that supports the oral tall-tale tradition.

quiz.q: Hawthorne, Poe and Irving all use setting to reinforce theme. Which pairing correctly matches setting to function?
o: Hawthorne’s village is comic; Poe’s tarn is cheerful; Irving’s mountains are a realistic part of the setting
All three settings are neutral backdrops that serve to identify the place of the action and have no further purpose
Hawthorne’s forest symbolizes industry; Poe’s house, wealth; and Irving’s mountains, the freedom of the new republic
Irving’s mountains symbolize wealth; Hawthorne’s forest, the frontier; and Poe’s house, the pride of a noble family
Poe’s house is a real historical site that Poe visited, and the details of its description are drawn from life
Hawthorne's dark forest externalizes moral doubt; Poe's decaying house mirrors a family's ruin; Irving's mountains create a folkloric otherworld
quiz.e: Each author's setting is symbolic or atmospheric, extending the story's meaning.

quiz.q: Compare the endings of "Rip Van Winkle" and "Young Goodman Brown." Which statement is most accurate?
o: Rip is reintegrated into a community that values his stories, while Brown is permanently alienated by what he believes he has learned
Both endings are happy, since each protagonist is restored to the community and to the people who had known him
Both protagonists die, and the villagers remember each of them with respect and with a sense of loss
Both end with a return to the forest, where the hero finds the peace that he had been unable to find at home
Rip is exiled while Brown is welcomed, since the village rejects the one and gives the other a place of honor
Both end with the revelation that the events were a dream, and that the heroes have lost nothing by their journeys
quiz.e: Irving's ending is gently comic and restorative, whereas Hawthorne's is bleak and isolating.

quiz.q: Which of the following best explains why Keats's poem is often paired with the prose works in this unit as an example of Romanticism?
o: It is a historical novel, set in a medieval castle and based on events recorded in the chronicles of the period
It is a satire in prose, in which the vices of the aristocracy are exposed in an elaborate and comic allegory
It shares with them an interest in imagination, atmosphere and intense experience, though in verse form
It was written by the same author as “Usher,” and the two works are by a single hand and share its style
It is a realistic account of an American town, whose people are described with care and with attention to detail
It is a hymn, intended to be sung in churches on St. Agnes’ Eve in memory of the saint
quiz.e: The unit connects Romantic and Gothic works that foreground imagination, mood and heightened feeling.

quiz.q: In which of the following ways do the narrators of "The Fall of the House of Usher" and "Rip Van Winkle" differ most significantly in their reliability and function?
o: Poe's narrator is a participant whose emotional perceptions shape the account; Irving's is an amused, self-conscious historian who comments on events from a distance
Both are unreliable first-person narrators, whose accounts are shaped by their fears and by their desire to be believed
Both are objective and scientific observers, who report the events in the order that they occurred and without comment
Irving’s narrator is a participant in the story, and Poe’s is a distant historian who comments on the events
Both narrators are the stories’ main characters, Rip and Usher, who describe their own experiences in the first person
Neither narrator comments on the events, since both are content to describe what happens and to let the reader judge
quiz.e: Poe's narrator is immersed in the events, while Irving's is a comic storyteller who stands outside them.

quiz.q: A student argues that all five texts in the unit deal with the tension between appearance and reality. Which choice offers the best textual support for this claim across at least three texts?
o: Brown's discovery behind the pious facade, the cracks in Usher's seemingly solid house, and Keats's contrast between ascetic piety and sensuous warmth
The cold weather in three of the texts, which the authors describe in similar terms and which affects their characters
The use of first-person narration in three texts, which allows the narrators to describe things as they seem to them
The mention of animals in three texts, which are shown to behave in ways that differ from what one would expect
The presence of a female character in three texts, each of whom is found in the end to be other than she seemed
Three texts that have the word “house” in the title or in the first paragraph and describe it in detail
quiz.e: Each cited example shows a surface that conceals something different beneath.

quiz.q: Which of the following best describes the different uses of irony in "Rip Van Winkle" and "Young Goodman Brown"?
o: Both authors use irony only at the very end, where the endings turn the meaning of the earlier events upside down
Irving's irony is gentle and comic, arising from Rip's obliviousness; Hawthorne's irony is darker, as in the name Faith and the 'virtue' of the community
Neither uses irony, since the authors’ concern is to describe events and not to make the reader see them differently
Irving’s irony is bitter and Hawthorne’s is playful, since each writer adopts a tone that suits his subject
Both use irony only in dialogue, where the characters say the opposite of what they mean to the people they address
Both use irony as a minor device, which is of less importance in each story than the plot and the setting
quiz.e: The tone of the irony differs: Irving's is comic and Hawthorne's is moral and bleak.

quiz.q: Which of the following would best support the claim that Poe's "House of Usher" prioritizes mood over plot?
o: The story contains no dialogue between the characters, since the narrator’s account is made up entirely of description
The story is told in the third person, which allows the reader to know what each character is thinking and feeling
The story has multiple settings, which the narrator describes in turn as he moves from place to place
The plot has many twists, each of which surprises the reader and leaves the story’s outcome in doubt
The narrator changes in the middle of the story, so that the reader sees the events from two different points
Extended descriptions of the setting and Usher's behavior precede the minimal action that makes up the climax
quiz.e: Atmosphere is built through lengthy description before a brief, intense climax.

quiz.q: Which of the following is the best example of personification in the unit's texts?
o: Irving’s description of Rip as lazy and goodhearted, a man who would do anything for others but his own work
Hawthorne’s description of the village as small and quiet, with a single street and a meetinghouse at its center
Poe's description of the house's "vacant eye-like windows"
Keats’s mention of the moon shining through a window, which casts a pale light upon the floor of Madeline’s chamber
Twain’s mention of miners who have left the cabin empty and gone elsewhere in search of a better claim
Hawthorne’s description of the minister as a man of grave bearing, whose sermons are known to the whole village
quiz.e: Giving a house eyes is personification.

quiz.q: In the context of the unit, which choice best describes a Gothic element shared by Hawthorne's and Poe's stories?
o: A brooding atmosphere in which hidden guilt and dread overshadow ordinary reality
A comic reversal in which a frightening event proves to have a harmless and amusing explanation at the end of the tale
A happy ending in which the central characters are reconciled to their families and restored to their former lives
An epistolary structure in which the events are revealed through letters, diaries and other private documents
A rural setting with farm animals and cheerful villagers, which stands in contrast to the story’s darker events
A focus on political reform, in which the characters’ private troubles are the result of the failures of government
quiz.e: Both use dark settings and psychological terror.

quiz.q: If a student wanted to show how an author uses a symbol to develop theme, which pairing would be strongest?
o: Irving’s mention of a dog and a barn, which appear in the opening paragraphs and recur in the story’s ending
Hawthorne's pink ribbon and the question of Faith's integrity
Poe’s mention of a candle and a table, which appear in the narrator’s first view of Usher’s room
Keats’s mention of the weather and a shoe, which appear in the stanzas that describe the lovers’ flight
Twain’s mention of a pitcher and a gate, which appear in the narrator’s opening account of Baker’s cabin
Hawthorne’s mention of a stream and a tree, which appear in the forest’s landscape as Brown goes along the path
quiz.e: The ribbon is a recurring object whose meaning is central to the theme of faith and doubt.

quiz.q: Which statement best distinguishes Twain's use of humor from Irving's?
o: Twain’s humor is gentle and affectionate, whereas Irving’s is harsh and aimed at the weaknesses of the people he describes
Neither writer is humorous, since each treats his subject with a gravity that the reader is meant to respect
Twain’s humor is based on rhyme and verse, while Irving’s depends on the sound of the names of his characters
Irving’s humor is based on puns only, while Twain’s depends on the situations in which his characters are placed
They use identical techniques, since each combines dialect, exaggeration and a sober manner to amuse the reader
Twain's humor arises from deadpan exaggeration in a dialect voice, whereas Irving's arises from mock-formal diction and gentle irony
quiz.e: Voice and diction differ: oral deadpan versus mock-scholarly irony.

quiz.q: Which of these claims about narrative point of view across the unit is most accurate?
o: The unit includes a framed omniscient historian, an anonymous first-person observer, a limited third-person view, and a character narrator
All texts use first-person narration, in which a participant tells of the events and offers a view of their meaning
All texts use a third-person omniscient narrator who knows what each character thinks and explains it to the reader
All texts are told by their protagonists, who describe their own experiences and are the only authorities for what occurred
None of the texts uses a frame, since each begins with the story itself and ends when the action has ended
Only the poem has a narrator, since the prose texts present events directly and without any voice to tell them
quiz.e: The works use varied perspectives: Irving's frame, Poe's first person, Hawthorne's limited third, Twain's character narrator.

quiz.q: What do Brown's and Rip's returns to their villages have in common?
o: Both return to find their wives alive and waiting, so that each is able to take up his earlier life without change
Both return as heroes whose absence has given them a new authority among the people who had known them
Both return to find their villages unchanged, so that each is struck by how little time has passed in his absence
Both regret leaving their homes, and each resolves never again to go away from the village or from his family
Each returns changed in a way that alters his relationship to a community that did not experience the same event
Both are accused of a crime by the villagers, and each must prove his innocence before the town is satisfied
quiz.e: Both protagonists return after an extraordinary experience; their relationship to the community has been altered.

quiz.q: Which of the following best describes the thematic role of the supernatural in "Rip Van Winkle" compared with "Young Goodman Brown"?
o: In both it is purely comic, since each author uses the supernatural to amuse the reader and to make light of fear
In both it is realistic, since the events are given natural explanations at the end and the characters are not deceived
In Irving it is a folkloric device that makes comic social commentary possible; in Hawthorne it is a vehicle for moral and psychological exploration
In Irving it is tragic, since Rip’s sleep costs him his family, while in Hawthorne it is a source of comedy
In Hawthorne it is a minor detail, which gives the story its setting but has no bearing on Brown’s conduct
In neither does it matter, since the stories’ themes would be the same if no supernatural event had occurred
quiz.e: The supernatural functions differently: whimsy versus moral allegory.

quiz.q: In both "The Haunted Palace" and "The Eve of St. Agnes," the poems rely on imagery that appeals to the senses. How does the effect of that imagery differ?
o: Both produce horror, since each poem moves from beauty to fear and leaves the reader with a sense of dread
The Haunted Palace's imagery turns from splendor to horror as an allegory of mental decay, while St. Agnes's imagery builds warmth and sensuous richness
Both produce comedy, since the imagery in each is so extravagant that it cannot be taken seriously by a reader
“St. Agnes” is a satire, in which sensuous imagery is used to mock the lovers and their belief in the legend
“The Haunted Palace” is a lullaby, whose imagery of gold and music is meant to soothe the narrator to sleep
They use no imagery, since each poem relies on abstract statements and on the rhythm of its lines for its effect
quiz.e: Poe's poem charts a decline; Keats's builds romantic abundance.

quiz.q: Across the unit, which choice best identifies a shared concern about human nature?
o: That human beings are always rational, and that their conduct can be explained by the reasons that they give for it
That human beings are always good, and that their faults are the result of the conditions in which they live
That human beings struggle to reconcile ideals with the imperfections of themselves and others
That human beings are free from conflict, since each text shows how a quiet and orderly life may be maintained
That nature is hostile to human beings, who are punished in each text for their attempts to master it
That technology improves society, and that each text shows how the new age has made life better than the old
quiz.e: Brown's loss of trust, Usher's fear, Rip's evasions and the lovers' risk all involve gaps between ideal and real.

quiz.q: A student writes that Hawthorne's story is a critique of Puritan society and not just a story of individual doubt. Which detail most strongly supports the student's claim?
o: The brief mention of a child whom Brown snatches from Goody Cloyse and whom he regards as the only innocent person
The mention of a staff that resembles a serpent, which is carried by the traveler and given to the old woman
The forest’s darkness, which Hawthorne describes in detail and which frightens Brown as he goes along the path
The use of the word “Faith” as a name, which gives the story a second meaning and unites its themes
The return of Brown to his village, where he is shown to be a stern and gloomy man for the rest of his life
The presence of respected church leaders at the devil's gathering and the traveler's references to violent acts by the community's forebears
quiz.e: The implication that the community's pillars are complicit in evil shifts the focus to the society.

quiz.q: In “Rip Van Winkle,” Dame Van Winkle is repeatedly described as a “termagant.” In context, the word most closely means
o: A thrifty and careful housekeeper
A woman of great wealth and rank
A fearful woman who avoids all conflict
A violent, overbearing, quarrelsome woman
A traveling seller of household goods
A woman skilled in folk medicine
quiz.e: The narrator uses termagant (with virago) for her scolding, domineering temper.

quiz.q: “The opinions of this junto were completely controlled by Nicholas Vedder.” In “Rip Van Winkle,” the word “junto” most closely means
o: A single powerful landowner whose authority extends over the whole village and whose word is accepted as law
A noisy annual festival at which the villagers gather to sing, to dance and to drink in the inn’s yard
A small group joined together for a common purpose
A court that settles village disputes by hearing both parties and by reaching a judgment in accordance with custom
A traveling troupe of actors who entertain the villagers with plays on their way through the Hudson Valley
A line of soldiers on parade who march through the village on the days when the militia is called out
quiz.e: The village sages at the inn form a small clique that gathers to talk politics.

quiz.q: The inn’s sign is described as “a rubicund portrait of His Majesty George the Third.” The word “rubicund” most closely means
o: Pale and thin
Newly painted
Cracked and faded
Ruddy or reddish
Golden and grand
Stern and unsmiling
quiz.e: Rubicund describes a ruddy, reddish complexion.

quiz.q: Irving writes that men “under the discipline of shrews at home” are apt to be “obsequious and conciliating abroad.” The word “obsequious” most closely means
o: Openly rebellious
Physically weak
Cleverly cruel
Overly eager to please
Suspicious of strangers
Careless with money
quiz.e: The point is that henpecked men behave in a servile, people-pleasing way in public.

quiz.q: Rip’s “patrimonial estate had dwindled away.” The word “patrimonial” most closely means
o: Recently purchased by the owner, who paid for the land with the savings of his earlier years in the village
Owned by the village as a whole, and used by the farmers for grazing their cattle and for cutting wood
Inherited from one’s father or ancestors
Held in common by neighbors who divide the produce of the land among them at the end of each season
Taxed by the crown at a rate that the owner could not meet, and so reduced by the sale of its parts
Mortgaged to a merchant in the town, who has taken the land in payment for the debts that Rip has incurred
quiz.e: Patrimonial refers to what is inherited from a father; his inherited land has shrunk through neglect.

quiz.q: Rip has an “insuperable aversion to all kinds of profitable labor.” The word “insuperable” most closely means
o: Slightly noticeable
Newly developed
Entirely hidden
Pleasantly mild
Impossible to overcome
Easily corrected
quiz.e: An insuperable aversion cannot be overcome.

quiz.q: In “Young Goodman Brown,” Goody Cloyse says, “Ah, forsooth, and is it your worship indeed?” The word “forsooth” most closely means
o: Forgive me
Truly or in truth
Before noon
At last
Gently
Without doubt a sin
quiz.e: Forsooth is an archaic intensifier meaning “in truth.”

quiz.q: In “The Fall of the House of Usher,” the house stands beside a “tarn.” The word “tarn” most closely means
o: A narrow stream
A small mountain lake
A stone wall
A walled garden
A marshy field
An underground cellar
quiz.e: A tarn is a small lake, here a black, still one beside the house.

quiz.q: In “The Eve of St. Agnes,” the “Beadsman” is introduced counting his rosary in the cold chapel. The word “Beadsman” most closely means
o: A man paid to pray for others, using prayer beads
A seller of jewelry who travels from castle to castle with a stock of beads, rings and ornaments for sale
A servant who guards the castle’s gate and keeps watch over the lord’s guests when they arrive for the feast
A soldier loyal to a noble family, who carries a rosary of beads in order to protect himself in battle
A traveling minstrel who plays and sings at festivals, and who is paid in gifts of food and drink
A monk who has left his order and now lives by begging, and who is known in the neighborhood for his poverty
quiz.e: A beadsman prays for the souls of his patrons and tells his beads.

quiz.q: In “The Eve of St. Agnes,” the Beadsman’s breath is “Like pious incense from a censer old.” The word “censer” most closely means
o: A person who judges others harshly, and who is known for his willingness to criticize the faults of his neighbors
A heavy chain by which a lamp or a lantern is hung in the roof of a church or in the hall of a castle
A small bell rung during the service to mark the moments of the ritual and to call the people to prayer
A prayer book carried by the priest, who reads from it at the altar during the celebration of the mass
A container in which incense is burned
A candle stand that holds the lights burning before the saint’s image in the chapel on the evening of her feast
quiz.e: A censer swings and holds burning incense in religious ritual.

quiz.q: In “Rip Van Winkle,” which word from the story is best defined as “inherited from one’s father”?
o: Rubicund
Obsequious
Insuperable
Conciliating
Peevish
Patrimonial
quiz.e: Patrimonial refers to paternal inheritance.

quiz.q: Identify the speaker of: “I am a poor quiet man, a native of the place, and a loyal subject of the King, God bless him!”
o: Nicholas Vedder
Peter Vanderdonk
Judith Gardenier
The stranger with the keg
Rip Van Winkle
Diedrich Knickerbocker
quiz.e: Rip says this in the village after his sleep, not knowing that a king no longer rules.

quiz.q: To whom is Rip speaking when he says, “I am a poor quiet man, a native of the place, and a loyal subject of the King, God bless him!”
o: The crowd of villagers who have surrounded and questioned him
His daughter Judith, who stands near him in the crowd and has asked him who he is and where he has come from
The innkeeper alone, who has come out of the tavern and demands to know what sort of person he is
The ghostly crew of the ninepins players, whom he meets again as he returns to the mountain and tells his story
The historian Peter Vanderdonk, to whom he has gone for advice about how to prove his identity to the village
His dog Wolf, which has followed him into the village and which he addresses in a gentle and bewildered tone
quiz.e: He is answering the hostile townspeople who ask which party he supports.

quiz.q: Identify the speaker of: “Faith kept me back a while.”
o: Goodman Brown
The devil
Deacon Gookin
The minister
Goody Cloyse
Faith
quiz.e: Brown explains his lateness to the traveler; the line puns on his wife’s name.

quiz.q: Identify the speaker of: “Ah, forsooth, and is it your worship indeed?”
o: Faith
Goodman Brown
The minister
Goody Cloyse
Deacon Gookin
The devil
quiz.e: Goody Cloyse greets the traveler as though recognizing a respected acquaintance.

quiz.q: Identify the speaker of: “Come, devil! for to thee is this world given.”
o: The traveler
Faith
Goodman Brown
Deacon Gookin
Goody Cloyse
The minister
quiz.e: Brown cries this out in despair after he thinks Faith is lost.

quiz.q: Identify the speaker of: “Madman! I tell you that she now stands without the door!”
o: The narrator
Roderick Usher
Madeline
A servant of the house
The physician
Sir Launcelot Canning
quiz.e: Usher shrieks this to the narrator as the sounds from the romance seem to come true.

quiz.q: In “Rip Van Winkle,” what does Rip carry up the mountain for the stranger he meets?
o: A bundle of firewood
A stack of ninepins
A sack of acorns
A fowling piece
A lantern
A keg
quiz.e: The stranger in antique Dutch dress asks Rip to help him carry a keg of liquor.

quiz.q: In “Rip Van Winkle,” what are the odd figures in the mountain hollow doing when Rip first sees them?
o: Drinking and singing
Digging for treasure
Praying around a fire
Dancing in a circle
Playing ninepins in silence
Arguing about politics
quiz.e: They play ninepins without speaking; the only sound is the rolling balls, like distant thunder.

quiz.q: In “Rip Van Winkle,” who is the village historian who recognizes the legend of the mountain?
o: Nicholas Vedder
Derrick Van Bummel
Brom Dutcher
Diedrich Knickerbocker
Jan Gardenier
Peter Vanderdonk
quiz.e: Peter Vanderdonk, the oldest inhabitant, tells that Hendrick Hudson’s crew returns every twenty years.

quiz.q: In “Rip Van Winkle,” whom does Rip recognize first in the changed village as a family member?
o: His son Rip Jr., who looks exactly like him as he was in youth and who is lounging against a tree
His wife, who is still living and who greets him with the same scolding that he had heard when he left
His friend Nicholas Vedder, who is seated before the inn and who recognizes him by his old manner of speaking
His brother, who keeps the inn and who has been waiting for him since the morning he failed to return
His neighbor Brom Dutcher, who calls out to him from the road and asks where he has been for so long
His grown daughter, Judith Gardenier, carrying a child
quiz.e: Judith Gardenier, now married with a baby, welcomes her father home.

quiz.q: In “Young Goodman Brown,” what does Faith wear in her cap that Brown later sees fall from the sky?
o: A silver cross
A white veil
A blue shawl
A gold locket
Pink ribbons
A green wreath
quiz.e: The pink ribbon floating down convinces Brown that Faith has gone to the forest meeting.

quiz.q: In “Young Goodman Brown,” what does the traveler give to Goody Cloyse that makes her suddenly vanish?
o: His staff
A letter
A bottle
A cloak
A ring
A coin
quiz.e: She seizes the staff, which looks like a snake, and flies away on it.

quiz.q: In “Young Goodman Brown,” the traveler claims to have known Brown’s father and grandfather. Which of the following does he say Brown’s ancestors did?
o: Fought against the Indians as soldiers
Signed the Declaration of Independence
Served as ministers of Salem village
Built the village meetinghouse
Helped persecute Quakers
Sailed from England on the Mayflower
quiz.e: The traveler says Brown’s grandfather helped scourge a Quaker woman and his father burned an Indian village.

quiz.q: In “Young Goodman Brown,” what is Brown’s state of mind when he returns to Salem village the next morning?
o: Relieved and cheerful, since the night has shown him that the village is safe and that his fears were groundless
Certain it was only a dream, and glad to put the events of the night out of his mind and take up his life
Eager to confess to the minister what he has seen, and to ask his advice on how he should regard it
Determined to leave the village forever, since he has concluded that no honest man can live among such people
Suspicious and recoiling from the people he meets
Joyful at seeing his wife, whom he greets with a warm embrace and with a promise that he will not leave her
quiz.e: He shrinks from the minister, Goody Cloyse and Faith, as if they all were part of the forest meeting.

quiz.q: In “The Fall of the House of Usher,” what does the narrator read to Roderick Usher during the storm?
o: A romance called the “Mad Trist”
A poem by Roderick himself
A medical text about catalepsy
A letter from Madeline
A prayer book
A history of the Usher family
quiz.e: The narrator reads the “Mad Trist” of Sir Launcelot Canning, whose sounds seem to match noises in the house.

quiz.q: In “The Fall of the House of Usher,” why do Usher and the narrator place Madeline in the vault?
o: They want to hide a murder, and the vault is a place where the body will not be found by the servants
The family tradition requires burial inside the house, and the vault is where all the Ushers have been placed
They believe she has died and wish to keep her body for a time
The physician has recommended it, for he believes that the cool air of the vault will protect the body from decay
They plan to move her to another house for burial, and the vault is a temporary place of rest on the way
Roderick wants to prove his theory of the sentience of the house by placing his sister within its stones
quiz.e: Madeline suffers from catalepsy and appears dead; Usher wants to entomb her temporarily in the vault.

quiz.q: In “The Fall of the House of Usher,” what happens to the house at the end?
o: It burns to the ground
It splits and sinks into the tarn
It is abandoned and left empty
It is sold to a distant relative
It collapses in the storm but is rebuilt
It becomes a hospital
quiz.e: The narrator flees and watches the fissure widen until the house falls into the tarn.

quiz.q: In “The Eve of St. Agnes,” what does Porphyro bring into Madeline’s chamber?
o: A gift of jewels
A feast of delicacies
A letter from her father
A love potion
A lute only
Warm clothing
quiz.e: He sets out a banquet of fruits, sweets and wine while she sleeps.

quiz.q: In “The Eve of St. Agnes,” what is Angela’s role in Porphyro’s plan?
o: She warns the Baron of his arrival, and so brings about the discovery that the lovers must flee from the castle
She tries to marry Madeline to a rival of Porphyro’s, whom she regards as a more suitable husband for the girl
She hides Madeline in the chapel, where the lovers are afterward united in the presence of the Beadsman
She leads him secretly to Madeline’s chamber
She poisons the guests at the feast, in order to give Porphyro a chance to enter the castle unobserved
She declares him a trespasser and calls the servants, who drive him from the castle before he can speak to her
quiz.e: Angela, the old nurse, reluctantly helps him hide near Madeline’s room.

quiz.q: In “The Eve of St. Agnes,” the legend says that a maiden who goes to bed without supper will
o: See her future husband in a dream
Receive a gift from the saint
Hear the voice of her mother
Be protected from illness
Wake with the gift of prophecy
Meet her enemy in a vision
quiz.e: Maidens hope to dream of their lover on St. Agnes’ Eve.

quiz.q: In “The Eve of St. Agnes,” what do Madeline and Porphyro do at the end of the poem?
o: They marry in the chapel
They are discovered and punished
They stay in the castle
They flee into the stormy night
They return to Porphyro’s castle by daylight
They part forever
quiz.e: They slip past the sleeping revelers and out into the storm.

quiz.q: In “Baker’s Bluejay Yarn,” who tells the story of the jay and the cabin?
o: Mark Twain’s narrator’s mother
A traveling preacher
Jim Baker
The jay himself
A schoolmaster
Tom Sawyer
quiz.e: Jim Baker, a California miner, tells the narrator about jays.

quiz.q: In “Baker’s Bluejay Yarn,” what does the jay try to fill with acorns?
o: A hollow log that stands at the edge of the clearing, and into which the jay drops the acorns one by one
A hole in the roof of an empty cabin
A rain barrel behind the cabin, which the jay believes is the storehouse where the miner keeps his supplies
A nest in the branches of a pine, which the jay has built for the winter and which he wishes to stock
A well near the cabin, whose depth the jay is unable to judge from the edge, and which swallows each acorn
A mine shaft on the hillside, which opens into a chamber that is too large for the jay’s acorns to fill
quiz.e: The jay drops acorns into the hole in the roof, but the acorns disappear into the empty cabin.

quiz.q: In “Baker’s Bluejay Yarn,” why do the other jays come to look at the hole?
o: They want to nest in the cabin, and they have come to see whether the hole is large enough for their use
They have heard of the first jay’s odd task
They hope to steal acorns that the first jay has gathered, and they gather round the hole to see where they are
They are chasing a hawk that has entered the cabin, and the hole is the place through which the bird escaped
They want to warn Baker that the jay has damaged the roof of his cabin, and that he should take care
They are lost, and have followed the first jay to the cabin in the hope that he will show them the way
quiz.e: News of his labor spreads among jays, and a crowd gathers to laugh at his predicament.

quiz.q: Based on “Young Goodman Brown,” which of the following would Faith most likely agree with?
o: Brown should join the traveler on his journey, since the errand is a harmless one and will be over by morning
Brown should trust the minister less, since he has been heard to speak in a manner unbecoming to his office
Brown should stay at home on the night of the journey
Brown should leave the village and take her with him, since the place has become hostile to honest people
The forest is a place of safety, and it is better for Brown to go there than to remain at home at night
Salem is a wicked town, and no one who lives in it can be sure of avoiding the temptations that surround him
quiz.e: Faith begs him to put off his journey and sleep in his own bed.

quiz.q: Based on “Baker’s Bluejay Yarn,” Jim Baker would most likely disagree with which statement?
o: Jays use language as well as humans do, and they are able to say whatever they wish with great force and variety
Jays have a sense of humor, which allows them to enjoy a joke and to laugh at the misfortunes of their kind
Jays can be quite expressive, and a person who listens to them will learn what they feel from their voices
Jays are less intelligent than other animals
Jays understand human speech, and are able to follow what a person says if he speaks to them with care
Jays have a good sense of what is funny, and are always ready to enjoy a joke at another bird’s expense
quiz.e: Baker insists that jays are remarkably expressive, so he would reject the claim that they are dull.

quiz.q: Which of the following statements about “Rip Van Winkle” is accurate?
o: The story is told in the first person by Rip, who describes his own experiences to the villagers in a plain style
The story is presented as the papers of Diedrich Knickerbocker
The story takes place in New England, in a village whose customs are those of the Puritan colonists
Rip is a leader of the Revolution, whose long absence is due to his service in the army of the colonies
The story ends with Rip’s death, which comes on the day he returns to the village and sees his daughter
Rip’s wife lives to see him return, and she welcomes him with the same scolding that she had given before
quiz.e: A postscript and headnote attribute the tale to Knickerbocker.

quiz.q: Which of the following statements about “Young Goodman Brown” is accurate?
o: It is a first-person account by Brown
It is set in the nineteenth century
It ends with Brown’s joyful reunion with Faith
The traveler is a stranger Brown has never heard of
Brown is a minister
It is set in Puritan Salem Village
quiz.e: Hawthorne sets the tale in seventeenth-century Salem Village.

quiz.q: Which of the following statements about “The Fall of the House of Usher” is accurate?
o: The narrator is Madeline’s husband
The narrator is Roderick’s physician
The narrator is a friend of Roderick’s youth
The narrator is Roderick’s brother
The narrator is Madeline’s twin
The narrator is the owner of the house
quiz.e: The unnamed narrator was a boyhood friend of Usher who is summoned by a letter.

quiz.q: Which of the following statements about “The Eve of St. Agnes” is accurate?
o: It is a narrative in free verse
It is a play in blank verse
It is written in Spenserian stanzas
It is a sonnet sequence
It is composed in ballad meter
It is written in heroic couplets
quiz.e: Keats uses nine-line Spenserian stanzas ending in an alexandrine.

quiz.q: Which of the following statements about “Baker’s Bluejay Yarn” is accurate?
o: It is told by a jay, who describes the events in a voice that is a mixture of human speech and birdsong
It is set in New England, in a village where the people speak in the dialect of the region’s farmers
It was written as a lecture, which Twain delivered to an audience in the course of a tour of the Western states
It is told in a Western vernacular by a miner
It is a poem, in which Baker’s story is told in a series of rhymed couplets with a regular rhythm
It is told in formal, ornate language, which the narrator adopts in order to give the story an air of dignity
quiz.e: Twain gives Baker a colloquial Western voice and has him present the story as true.

quiz.q: “Rip Van Winkle” is set in the years surrounding the American Revolution. Which detail best shows the change in the village?
o: The village has a new church, which was built after the Revolution and which replaces the old meetinghouse
Rip’s house is repaired, and the garden that his wife had kept is now in better condition than it had been
The Catskill Mountains have moved, and the villagers say that the hills are not where they stood before
The villagers wear different hats, and Rip’s own hat is a mark of the fashion that has gone out of use
The inn is closed, and the villagers meet in a private house to discuss the news of the day and the war
The tavern sign changes from King George to General Washington
quiz.e: The sign is a concrete marker of the transformation from colony to republic.

quiz.q: Hawthorne’s Puritan setting in “Young Goodman Brown” most directly supports which theme?
o: The conflict between outward piety and hidden sin
The value of free enterprise, since the story shows that a man who works for himself is better than one who serves others
The danger of exploring the frontier, since Brown’s journey into the forest leads him into peril and into error
The hopefulness of democratic reform, since the story presents the new world as a place of freedom from the past
The power of love to cure fear, since Brown’s affection for Faith is shown in the end to have restored his trust
The rise of industrial society, since the story shows how the old village is changed by the new age and its habits
quiz.e: The Puritan community stresses piety, and the story suggests hypocrisy and doubt beneath it.

quiz.q: “The Fall of the House of Usher” is an example of which literary tradition?
o: Gothic fiction
Realism
Naturalism
Regionalism
Transcendentalism
Modernism
quiz.e: Poe uses the decaying mansion, madness, and supernatural dread typical of the Gothic.

quiz.q: “The Eve of St. Agnes” is a poem of which literary movement?
o: Romanticism
Neoclassicism
Realism
Modernism
Metaphysical poetry
Naturalism
quiz.e: Keats is a major second-generation English Romantic poet, and the poem emphasizes sensuous imagery.

quiz.q: “Baker’s Bluejay Yarn” is an example of which literary tradition?
o: American regionalism and frontier humor
Gothic fiction, in which a decaying setting and a sense of dread combine to produce a mood of terror in the reader
Transcendentalism, in which the writer’s interest is in the individual’s relation to nature and to the divine spirit
Romantic nature poetry, in which the writer describes the beauty of the landscape in a style marked by feeling
Puritan sermon, in which the writer instructs the congregation on the dangers of sin and the need for repentance
Neoclassical satire, in which the writer exposes the follies of society in a formal style governed by reason
quiz.e: Twain uses Western dialect and tall-tale humor.

quiz.q: One can infer about Irving’s attitude toward Rip’s neighbors from the portrait of the inn’s “junto” of village sages that
o: He admires their wisdom and means readers to treat their judgments as the story’s authority
He finds their self-importance amusing, since their solemn politics rest on a few old newspapers
He fears their influence on the village and wishes to warn readers against idle gossip
He resents their leisure because it contrasts with the hard labor of his own readers
He is indifferent to them and mentions them only to complete the setting
He regards them as dangerous radicals who have prepared the way for the Revolution
quiz.e: The sages’ gravity is mock-heroic: Nicholas Vedder’s silent pipe-smoking governs their opinions, and Irving is gently amused.

quiz.q: By commenting that Rip would “rather starve on a penny than work for a pound,” the narrator chiefly emphasizes that Rip’s idleness is
o: A calculated strategy by which he hopes to avoid paying taxes to the crown
A habit he has recently acquired in imitation of the village’s wealthier men
A condition brought on by illness that the villagers misread as laziness
A settled principle of his temperament, which no practical reward can overcome
A deliberate protest against the authority of his wife and the village council
A form of religious scruple that the narrator treats with respectful seriousness
quiz.e: The narrator treats the trait as built into Rip’s nature, so even a large payment cannot change it.

quiz.q: In the phrase “petticoat government,” the narrator is suggesting that Rip
o: Opposes all forms of government and therefore resents the Revolution as much as he had resented the king’s rule
Believes that women should hold political office in the new republic, and regards his wife as a fit ruler
Has joined the Revolution in order to escape his wife’s authority, and sees the war as a means of freedom
Considers his wife a traitor to the cause of the colonies, whose quarrels with him are a form of rebellion
Understands domestic power as a form of tyranny, and so mixes small and large subjects for comic effect
Regards the king’s ministers as no better than a household of women, and so as unfit to govern the colonies
quiz.e: Rip’s grievance is the scolding at home; the narrator’s mock-political phrase makes it comic.

quiz.q: The chief effect of the opening paragraphs describing the Catskill Mountains is to
o: Provide the geographical details that a reader needs to find the village on a map
Argue that the mountains are the most important natural feature of the Hudson Valley
Introduce a conflict between the villagers and the mountain’s inhabitants
Establish a legendary, almost enchanted setting in which the later events will seem natural
Contrast the beauty of nature with the ugliness of the village’s politics
Prepare readers for a realistic description of the Dutch colonial economy
quiz.e: The mountains change color with the weather and are described with a lyrical, storybook quality that prepares for the supernatural.

quiz.q: The final paragraph of “Rip Van Winkle,” in which Rip tells his story to visitors, primarily reveals that
o: Rip has regained the wealth that he lost through his neglect of the farm
Rip has become a bitter critic of the new government and its officials
Rip has ceased to believe that his story is true
Rip has learned from his experience that industry is the only virtue
Rip regrets the years that his sleep has taken from his family
Rip has become a local legend whose idleness is now honored as a form of wisdom
quiz.e: He sits on the bench outside the inn, a respected patriarch in the new village, free of his wife and his farm work.

quiz.q: The speaker of “Come, devil! for to thee is this world given” can best be described as
o: A man who has just resolved to resist evil and defies the devil to tempt him
A skeptic who mocks the devil’s power in order to show that it is imaginary
A minister delivering a sermon on the danger of despair in a Puritan community
A man in despair who gives himself up to evil after concluding that goodness is a delusion
A traveler who feels that he has lost his way and calls for any guide
A man in a fever whose words have no connection to what he has seen
quiz.e: Brown cries out when he believes Faith has fallen, and he abandons his resistance.

quiz.q: Which of the following would the minister and Deacon Gookin, as Brown first knows them, probably not approve of?
o: A villager’s attendance at the evening prayers in the meetinghouse
A villager’s decision to walk alone in the forest after dark to attend a secret meeting
A villager’s habit of reading scripture to his family at night
A villager’s support for the minister’s sermons on sin and judgment
A villager’s loyalty to the village’s ancient customs and laws
A villager’s willingness to listen to the counsel of the community’s elders
quiz.e: Their public piety makes them ostensible opponents of the forest meeting, which is what makes their presence there shocking.

quiz.q: Which of the following best paraphrases the meaning of the sentence “A stern, a sad, a darkly meditative, a distrustful, if not a desperate man did he become, from the night of that fearful dream”?
o: Brown became a more careful man, a better husband and a firmer believer in his faith
Brown became a respected leader who used the dream to make his community better
Brown remained as cheerful as he had been, though the dream gave him an interest in scripture
Brown’s experience in the forest left him gloomy, suspicious and distant for the rest of his life
Brown grew steadily more fearful of the forest, which he never entered again in his life
Brown became a desperate man because he had committed a crime on the night of the dream
quiz.e: The sentence lists traits of lasting disillusionment; the dream permanently altered his view of the people around him.

quiz.q: In context, “vacant eye-like windows” suggests that the house
o: Has recently been abandoned and shows signs of having been looted by the people who lived near it before
Appears to gaze back at the narrator, lifeless yet watchful, which prepares for its sentient menace
Is being rebuilt after a fire and has no glass in its frames, which the builders will supply in the spring
Is a modern building designed by an architect with an interest in symmetry and in the effects of light
Offers a bright and welcoming view of the surrounding countryside, which the narrator enjoys on his arrival
Contains a collection of paintings of eyes that Roderick has assembled, and which can be seen from outside
quiz.e: The simile gives the house a blank, staring look and begins the story’s identification of house and family.

quiz.q: The speaker gives explicit symbolic significance to the house in the sentence in which the narrator says that “the mansion and the family” are
o: Likely to be rebuilt by the surviving member of the family
Identified in the peasantry’s mind as a single entity, the “House of Usher”
Separated by a legal dispute that has lasted several generations
Known to the narrator only through letters and not from experience
Described as a refuge from the hostile countryside outside the grounds
Compared by the physician to a hospital in need of repair
quiz.e: The name “House of Usher” refers to both the building and the family line, and Poe makes the identification explicit.

quiz.q: In the lines describing the “Haunted Palace,” the palace is compared to
o: A real castle that once stood in the narrator’s homeland
A ship that wanders the sea after a great storm
A church whose bells ring at the death of the king
A garden that withers when the seasons change
The human head and mind, whose ruin the poem allegorically traces
A battlefield where the monarch’s armies were defeated
quiz.e: Usher’s ballad is an allegory of a mind that falls from reason into madness.

quiz.q: It can be inferred that the narrator’s attitude toward Roderick’s theory that the stones of the house are sentient is
o: Complete acceptance, since he has seen the phenomenon himself
Amused contempt for a delusion that he thinks will be cured by company
Scholarly interest in a theory that he has read about in books
Indifference, because he never mentions it in his account
Uneasy skepticism that is overcome by the evidence of the house’s effect on him
Open hostility, because he thinks it a sign of Roderick’s deceit
quiz.e: He narrates the theory with doubt but grows more susceptible to the house’s atmosphere.

quiz.q: In lines in which Keats describes “the sculptured dead” in the chapel, the speaker seeks to convey a feeling of
o: Chill, stillness and mortality that makes the lovers’ warmth seem more vivid by contrast
Warmth and comfort that the chapel provides to those who pray in it, even in the coldest season of the year
Excitement and anticipation at the approach of the festival, which the people of the castle are preparing to celebrate
Bitterness at the way the dead have been neglected by the living, who no longer visit the chapel or pray for them
Amusement at the ornate carving that decorates the tombs, which the speaker finds excessive and a little foolish
Joyful reverence for the saints whose images are painted on the walls, and whose presence is felt by the Beadsman
quiz.e: The opening stanzas stress cold and death, which sets off the warmth of the main story.

quiz.q: The “Beadsman” in the first stanzas is best described as
o: A figure of renunciation whose cold devotion contrasts with the sensuous love that follows
A servant of the Baron who watches over Madeline and reports her movements
A traveling pilgrim who seeks shelter in the castle for the night
A priest who conducts the marriage of the lovers at the end of the poem
A guest at the feast who denounces the revelers for their worldliness
A madman whose prophecies foretell the lovers’ downfall
quiz.e: He prays for others’ sins and then fades from the poem; his asceticism is the foil for Madeline and Porphyro.

quiz.q: In the stanza in which Madeline undresses, the speaker’s attitude toward her is best described as
o: Tender and reverent, treating her innocence with a sensuous delicacy
Hostile and critical, since she violates the rules of her household
Clinical and detached, as in a scientific study of her behavior
Satirical, mocking the superstition that leads her to bed supperless
Fearful, since the scene seems to threaten her with violence
Indifferent, as the speaker is occupied with Porphyro’s preparations
quiz.e: Keats’s diction (“warmed jewels”) is lush and admiring.

quiz.q: The tall tale’s final scene, in which the jays shriek with laughter at the jay’s hopeless task, suggests that
o: Mockery of another’s foolishness is a human trait that Twain attributes to the jays
Jays are cruel animals who enjoy the sufferings of other creatures, and who take pleasure in the failure of their kind
The jay has been punished for stealing from the miner’s cabin, and the other jays are gathered to see his penalty
Baker is a poor judge of the animals he has lived among, and his account of their behavior is not to be trusted
The jays have a language that Baker alone can understand, and the story is his translation of what they said
The scene is meant to teach readers to respect the work of birds, however foolish its object may seem
quiz.e: The jays’ jeering at the stubborn jay is a satire of human behavior in a social group.

quiz.q: The speaker’s account of the hole in the cabin roof is best described as
o: Lyrical, in the manner of a nature poem about the western landscape
Defensive, as though Baker expected to be accused of exaggeration
Learned, as though the narrator were reporting a scientific observation
Deadpan, with the narrator treating a ridiculous event as plain and serious fact
Sentimental, inviting readers to pity the labor of the bird
Satirical in a bitter way, aimed at the miners who left the cabin
quiz.e: Twain’s humor depends on the narrator’s straight face while he narrates absurdity.

quiz.q: The “Fall of the House of Usher” is an example of which genre?
o: A realistic novel of manners about a declining aristocratic family
Gothic horror, in which setting and psychology are fused to produce dread
A pastoral romance set in the countryside of the narrator’s youth
A satirical sketch that mocks the gloom of Romantic poets
A didactic tale about the moral dangers of excessive learning
A travel narrative that records the narrator’s journey through Europe
quiz.e: Poe’s tale uses a decaying house, a doomed family and an unreliable narrator typical of Gothic fiction.

quiz.q: According to the editors, which pair of criteria governed their choice of stories?
o: Popularity with earlier anthologists and the length of the story in printed pages
Fame of the author and the story’s success with the magazine readers of its day
Freedom from Gothic effects and an optimistic view of American life
A balance of regions and the inclusion of one story from every decade since 1832
Excellence of the story itself and its value in showing how the American form developed
Moral lessons suitable for students and a plot that resolves in a single sitting
quiz.e: The Introduction says the criteria were “double”: a story’s excellence in itself and its representativeness in the story’s development in the United States.

quiz.q: The editors reject “Marjorie Daw” and “The Lady, or the Tiger?” mainly because they
o: Were written before Poe’s work and so cannot show the form’s development
Lack the moral or intellectual weight that serious American stories carry
Imitate European Gothic fiction too closely to count as American stories
Use dialect and local color in ways that the editors find offensive
Were never popular with the readers of the magazines in which they appeared
Rely on a long plot of linked incidents rather than a single effect
quiz.e: They are called pleasant contrivances or jokes without psychological depth; this missing quality is what Canby called “specific gravity.”

quiz.q: Which of the following would the editors most likely regard as having “specific gravity”?
o: A mystery whose clever solution surprises the reader in the final sentence
A tale of local scenery whose chief pleasure is in its colorful description
A well-bred joke told with great technical polish and a neat ending
A fable about animals that teaches a plain moral to young readers
A romantic adventure that ends with the union of two lovers
A comic story that is also a serious reflection on manners or national character
quiz.e: The editors say that even when it is funny, the typical American story asks to be taken seriously as a reflection of life, manners or morals.

quiz.q: In the Introduction, the contrast between Irving’s and Poe’s methods is best described as one between
o: A tale of the supernatural and a tale of ordinary domestic life in a village
A graceful chronological chain of incidents and a concentrated tale aimed at a single effect
A humorous satire of society and a sober defense of its institutions
A story told by a participant and a story told by an all-knowing author
An early form based on plot and a later form based on character alone
A story rooted in local color and a story rooted in historical fact
quiz.e: Irving’s “Rip Van Winkle” is the orderly tale of linked incidents; Poe’s is the concentrated tale of effect.

quiz.q: The editors’ claim that Poe’s terror is “not of Germany but of the soul” is best understood as
o: The editors’ praise of Poe as the most profound psychologist of the century
A criticism of Poe’s imitation of the German Romantics in his early tales
Poe’s own statement, which the editors find only partly justified by his actual effects
A definition of the Gothic tradition in all its American and European forms
A comparison of Poe’s style with that of Hawthorne in “Young Goodman Brown”
An argument that Poe’s stories belong to the tradition of realism
quiz.e: Poe made the claim, but the editors say his effects are mostly physiological and literary, his “madness” more literary than observed.

quiz.q: Which of the following is credited to Poe in the Introduction?
o: The local-color sketch of life in the Western mining camps
The character-centered story of a “situation revealed”
The fable in which animals speak in a frontier dialect
The tale of ratiocination, the parent of the detective story
The comic tale of an idle man who sleeps through a revolution
The impressionistic tale of men adrift at sea in an open boat
quiz.e: “The Murders in the Rue Morgue” is the model of the tale of ratiocination, with its amateur detective, dull assistant and false clues.

quiz.q: Which of the following statements best describes how the Introduction compares Poe and Hawthorne?
o: Poe’s stories are realistic, while Hawthorne’s are pure fantasy without moral meaning
Both authors depend on a single effect and neither is concerned with character
Hawthorne’s story is less serious than Poe’s because it relies on a historical setting
Poe is a New England moralist and Hawthorne a Southern writer of horror tales
Both write of witchcraft, and the two differ only in the length of their stories
Poe’s darkness is theatrical, whereas Hawthorne’s forest stands for the darkness of the human soul
quiz.e: The editors call Hawthorne’s story “granite” to Poe’s “pine” in specific gravity, a difference of soul versus stage effect.

quiz.q: The phrase “granite to pine” in the comparison of Hawthorne’s story with Poe’s suggests that Hawthorne’s story is
o: Easier to read and more popular with students than Poe’s
Older in its sources and more Gothic in its details than Poe’s
Shorter and more tightly constructed than Poe’s
More flexible in its use of symbol and dialect than Poe’s
Heavier in moral and psychological substance than Poe’s
More dependent on setting and less on character than Poe’s
quiz.e: Granite is dense and hard, pine soft; the metaphor ranks Hawthorne’s “specific gravity” above Poe’s.

quiz.q: According to the Introduction, what weakness does “Young Goodman Brown” show as a piece of craftsmanship?
o: Its use of a forest setting that has no connection with its theme
Its reliance on a Gothic house in the manner of Poe
Its use of dialect that distracts from the story’s meaning
Its failure to give Brown’s experience a symbolic significance
Its return section is followed by a lame, anticlimactic appendix
Its excessive dependence on a single effect in the final scene
quiz.e: The editors say Poe would never have left the story with an anticlimactic appendix; Hawthorne is not as impeccable a craftsman.

quiz.q: The Introduction says the American story has moved “away from plot” toward what Henry James called a
o: “Central intelligence”
“Situation revealed”
“Slice of life”
“Moral fable”
“Local color”
“Unity of effect”
quiz.e: The editors say the form has tended to become less a complication resolved than a situation revealed.

quiz.q: According to the Introduction, Mark Twain’s mastered forms were
o: The tale of effect and the tale of ratiocination
The local-color story and the impressionist sketch
The novelette and the historical romance
The psychological story and the situation revealed
The allegory and the Gothic romance
The humorous frontier sketch and the fable
quiz.e: The Introduction says he never wrote a good short story; the forms he mastered were the humorous frontier sketch (“How to Tell a Story”) and the fable.

quiz.q: The editors’ remark that “Baker’s Bluejay Yarn” is “superb in its own kind” most nearly implies that the piece
o: Is the best example of the single-effect tale in the anthology
Is a failed imitation of Poe that is saved by its humor
Is better in technique than the stories of Hawthorne and Irving
Is a historical document of the mining camps rather than a work of art
Belongs to the beast-story tradition and should be judged by its own standards, not as a strict short story
Is a satire of the local-color movement and its writers
quiz.e: Twain’s yarn belongs to the ancient beast-story tradition (cf. Uncle Remus) and is not a short story by Matthews’s definition, yet is excellent in its kind.

quiz.q: Which of the following does the Introduction credit to Bret Harte?
o: Inventing the tale of ratiocination in the first half of the century
Introducing the point-of-view experiments of the central intelligence
Writing the first story to use the single effect in 1832
Creating the impressionist sketch with a nervous, tense style
Popularizing the short story and giving it standing as a distinct form
Bringing the humorous frontier sketch into the pages of the Atlantic
quiz.e: After “The Luck of Roaring Camp” (1868) he gave the story status; his characters combine contradictory qualities.

quiz.q: The editors’ treatment of Henry James emphasizes that he
o: Rejected Poe’s concentration in favor of the long chronological tale
Developed local color into a distinct form through stories of the West
Took Poe’s concentration, dropped the Gothic machinery, and applied the method to observed experience
Wrote stories of effect on the model of Irving’s Sketch Book
Is the only writer in the anthology who depends on dialect
Added moral weight to the story, a quality that Hawthorne lacked
quiz.e: James took Hawthorne’s serious situation and moral preoccupations, kept Poe’s concentration, and discarded the Gothic and sensational.

quiz.q: In the Introduction, the writing of the editors can best be characterized as
o: Neutral summary that avoids judging the quality of any story
Nostalgic memoir about the editors’ own early reading of the stories
Satirical commentary on the weaknesses of the American public
Technical analysis of rhetorical devices in each of the stories
Personal narrative about the editors’ travels through the United States
Confident literary-historical argument that praises and criticizes the writers it discusses
quiz.e: They rank writers (Poe vs. Hawthorne), name weaknesses (Howells, Twain) and defend their selection.

hardQuiz.q:
Merchants on Larkin Street predicted ruin when the council proposed closing four blocks to cars. They pointed, understandably, to the parking spaces. But parking was never the product. In the three summers since the pilot began, foot traffic has doubled, two vacant storefronts have filled, and the only complaint I hear at my own café is that the sidewalk tables are always full. A street is not a pipe for moving vehicles; it is the largest piece of public property most of us will ever share. The council should make the closure permanent, and it should do so before the next budget cycle ends, when the cost of delay will come due in leases not renewed.

Which description best captures the rhetorical situation of this passage?
o: A journalist for a local paper neutrally reports a dispute between merchants and the council, quoting both sides evenly
A resident writes to all neighbors, urging them to oppose any change to parking in the district before the vote
An economist presents a predictive model of retail traffic to the council, asking it to wait for further data
A council member defends a closure already approved, explaining to merchants why their objections came too late
A business owner addresses the council and skeptical merchants, using a local pilot's results to urge a timely decision
hardQuiz.e: The writer speaks as a café owner, addresses both the council ("should make ... permanent") and merchants ("Merchants ... predicted ruin"), and ties the argument to a deadline. It is advocacy, not neutral reporting.

hardQuiz.q:
Merchants on Larkin Street predicted ruin when the council proposed closing four blocks to cars. They pointed, understandably, to the parking spaces. But parking was never the product. In the three summers since the pilot began, foot traffic has doubled, two vacant storefronts have filled, and the only complaint I hear at my own café is that the sidewalk tables are always full. A street is not a pipe for moving vehicles; it is the largest piece of public property most of us will ever share. The council should make the closure permanent, and it should do so before the next budget cycle ends, when the cost of delay will come due in leases not renewed.

The phrase "They pointed, understandably, to the parking spaces" most directly serves to:
o: Establish the writer’s expertise in retail economics so that later statistical claims will be trusted without question
Mock the merchants by implying that their worry about parking is trivial and not worth the council’s serious attention
Concede the objection's reasonableness in order to present the writer as fair before redirecting the argument
Introduce the first piece of statistical evidence about parking, which the rest of the paragraph then builds upon
Shift the tone from persuasive to purely informational so that the reader can weigh both sides without pressure
hardQuiz.e: 'Understandably' grants the merchants a reasonable motive, which builds the writer's credibility and prepares the redirect in 'But parking was never the product.' It does not ridicule them.

hardQuiz.q:
Merchants on Larkin Street predicted ruin when the council proposed closing four blocks to cars. They pointed, understandably, to the parking spaces. But parking was never the product. In the three summers since the pilot began, foot traffic has doubled, two vacant storefronts have filled, and the only complaint I hear at my own café is that the sidewalk tables are always full. A street is not a pipe for moving vehicles; it is the largest piece of public property most of us will ever share. The council should make the closure permanent, and it should do so before the next budget cycle ends, when the cost of delay will come due in leases not renewed.

The sentence "A street is not a pipe for moving vehicles; it is the largest piece of public property most of us will ever share" relies primarily on:
o: A simile that likens the street to private property, so that its value is measured in what a business could earn from it
Hyperbole that inflates the size of the street in order to make the merchants’ parking complaints seem small by comparison
A metaphor paired with an antithetical structure that redefines what a street is for
An allusion to a historical dispute over public land, which gives the closure the weight of a long civic tradition
Understatement that deliberately minimizes the merchants’ concern so that the council will regard it as not worth debating
hardQuiz.e: The 'pipe' metaphor is rejected and replaced with a new definition in a 'not X; it is Y' construction. That reframing changes the terms of the debate.

hardQuiz.q:
Merchants on Larkin Street predicted ruin when the council proposed closing four blocks to cars. They pointed, understandably, to the parking spaces. But parking was never the product.
