In the three summers since the pilot began, foot traffic has doubled, two vacant storefronts have filled, and the only complaint I hear at my own café is that the sidewalk tables are always full. A street is not a pipe for moving vehicles; it is the largest piece of public property most of us will ever share. The council should make the closure permanent, and it should do so before the next budget cycle ends, when the cost of delay will come due in leases not renewed.

Which statement best describes the shift in tone from the first four sentences to the final sentence?
o: From open hostility toward the merchants in the opening sentences to a grudging admiration for how they have endured
From personal reminiscence about the street’s past to a detached, statistical analysis of what the closure might cost
From playful humor at the start of the passage to a solemn, grieving note about the street’s lost businesses
From neutral reporting of the pilot’s results to a tone of weary resignation that the council will not act
From measured, wry observation to pointed urgency tied to a consequence
hardQuiz.e: The opening is measured and a little wry ('understandably,' 'never the product'). The last sentence turns urgent with a deadline and consequence ('before... will come due').

hardQuiz.q:
Merchants on Larkin Street predicted ruin when the council proposed closing four blocks to cars. They pointed, understandably, to the parking spaces. But parking was never the product. In the three summers since the pilot began, foot traffic has doubled, two vacant storefronts have filled, and the only complaint I hear at my own café is that the sidewalk tables are always full. A street is not a pipe for moving vehicles; it is the largest piece of public property most of us will ever share. The council should make the closure permanent, and it should do so before the next budget cycle ends, when the cost of delay will come due in leases not renewed.

Which additional evidence would most effectively strengthen the writer's claim that the closure has helped businesses?
o: Sales tax receipts for the four blocks compared with similar commercial streets that remained open to cars over the same period
A quotation from a longtime resident who says she enjoys the sidewalk tables and has begun to shop on the street more often
The writer’s own estimate of how many pedestrians now walk along the four blocks on a typical weekday afternoon
The number of parking spaces lost to the closure, set beside the total number of spaces that remain in the district
A description of the street’s commercial history before the pilot, including which shops had opened and closed in earlier decades
hardQuiz.e: A comparison group across the same period addresses whether the gains came from the closure rather than from general trends. The other options are anecdotal, irrelevant, or the objection itself.

hardQuiz.q:
Merchants on Larkin Street predicted ruin when the council proposed closing four blocks to cars. They pointed, understandably, to the parking spaces. But parking was never the product. In the three summers since the pilot began, foot traffic has doubled, two vacant storefronts have filled, and the only complaint I hear at my own café is that the sidewalk tables are always full. A street is not a pipe for moving vehicles; it is the largest piece of public property most of us will ever share. The council should make the closure permanent, and it should do so before the next budget cycle ends, when the cost of delay will come due in leases not renewed.

The final sentence functions most significantly to:
o: Introduce a counterargument that the writer will refute in a later paragraph, so that the piece appears balanced to its readers
Summarize the evidence from the first half of the passage so that the council can recall each point before it votes
Soften the argument by acknowledging uncertainty about the pilot’s results and inviting the council to gather more data
Move from the argument to a specific request with a deadline, and attach a concrete cost to inaction
Shift the focus away from the council and toward the merchants, who are now asked to change their own practices
hardQuiz.e: It states the demand ('make the closure permanent'), sets a timeframe, and names the cost of delay, which turns the argument into a call to action.

hardQuiz.q:
Merchants on Larkin Street predicted ruin when the council proposed closing four blocks to cars. They pointed, understandably, to the parking spaces. But parking was never the product. In the three summers since the pilot began, foot traffic has doubled, two vacant storefronts have filled, and the only complaint I hear at my own café is that the sidewalk tables are always full. A street is not a pipe for moving vehicles; it is the largest piece of public property most of us will ever share. The council should make the closure permanent, and it should do so before the next budget cycle ends, when the cost of delay will come due in leases not renewed.

Which sentence would serve best as a thesis for a rhetorical analysis of this passage?
o: The writer uses metaphor, concession and a call to action to persuade the council and the merchants to support a permanent closure
By conceding the merchants' concern and then redefining the street's purpose, the writer reframes the debate so that a permanent closure seems the logical conclusion
The passage is persuasive because it uses evidence and emotional appeals to move an audience that began by disagreeing
The writer argues that Larkin Street should be closed to cars permanently, and he supports his argument with a pilot program
The author’s use of a pipe metaphor shows creativity and effectively changes how readers might think about a city street
hardQuiz.e: A strong thesis names specific choices, explains how they work and ties them to purpose. The first option does all three; the others list devices, make a generic judgment, or restate the argument.

hardQuiz.q:
Merchants on Larkin Street predicted ruin when the council proposed closing four blocks to cars. They pointed, understandably, to the parking spaces. But parking was never the product. In the three summers since the pilot began, foot traffic has doubled, two vacant storefronts have filled, and the only complaint I hear at my own café is that the sidewalk tables are always full. A street is not a pipe for moving vehicles; it is the largest piece of public property most of us will ever share. The council should make the closure permanent, and it should do so before the next budget cycle ends, when the cost of delay will come due in leases not renewed.

Which revision of the third sentence ("In the three summers since the pilot began, foot traffic has doubled, two vacant storefronts have filled, and ...") would introduce an error?
o: Changing "has doubled" to "doubled"
Replacing the first comma with a semicolon
Changing "has doubled" to "have doubled"
Changing "filled" to "been filled"
Replacing "pilot began" with "pilot had begun"
hardQuiz.e: 'Foot traffic' is a singular subject, so 'have doubled' would be an agreement error. The other changes alter tense, punctuation or voice without creating a grammatical error in context (although some change meaning slightly).

hardQuiz.q:
Brothers and sisters: the owners tell us that the mill is a family, and I do not doubt it. I have worked beside this family twenty-two years, and I have noticed how the family eats. The mill's lamps burn all night; it is our eyes that pay for the oil. The mill's profits rose by a fifth this year; it is our wages that were cut by a tenth. I do not ask the owners to love us. Love is a luxury no ledger records. I ask only that they count us as they count their looms: as property worth keeping in repair.

The speaker's address "Brothers and sisters" and the references to "our eyes" and "our wages" most clearly indicate that the primary audience is:
o: Fellow workers whom the speaker hopes to unite and move to act
The mill owners themselves, whom the speaker hopes to persuade directly by appealing to their pride in the family they describe
A neutral public audience reading a newspaper, who need to be informed about conditions inside the mill before they judge
Government regulators reviewing labor practices at the mill, to whom the speaker presents evidence in the hope of an inspection
The speaker’s own family and neighbors, whom the speaker wants to reassure that the mill’s troubles will soon pass
hardQuiz.e: The speaker uses the inclusive 'our' and a salutation of solidarity. The owners are discussed in the third person ('they'), so they are the object, not the addressee.

hardQuiz.q:
Brothers and sisters: the owners tell us that the mill is a family, and I do not doubt it. I have worked beside this family twenty-two years, and I have noticed how the family eats. The mill's lamps burn all night; it is our eyes that pay for the oil. The mill's profits rose by a fifth this year; it is our wages that were cut by a tenth. I do not ask the owners to love us. Love is a luxury no ledger records. I ask only that they count us as they count their looms: as property worth keeping in repair.

The statement "I have noticed how the family eats" most directly establishes:
o: A sincere endorsement of the mill as a family, offered by a speaker who has watched the owners care for the workers
An ironic challenge to the owners' metaphor by implying the family relationship is exploitative
A logical appeal supported by data on food spending, intended to prove that the owners’ claim is statistically false
An appeal to the speaker’s authority as a physician, whose professional judgment gives the observation its credibility
A neutral transition that closes one paragraph and opens the next without adding any new idea to the argument
hardQuiz.e: The speaker accepts the owners' 'family' language and turns it ironic: noticing 'how the family eats' implies that some members consume while others pay.

hardQuiz.q:
Brothers and sisters: the owners tell us that the mill is a family, and I do not doubt it. I have worked beside this family twenty-two years, and I have noticed how the family eats. Love is a luxury no ledger records. I ask only that they count us as they count their looms: as property worth keeping in repair.

The structure of the sentences "it is our eyes that pay for the oil" and "it is our wages that were cut by a tenth" is best described as:
o: Parallel clauses that contrast the owners' gains with the workers' costs
Anaphora that repeats the same opening phrase to build toward an emotional climax about the workers’ suffering
A series of rhetorical questions that invite the owners to defend themselves before an audience of the mill’s workers
An extended metaphor that compares the mill to a family and then carries the comparison through the whole sentence
Asyndeton that removes conjunctions so that the list of the workers’ grievances moves quickly and without pause
hardQuiz.e: Each clause pairs an owner-side benefit (lamps burning, profits rising) with a worker-side cost in a parallel pattern, which makes the contrast vivid.

hardQuiz.q:

Love is a luxury no ledger records. I ask only that they count us as they count their looms: as property worth keeping in repair.

Which statement best characterizes the speaker's tone in the passage?
o: Warmly sentimental toward the owners, whom the speaker credits with sincere though sometimes misguided generosity
Angry and chaotic, with sentences that break down as the speaker loses control of the argument in front of the workers
Bitterly ironic yet controlled, with a dignified refusal to beg
Neutral and academic, as though the speaker were analyzing conditions at the mill for a professional journal
Playful and lighthearted, with jokes at the owners’ expense meant to put the audience at ease before the argument
hardQuiz.e: The irony ('how the family eats') and the restrained, concrete diction ('I do not ask the owners to love us') produce disciplined bitterness, not rage or neutrality.

hardQuiz.q:
Brothers and sisters: the owners tell us that the mill is a family, and I do not doubt it. I have worked beside this family twenty-two years, and I have noticed how the family eats. The mill's lamps burn all night; it is our eyes that pay for the oil. The mill's profits rose by a fifth this year; it is our wages that were cut by a tenth. I do not ask the owners to love us. Love is a luxury no ledger records. I ask only that they count us as they count their looms: as property worth keeping in repair.

The juxtaposition of "profits rose by a fifth" and "wages ... cut by a tenth" is most effective because it:
o: Provides a complete financial analysis of the mill, so that listeners can judge for themselves whether the owners can afford a raise
Appeals to the owners’ sense of pity by describing in detail how the workers’ families have suffered since the cut
Relies on a single anecdote rather than on data, so that the audience feels the cut as a personal story
Uses specific, parallel proportions that let listeners compare gain and loss immediately
Contradicts the claim that the mill is a family by showing that the owners never speak to the workers at all
hardQuiz.e: Numbers expressed as fractions, placed in parallel, make the disparity easy to grasp aloud. The passage does not offer a full financial analysis.

hardQuiz.q:

Love is a luxury no ledger records. I ask only that they count us as they count their looms: as property worth keeping in repair.

The final sentence ("I ask only that they count us as they count their looms") functions primarily as:
o: A concession that the owners have been generous, which prepares the audience to accept a smaller request
An analogy that reduces the demand to a modest request based on the owners' own values
A shift to a neutral tone in which the speaker steps back from the argument and invites the audience to decide
A summary of every piece of evidence offered earlier so that the audience can remember the argument as a whole
A rhetorical question that leaves the owners to answer for themselves whether workers deserve the same care as machines
hardQuiz.e: The comparison to looms frames the request as modest and uses the owners' own standards (maintenance of valuable property) against them.

hardQuiz.q:

Which choice best describes how the speaker uses the word "family" in the passage?
o: The speaker rejects the term entirely in the opening sentence and never returns to the idea of a family again
The speaker uses it literally to describe real relatives who work together in the mill under the owners’ supervision
The speaker uses it to praise the owners’ kindness and so earns the goodwill of the owners before making a demand
The speaker adopts the owners' term and then reveals its inadequacy by describing unequal consequences
The speaker uses it only in the final sentence, where it becomes a sudden and unexpected turn in the argument
hardQuiz.e: The word is introduced as the owners' claim and then tested against evidence (eyes, wages), which exposes the metaphor's hypocrisy.

hardQuiz.q:
Brothers and sisters: the owners tell us that the mill is a family, and I do not doubt it. I have worked beside this family twenty-two years, and I have noticed how the family eats. The mill's lamps burn all night; it is our eyes that pay for the oil. The mill's profits rose by a fifth this year; it is our wages that were cut by a tenth. I do not ask the owners to love us. Love is a luxury no ledger records. I ask only that they count us as they count their looms: as property worth keeping in repair.

If an owner wished to rebut the speaker, which response would most directly address the passage's central comparison?
o: Asserting that the speaker is ungrateful for the steady employment the mill has given his family over many years
Saying that the lamps are expensive to keep burning, so the owners could not be expected to pay for workers’ eyes
Stating that the speaker has worked at the mill for twenty years and has never before complained about his pay
Claiming that all families have disagreements, so a quarrel over wages does not prove that the mill is not one
Arguing that wage reductions were necessary to keep the mill solvent despite profits in a single year
hardQuiz.e: The central comparison pits rising profits against falling wages. A rebuttal must explain or challenge that relationship, for example by pointing to solvency concerns.

hardQuiz.q:
To the Editor: Your headline calls gene-edited wheat "a gamble with the food supply." I have spent nineteen years breeding wheat, conventionally and otherwise, and I would put it differently. Every cultivar on your readers' tables was altered, by crossing, by radiation, by selection; the question has never been whether we change crops, only how precisely and how openly. Precision is not safety, and I would not claim that it is. But the trials your article calls "secret" are published, and their data on off-target edits are available to anyone willing to read a table. Skepticism is healthy. Let it be aimed at the evidence rather than at the word "engineered."

The writer's choice to identify her nineteen years of wheat breeding in the second sentence primarily reflects which consideration?
o: Establishing credibility with readers who may doubt a challenge to the newspaper's framing
Providing the exigence for the letter by explaining that her own research was criticized in the original headline
Demonstrating that gene editing is safe by pointing to how long she has worked with these plants without harm
Appealing to the editor’s emotions by showing how much of her life she has devoted to a single crop
Narrowing the audience to other scientists who will recognize her credentials and read the rest with sympathy
hardQuiz.e: Experience is cited to support her authority (ethos) before she disputes the headline. It does not itself prove safety or define the exigence, which is the headline.

hardQuiz.q:

But the trials your article calls "secret" are published, and their data on off-target edits are available to anyone willing to read a table. Skepticism is healthy. Let it be aimed at the evidence rather than at the word "engineered."

Which statement best describes the effect of the sentence "Precision is not safety, and I would not claim that it is"?
o: It undermines her argument by admitting that the technology is unsafe, which gives the headline writer an opening
It shifts the argument from logos to pathos by asking readers to feel sympathy for a scientist who has been misjudged
It introduces a fallacy by oversimplifying a complicated question into a choice between safety and precision
It signals that the writer is uncertain about her own position and is preparing to retreat from it in the next paragraph
It concedes a limit of her position, which strengthens her credibility with a skeptical audience
hardQuiz.e: Qualifying her own claim shows fairness and anticipates objection. It does not abandon her thesis.

In the phrase "a gamble with the food supply," quoted from the headline, the word "gamble" functions as:
o: A literal description of the field trials, whose results were uncertain enough to be fairly called a risk
A loaded metaphor the writer must challenge because it frames the science as reckless
An example of understatement that makes a serious danger to the food supply sound like a minor inconvenience
A technical term used by breeders to describe the odds that a given cross will produce the desired trait
An allusion to a historical event in which an untested crop failed and brought hunger to a farming region
hardQuiz.e: The letter responds to the connotations of 'gamble' (risk, chance), which is why she then reframes the issue in terms of precision and openness.

Which feature of the passage's diction most contributes to a measured, professional tone?
o: Qualified, precise phrasing such as "I would put it differently" and "I would not claim"
Frequent use of slang and everyday idiom that lets the writer sound like an ordinary reader responding to the paper
Extended figurative language that compares the breeding of wheat to the work of an artist shaping her materials
Short, emphatic fragments that give each point the force of a slogan and keep the pace of the letter brisk
Direct address to the reader as “you,” which turns the letter into a personal appeal rather than a professional reply
hardQuiz.e: Hedged, restrained phrasing signals a measured, evidence-minded voice.

The writer's claim that "Every cultivar on your readers' tables was altered" is most vulnerable to which critique?
o: It relies on an emotional appeal that distracts the reader from the lack of any argument about the science
It does not distinguish between kinds of alteration that may carry different risks
It uses a statistic from an unreliable source, which makes every claim in the letter harder to trust
It contradicts her own later statement about precision, since the word “altered” undermines the distinction she draws
It is irrelevant to the headline, which concerned a single new crop and not the history of every cultivar
hardQuiz.e: Equating crossing with gene editing may overlook differences in kind and speed of change; she partially acknowledges this in the next sentence, but the claim as stated is broad.

The final two sentences primarily serve to:
o: Introduce a new claim unrelated to the earlier ones, so that the letter ends on a point the editor has not yet considered
Summarize each point from the letter in order, so that a hurried reader can carry away the whole argument
Retreat from her earlier argument by granting that the newspaper’s headline may be right after all
Redirect the audience's skepticism from a label toward evidence, offering a constructive stance instead of simple opposition
Appeal to the authority of the newspaper by praising its reputation and asking it to correct its own headline
hardQuiz.e: The conclusion accepts skepticism but reorients it ('aimed at the evidence rather than at the word'), tying back to the headline.

A student writing a synthesis essay on public trust in science uses this letter alongside a poll showing falling trust in agricultural research. Which use of the letter would best demonstrate synthesis?
o: Quoting the letter at length without commentary, so that the reader can judge the writer’s tone and reasoning unaided
Using the letter to prove that the poll is inaccurate, since a trusted scientist’s reasoning contradicts its findings
Using the letter to illustrate how a scientist attempts to rebuild trust through transparency, then evaluating whether the approach addresses the poll's concerns
Summarizing the letter and the poll in separate paragraphs, then concluding that both are interesting views of the topic
Using the letter as the only source in the essay, since it already addresses the issue of public trust directly
hardQuiz.e: Synthesis puts sources into conversation in service of the writer's argument. Summary, long quotation, or reliance on one source does not.

Which version of the underlined portion corrects the error in the following revision? "Every cultivar on your readers' tables were altered."
o: Every cultivar ... was altered
Every cultivar ... have been altered
All cultivar ... were altered
Every cultivar ... were being altered
Every cultivar ... are altered
hardQuiz.e: 'Every cultivar' is singular, so the verb must be singular: 'was altered.' 'All cultivar' would need a plural noun.

hardQuiz.q:
You will be told, in the weeks ahead, that the world is waiting for you. It is not. The world is busy. It is waiting for no one; it is filling itself with whoever shows up. So show up for the work no one has assigned. Show up for the neighbor whose name you have not learned. Show up when it is cold, when it is unnoticed, when the applause has gone home. You will not be remembered for the diplomas that hang in your offices. You will be remembered, if you are lucky, for the mornings you were still there.

The speaker's use of the phrase "in the weeks ahead" most directly acknowledges which element of the rhetorical situation?
o: The speaker’s expertise, which entitles her to offer advice that the graduates would not accept from other speakers
The occasion and audience of graduating students who will soon hear similar speeches
The text’s genre as a eulogy, which sets a solemn expectation about how much the audience should remember
A constraint on the length of the speech, which obliges her to compress her advice into a few sentences
The speaker’s disagreement with other speakers, whose advice she expects to contradict her own in later remarks
hardQuiz.e: The reference locates the speech in a graduation season and anticipates the platitudes the audience will hear, which the speaker then undercuts.

hardQuiz.q:
You will be told, in the weeks ahead, that the world is waiting for you. It is not. The world is busy. It is waiting for no one; it is filling itself with whoever shows up. So show up for the work no one has assigned. Show up for the neighbor whose name you have not learned. Show up when it is cold, when it is unnoticed, when the applause has gone home. You will not be remembered for the diplomas that hang in your offices. You will be remembered, if you are lucky, for the mornings you were still there.

The opening "It is not. The world is busy" is most likely intended to:
o: Establish the speaker’s authority through statistics about how the world treats graduates, so her advice appears well-founded
Insult the graduates by suggesting that the world will not notice them, so that they feel the need to prove themselves
Introduce a logical fallacy by treating a single bleak claim as though it were enough to settle the question
Surprise the audience by rejecting a familiar claim, and so win attention for a less conventional message
Appeal to nostalgia by recalling the speaker’s own graduation, so that the audience will trust her memories
hardQuiz.e: The deflationary reversal of a commencement cliché captures attention and sets up the speaker's alternative message.

hardQuiz.q:
You will be told, in the weeks ahead, that the world is waiting for you. It is not. The world is busy. It is waiting for no one; it is filling itself with whoever shows up. So show up for the work no one has assigned. Show up for the neighbor whose name you have not learned. Show up when it is cold, when it is unnoticed, when the applause has gone home. You will not be remembered for the diplomas that hang in your offices. You will be remembered, if you are lucky, for the mornings you were still there.

The repeated structure beginning "Show up" in the middle of the passage is an example of:
o: Antithesis, which sets two opposing ideas side by side so that the audience sees how much each differs from the other
Anaphora, which accumulates emphasis on a central imperative
Hyperbole, which exaggerates the graduates’ responsibilities so that ordinary duties seem as grand as heroic ones
Euphemism, which softens a harsh claim by describing the demands of adulthood in gentler and more polite terms
Apostrophe, which addresses an absent person or abstraction as though it could hear and respond to the speaker
hardQuiz.e: The repetition of the same opening words across successive sentences is anaphora, and it emphasizes the commandment to be present.

hardQuiz.q:

So show up for the work no one has assigned. Show up for the neighbor whose name you have not learned. Show up when it is cold, when it is unnoticed, when the applause has gone home. You will not be remembered for the diplomas that hang in your offices. You will be remembered, if you are lucky, for the mornings you were still there.

Which of the following best characterizes how syntax contributes to the passage's effect?
o: Short, declarative sentences create a blunt, almost aphoristic quality that rises into longer, rhythmic imperatives
Long, complex sentences throughout create a scholarly tone and slow the reader so that each qualification can be weighed
Rhetorical questions dominate the passage and keep the audience in doubt about which answer the speaker intends
Sentence fragments show the speaker’s confusion and make the passage seem like an unfinished set of private notes
Parenthetical asides convey humor, since the speaker keeps interrupting herself to qualify a point with a joke
hardQuiz.e: The speaker moves from terse statements to a rhythm of repeated imperatives, which makes the message memorable.

You will not be remembered for the diplomas that hang in your offices. You will be remembered, if you are lucky, for the mornings you were still there.

Which of the following would most strengthen the speaker's central claim about being remembered for presence rather than credentials?
o: A list of famous universities whose graduates were not remembered, which would show how little a credential can guarantee
A brief example of a person remembered for consistent small acts rather than formal achievements
A statistic on average starting salaries for graduates of different fields, which would show what credentials are worth
An explanation of what a diploma represents, including the years of study and the standards required to earn one
A quotation about the importance of success that praises ambition and suggests how graduates can be remembered
hardQuiz.e: A specific example would support the claim directly; the other options reinforce the value of credentials the speaker discounts.

You will not be remembered for the diplomas that hang in your offices. You will be remembered, if you are lucky, for the mornings you were still there.

The final two sentences function primarily to:
o: Provide a list of tasks the graduates should accomplish in their first year, so that the advice ends on specifics
Shift to a humorous tone that relaxes the audience after a serious passage and lets the speech end on laughter
Introduce a new topic, the value of friendship, which the speaker will take up in the remainder of her remarks
Offer a counterargument that the speaker will refute in the next paragraph, so that the speech appears balanced
Contrast what graduates may value with what lasting regard depends on, and so state the thesis in memorable form
hardQuiz.e: The sentences set 'diplomas' against 'mornings you were still there,' delivering the central claim in antithetical form.

hardQuiz.q:

You will not be remembered for the diplomas that hang in your offices. You will be remembered, if you are lucky, for the mornings you were still there.

Which analysis most accurately describes the speaker's use of the second person?
o: It creates distance between the speaker and the graduates, so the advice sounds like a general rule and not a personal wish
It indicates that the speaker is uncertain about her own advice and wants the audience to decide whether it applies
It signals a shift to a scientific register, in which the speaker reports the habits of people who succeed
It reflects the speaker’s disapproval of the graduates, whose assumptions about their futures she wishes to correct
It positions the speaker as a direct advisor and makes the imperative mood personal rather than abstract
hardQuiz.e: Direct address and imperatives create intimacy and urgency.

hardQuiz.q:
You will be told, in the weeks ahead, that the world is waiting for you. It is not. The world is busy. It is waiting for no one; it is filling itself with whoever shows up. So show up for the work no one has assigned. Show up for the neighbor whose name you have not learned. Show up when it is cold, when it is unnoticed, when the applause has gone home. You will not be remembered for the diplomas that hang in your offices. You will be remembered, if you are lucky, for the mornings you were still there.

In the sentence "You will be remembered, if you are lucky, for the mornings you were still there," the phrase "if you are lucky" is set off with commas because it is:
o: A restrictive modifier that limits the meaning of “remembered” and so cannot be removed without changing the sentence
A series item that belongs to a list of three conditions of being remembered and so needs commas on both sides
A coordinate adjective that modifies “mornings” together with another and is therefore separated by a comma
A parenthetical element that interrupts the main clause
The subject of the clause, which is why it needs to be separated from the verb that follows it
hardQuiz.e: Nonessential interrupting phrases are set off by commas on both sides.

hardQuiz.q:
The documentary promises "the untold story" of the dam, which is a curious claim for a film whose every sequence has been told before, mostly by the same three engineers, mostly at the same podium. We are shown the concrete in slow motion. We are shown the river in slow motion. The only thing not in slow motion is the film's opinion, which arrives at 90 seconds per minute: the dam was a triumph, its critics were sentimental, and the displaced families, whom we meet briefly, were "part of the cost of progress." The phrase is spoken as though cost were a kind of consolation. It is not. A film may admire a dam. It should not need to pretend that no one stood where the water now stands.

The reviewer's primary purpose in the passage is best described as:
o: To summarize the dam’s history for readers unfamiliar with it, so that they can decide whether to see the film
To evaluate a documentary's framing and argue that it ignores the dam's human costs while claiming novelty
To praise the film’s technical craft while regretting that its subject has already been treated by other films
To inform readers of the film’s release date and subject, together with a short guide to how it is organized
To persuade readers to visit the dam, whose history the film is said to have neglected, in order to judge it
hardQuiz.e: The review evaluates and criticizes; the concluding sentences make an argument about what the film should have done.

The statement "the film's opinion ... arrives at 90 seconds per minute" is best understood as:
o: A literal measurement of the film’s pace, offered by the reviewer to show how much opinion the film contains
A sarcastic exaggeration that criticizes the film for pressing its viewpoint relentlessly
A neutral comparison between the film’s opinion and its facts, meant to help the reader evaluate the balance
A statistical claim about how much of the running time is devoted to interviews, as opposed to narration
A compliment about the pacing of the film, which keeps its argument moving without ever losing the viewer’s attention
hardQuiz.e: The impossible rate is hyperbole used sardonically to suggest the film rushes and overstates its opinion.

The repetition in "We are shown the concrete in slow motion. We are shown the river in slow motion" primarily creates which effect?
o: A deadpan, mocking rhythm that portrays the film's visual style as repetitive
A sense of urgency that makes the film’s images seem to move faster as its argument gathers force
Admiration for the film’s artistry, as the reviewer lingers on each image to show how deliberately it was made
A shift in the reviewer’s tone to sympathy, since the repetition shows that the filmmakers meant well
Confusion about the film’s subject, since the repeated images leave the viewer unsure what the film is about
hardQuiz.e: The pairing of parallel sentences underscores sameness and mockery; the reviewer is not praising the visuals.

hardQuiz.q:

Which statement best describes the shift in tone in the last four sentences?
o: From sardonic mockery to a firm, serious moral claim
From admiration for the film’s craft to disappointment that it did not do more to explore the dam’s history
From light humor to confusion, as the reviewer finds that she can no longer state what the film is about
From neutral reporting of what the film contains to enthusiasm for the way it treats its subject
From sadness over the dam’s history to joy in discovering that the film offers a hopeful ending
hardQuiz.e: After mocking the film's style, the reviewer turns serious: 'It is not.' and 'It should not need to pretend...' present an ethical stance.

hardQuiz.q:
The documentary promises "the untold story" of the dam, which is a curious claim for a film whose every sequence has been told before, mostly by the same three engineers, mostly at the same podium. We are shown the concrete in slow motion. We are shown the river in slow motion. The only thing not in slow motion is the film's opinion, which arrives at 90 seconds per minute: the dam was a triumph, its critics were sentimental, and the displaced families, whom we meet briefly, were "part of the cost of progress." The reviewer quotes the phrase "part of the cost of progress." The use of the quotation is most effective in supporting which point?
o: That the dam was not a triumph of engineering, since its builders failed to anticipate the problems it caused
That the film adopts a language of rationalization that minimizes displaced families
That the engineers were incorrect in their estimates of cost, which rose well beyond what had been promised
That the film includes many interviews, which the reviewer treats as evidence that its makers did careful work
That progress is unavoidable, so that those displaced must accept the cost as the film’s speakers insist
hardQuiz.e: The quotation reveals the film's own wording, which the reviewer challenges as a euphemistic justification.

hardQuiz.q:
The documentary promises "the untold story" of the dam, which is a curious claim for a film whose every sequence has been told before, mostly by the same three engineers, mostly at the same podium. We are shown the concrete in slow motion. We are shown the river in slow motion. The final sentence ("A film may admire a dam. It should not need to pretend that no one stood where the water now stands.") functions primarily to:
o: Introduce a new argument, about the dam’s engineering, which the reviewer has not previously mentioned and does not develop
Concede a legitimate position while stating the reviewer's essential objection in a concise, memorable contrast
Summarize the film’s plot in two sentences so that readers who have not seen it can follow the review
Provide a logical proof that the film’s claim to be “untold” must be false because it repeats earlier films
Shift to a humorous tone that lightens the review and leaves the reader with a final joke at the film’s expense
hardQuiz.e: The sentence grants that admiration is acceptable and then pinpoints the objection, balancing fairness with a pointed conclusion.

hardQuiz.q:

Which of the following best explains how diction contributes to the reviewer's critique in the sentence "The phrase is spoken as though cost were a kind of consolation"?
o: The word “phrase” signals that the reviewer is neutral about the film’s language and merely reporting what it said
The comparison of 'cost' to 'consolation' exposes the illogic of treating a loss as a comfort
The word “spoken” shows that the film is silent about its subject, which the reviewer treats as its chief flaw
The word “kind” makes the sentence ambiguous, so that readers cannot tell whether the reviewer approves of the film
The word “cost” refers to money only, so that the sentence is a complaint about the dam’s budget
hardQuiz.e: The sentence juxtaposes two opposed ideas to reveal faulty logic.

hardQuiz.q:
The documentary promises "the untold story" of the dam, which is a curious claim for a film whose every sequence has been told before, mostly by the same three engineers, mostly at the same podium. We are shown the concrete in slow motion. We are shown the river in slow motion. The only thing not in slow motion is the film's opinion, which arrives at 90 seconds per minute: the dam was a triumph, its critics were sentimental, and the displaced families, whom we meet briefly, were "part of the cost of progress." The phrase is spoken as though cost were a kind of consolation. It is not. A film may admire a dam. It should not need to pretend that no one stood where the water now stands.

Which revision of the first sentence would most improve clarity without changing its meaning? "The documentary promises 'the untold story' of the dam, which is a curious claim for a film whose every sequence has been told before."
o: Replacing “promises” with “promised” only, which changes the tense of the verb but leaves the structure unchanged
Replacing "which is" with a dash before "a curious claim"
Deleting the word “curious,” which would leave the sentence grammatical but remove the reviewer’s skeptical judgment
Moving “before” to the start of the sentence, which would change the emphasis but not the sentence’s meaning
Replacing “whose” with “who’s,” which makes the clause a contraction and so makes the pronoun refer to the film
hardQuiz.e: A dash can set off the comment on the claim while keeping the grammar correct. 'Who's' would be an error, and the others alter meaning or tense.

hardQuiz.q:
I came to the marsh in March, when the ice had loosened its grip but not yet let go, when the reeds stood in last year's gold and the first red-winged blackbirds, who arrive before the weather has agreed to welcome them, were already shouting their claims from the cattails. I had expected silence. I had expected, I think, a kind of apology: the quiet of a place that has been drained, and filled, and drained again. Instead there was an insistence so complete that I stood for a long time not trying to name it, only learning what it is to be unnecessary to a place that is entirely alive.

The writer's account of expecting "silence" and "a kind of apology" most strongly suggests an audience that:
o: Is made up of professional ecologists who already know that marshes are far more resilient than they appear to visitors
Has never visited a marsh and so needs to be told that such places are alive with birds and other creatures
Shares assumptions about the damage human activity does to wild places, which the writer then complicates
Prefers an objective scientific report to a personal narrative and would therefore be impatient with the writer’s reflection
Is hostile to conservation and must be persuaded that marshes deserve protection from the effects of human visits
hardQuiz.e: The essay anticipates readers who would expect a diminished marsh and then surprises them. It does not use technical or hostile language.

hardQuiz.q:
I came to the marsh in March, when the ice had loosened its grip but not yet let go, when the reeds stood in last year's gold and the first red-winged blackbirds, who arrive before the weather has agreed to welcome them, were already shouting their claims from the cattails. I had expected silence. I had expected, I think, a kind of apology: the quiet of a place that has been drained, and filled, and drained again. Instead there was an insistence so complete that I stood for a long time not trying to name it, only learning what it is to be unnecessary to a place that is entirely alive.

The long opening sentence, with its accumulation of clauses, produces which effect?
o: It confuses the reader with complexity, a deliberate disorientation that mirrors the writer’s own bewilderment at the marsh
It creates a tone of urgency, as though the writer were anxious to describe everything before the scene could change
It immerses the reader in the scene's layered details, delaying the main point to mimic the slow arrival of spring
It states the writer’s thesis immediately, so that the rest of the passage can be read as support for one claim
It depicts a rapid sequence of events, so that the reader is carried quickly from one image to the next
hardQuiz.e: A periodic, cumulative sentence builds an impression of the season and slows the pace; the main clause is 'I came to the marsh in March.'

hardQuiz.q:
I came to the marsh in March, when the ice had loosened its grip but not yet let go, when the reeds stood in last year's gold and the first red-winged blackbirds, who arrive before the weather has agreed to welcome them, were already shouting their claims from the cattails. I had expected silence. I had expected, I think, a kind of apology: the quiet of a place that has been drained, and filled, and drained again. Instead there was an insistence so complete that I stood for a long time not trying to name it, only learning what it is to be unnecessary to a place that is entirely alive.

The phrase "who arrive before the weather has agreed to welcome them" is best characterized as:
o: A literal description of birds that arrive at the marsh earlier than the season’s warmth, which the writer reports as fact
Personification that humorously attributes a will to the weather
An example of apostrophe, in which the writer addresses the weather directly and asks it to welcome the arriving birds
A metaphor for human migration, in which the arrival of the birds stands for people who settle in a new country
Hyperbole about spring, which exaggerates how late the season is so as to dramatize the birds’ early arrival
hardQuiz.e: Weather 'agreeing' to welcome is personification; the humor suggests the birds' boldness.

hardQuiz.q:

Instead there was an insistence so complete that I stood for a long time not trying to name it, only learning what it is to be unnecessary to a place that is entirely alive.

The shift in the final sentence from description of the marsh to "what it is to be unnecessary to a place" most clearly reflects a change from:
o: Fact to fiction, as the writer leaves the observed marsh and begins to imagine events she did not witness
Argument to narrative, as the writer abandons her claim in order to tell a story about her visit
Humor to anger, as the writer’s playful opening gives way to a complaint about how the marsh is treated
Past to future tense, as the writer turns from what happened to what she hopes will happen on later visits
Observation to reflection, adding a note of humility
hardQuiz.e: The essay moves from what the writer saw to what the experience taught about human place in nature.

hardQuiz.q:

Instead there was an insistence so complete that I stood for a long time not trying to name it, only learning what it is to be unnecessary to a place that is entirely alive.

In the sentence "I had expected, I think, a kind of apology," the phrase "I think" most likely functions to:
o: Show that the narrator does not understand the marsh well enough to say what she expected to find there
Indicate tentative, reflective self-examination, which makes the narrator's candor more credible
Present an objective fact that the reader could confirm independently by consulting a record of the marsh
Create a humorous tone by having the narrator poke fun at her own foolish assumptions about the marsh
Introduce a logical fallacy by presenting a personal impression as though it were evidence about the marsh
hardQuiz.e: The hedge suggests honest self-reflection, building trust in a personal essay.

hardQuiz.q:

Instead there was an insistence so complete that I stood for a long time not trying to name it, only learning what it is to be unnecessary to a place that is entirely alive.

Which statement best describes the structure of the passage?
o: It presents a problem with the marsh’s condition and then offers a solution that the narrator hopes readers will adopt
It moves from a precise scene to an expectation that is overturned and then to a reflective conclusion
It compares two marshes, one in March and one in a later season, in order to show how much they differ
It argues for a policy of protecting the marsh from visitors and gives reasons for the policy in order
It moves chronologically through a single day, beginning at dawn and ending at dusk, with each event in sequence
hardQuiz.e: The movement from observation to anticipated silence, to 'instead,' to an insight is a turn structure.

hardQuiz.q:

Which of the following claims about the writer's use of the word "insistence" is best supported by the passage?
o: It indicates the writer’s irritation at the birds’ noise, which interrupts her attempt to reflect on the marsh
It conveys the marsh's vitality as a force that does not depend on human approval

hardQuiz.e: The 'insistence' of sound and life contrasts with the writer's expectation of apology.

hardQuiz.q:

The sentence "I had expected silence. I had expected, I think, a kind of apology" contains repetition of "I had expected." Which description is most accurate?
o: Faulty parallelism that should be revised, since the second clause repeats the first without adding a new idea
A comma splice that joins two independent clauses without a conjunction and should be corrected in revision
A run-on sentence in which the clauses are fused without punctuation and so confuse the reader about the point
Anaphora that emphasizes the narrator's mistaken assumptions
Redundancy that should be deleted for concision, since repeating “I had expected” adds no information to the sentence
hardQuiz.e: The repetition is deliberate, creating rhythm and underscoring the contrast with what follows.

hardQuiz.q:
Mistakes were made in the handling of customer data, and we regret any inconvenience that may have been experienced. Steps are being taken to ensure that such matters are addressed going forward. We want our customers to know that their privacy remains a priority and that the company has always been committed to the highest standards. An internal review has been initiated, and its findings will be shared as appropriate.

Which of the following best describes the likely purpose of this statement?
o: To announce a new privacy policy that will protect customers’ records from the kind of incident just described
To inform customers of the specific steps they should take at once to protect their own accounts and passwords
To manage public reaction to a data incident while limiting acceptance of responsibility
To persuade investors to keep their shares by showing that the company is acting quickly to contain the damage
To explain the technical cause of the incident so that outside experts can judge whether it could recur
hardQuiz.e: The vague language and avoidance of a clear agent suggest damage control rather than full accountability.

hardQuiz.q:
Mistakes were made in the handling of customer data, and we regret any inconvenience that may have been experienced. Steps are being taken to ensure that such matters are addressed going forward. We want our customers to know that their privacy remains a priority and that the company has always been committed to the highest standards. An internal review has been initiated, and its findings will be shared as appropriate.

The sentence "Mistakes were made" is most significant because of:
o: The use of passive voice that omits who made the mistakes, which distances the company from responsibility
The use of the past tense, which reveals that the company regards the problem as already completely resolved
The use of the word “mistakes,” which is too strong and so makes the company sound more guilty than it intends
The sentence’s brevity, which gives it a blunt force that no longer sentence in the statement could equal
Its appeal to pathos, which invites customers to feel sympathy for the employees who made an honest error
hardQuiz.e: The passive voice conceals the actor, a common evasive strategy.

hardQuiz.q:
Mistakes were made in the handling of customer data, and we regret any inconvenience that may have been experienced. Steps are being taken to ensure that such matters are addressed going forward. We want our customers to know that their privacy remains a priority and that the company has always been committed to the highest standards. An internal review has been initiated, and its findings will be shared as appropriate.

The phrase "any inconvenience that may have been experienced" is best understood as which of the following?
o: A precise statement of fact in which the company reports exactly how many customers experienced a problem
A metaphor for stress in which the customers’ worry about their data is likened to a physical burden
A euphemism that minimizes the effect on customers and hedges whether harm occurred
Hyperbole about customers’ feelings that inflates their annoyance so as to make the company’s apology seem larger
An allusion to a similar incident at another firm, which suggests that the problem is common to the industry
hardQuiz.e: 'Inconvenience' understates a data breach, and 'may have been' hedges even the existence of harm.

hardQuiz.q:
Mistakes were made in the handling of customer data, and we regret any inconvenience that may have been experienced. Steps are being taken to ensure that such matters are addressed going forward. We want our customers to know that their privacy remains a priority and that the company has always been committed to the highest standards. An internal review has been initiated, and its findings will be shared as appropriate.

The tone of the statement is best described as:
o: Warm and conversational, with plain words and short sentences that address customers as though they were neighbors
Angry and defensive, with sharp phrasing that suggests the company resents being asked to account for itself
Humorous, with a light touch meant to make the problem seem small and keep the customers from becoming alarmed
Impersonal and guarded, with formal diction that avoids specifics
Personal and confessional, with a first-person admission of fault that invites forgiveness from the customers
hardQuiz.e: The corporate register, passive constructions and abstractions create distance.

hardQuiz.q:
Mistakes were made in the handling of customer data, and we regret any inconvenience that may have been experienced. Steps are being taken to ensure that such matters are addressed going forward. We want our customers to know that their privacy remains a priority and that the company has always been committed to the highest standards. An internal review has been initiated, and its findings will be shared as appropriate.

Which revision would most strengthen the credibility of the statement for a skeptical audience?
o: Adding more praise for the company’s long record of high standards, so that readers recall how seldom it has failed
Stating what data was affected, when it was discovered, who is responsible for the review and when results will be released
Using more formal language throughout, so that the statement sounds as authoritative as a report from a regulator
Repeating the company’s commitment to privacy in the opening and closing sentences so that readers remember it
Shortening the statement to two sentences, so that readers are not given time to notice what it leaves out
hardQuiz.e: Specifics and accountability build trust; vague reassurance does not.

hardQuiz.q:

The last sentence, "its findings will be shared as appropriate," most likely:
o: Guarantees complete transparency by promising that every finding of the review will be published in full
Leaves open whether and when information will be released, which weakens the promise
Provides a timeline by which customers can expect the results of the review and any resulting changes
Introduces a new argument about the company’s reputation that the previous sentences had not prepared the reader for

hardQuiz.e: 'As appropriate' gives the company discretion, making the promise noncommittal.

A rhetorical analysis of the passage would most appropriately focus on:
o: The statement’s use of statistics, which makes the incident seem small by comparing it with the company’s yearly volume

How passive voice, euphemism and abstraction serve the company's interest in limiting accountability
The writer’s use of dialect, which lends the statement a local flavor and makes the company sound approachable
The statement’s metaphors, which compare the data incident to a storm that has passed over the company
hardQuiz.e: The persuasive strategy lies in grammatical and lexical choices that obscure responsibility.

hardQuiz.q:
Mistakes were made in the handling of customer data, and we regret any inconvenience that may have been experienced. Steps are being taken to ensure that such matters are addressed going forward. We want our customers to know that their privacy remains a priority and that the company has always been committed to the highest standards.
