Which revision of "Mistakes were made" would most directly add an agent?
o: "We made mistakes in how we handled customer data."
“Mistakes had been made.” This changes the tense but leaves the doer of the action unnamed
“Some mistakes were being made.” This makes the action continuous but still does not say who made them
“There were mistakes made.” This begins with an expletive construction and so again leaves the actor out
“Mistakes occurred.” This uses an active verb, but the mistakes appear to happen with no one responsible
hardQuiz.e: Using the first-person active voice names the actor; the others remain passive or agentless.

hardQuiz.q:
Source A: "Circulation of printed books has fallen twelve percent in a decade, and library budgets should follow readers: toward screens, not shelves." Source B: "Visits to our branches rose in the same decade. People come for printing, for childcare programs, for job applications, and for the one room in town where nobody asks them to buy anything."

A student writes: "Although Source A is right that print circulation has fallen, Source B shows that falling circulation does not mean falling use." What synthesis move does the sentence make?
o: It summarizes both sources equally, giving each the same weight and leaving the reader to reach a conclusion alone
It dismisses Source A without evidence so that the writer may rest the whole argument upon Source B
It uses one source to qualify the conclusion drawn from the other, positioning the writer's own claim between them
It restates Source B in different words, adding no new idea that Source A had not already prepared
It introduces a new fallacy by assuming that one source’s evidence must cancel whatever the other source claims
hardQuiz.e: The sentence concedes part of A, then uses B to complicate A's inference, which is a synthesis move that advances an argument.

hardQuiz.q:
Source A: "Circulation of printed books has fallen twelve percent in a decade, and library budgets should follow readers: toward screens, not shelves." Source B: "Visits to our branches rose in the same decade. People come for printing, for childcare programs, for job applications, and for the one room in town where nobody asks them to buy anything."

Which statement best identifies the central disagreement between the sources?
o: Whether libraries should continue to exist at all in a period when so much reading has moved onto screens
Whether printed books are valuable to readers of any age, or whether only digital texts can serve them
Whether a decline in one measure of use (print circulation) should determine how library resources are allocated
Whether the sources use accurate statistics, since each of them cites figures that the other does not mention
Whether library visitors are satisfied with the services they receive, as both sources report different surveys
hardQuiz.e: Source A infers budget priorities from circulation; B argues that visits and uses are broader.

hardQuiz.q:
Source A: "Circulation of printed books has fallen twelve percent in a decade, and library budgets should follow readers: toward screens, not shelves." Source B: "Visits to our branches rose in the same decade. People come for printing, for childcare programs, for job applications, and for the one room in town where nobody asks them to buy anything."

A student argues that libraries should keep funding in-person programming. Which line of reasoning, drawing on the sources, would be strongest?
o: Libraries have always been important to their communities, and so the council should not question their funding
Source A is written by someone who does not like libraries, so its figures should be treated with suspicion
Visitors enjoy books and reading, which proves that the community will continue to support the library’s programs
The decade is a long enough period that the circulation decline must reflect a permanent change in how people read
Print circulation measures only one function; Source B's visit data and program uses indicate that libraries serve needs that screens do not replace
hardQuiz.e: The strongest reasoning explains why the evidence supports the position, linking specific data to a claim about function.

hardQuiz.q:
Source A: "Circulation of printed books has fallen twelve percent in a decade, and library budgets should follow readers: toward screens, not shelves." Source B: "Visits to our branches rose in the same decade. People come for printing, for childcare programs, for job applications, and for the one room in town where nobody asks them to buy anything."

Which additional information would most help evaluate Source A's recommendation?
o: The number of books held in each library, which would show whether the collections have grown or shrunk
The age of the library buildings, which would show whether the branches need costly repairs before long
The names of the library directors, which would show whether the system has been managed by the same people
The price of printed books over the decade, which would show whether readers could still afford to buy them
Whether digital circulation and database use increased in the same decade
hardQuiz.e: The claim to shift to screens depends on whether digital use is growing; that evidence addresses the inference.

hardQuiz.q:
Source A: "Circulation of printed books has fallen twelve percent in a decade, and library budgets should follow readers: toward screens, not shelves." Source B: "Visits to our branches rose in the same decade. People come for printing, for childcare programs, for job applications, and for the one room in town where nobody asks them to buy anything."

Source B's phrase "the one room in town where nobody asks them to buy anything" is primarily an appeal to:
o: Shared values about public space and equality of access
The authority of library experts, who are cited as proof that public libraries serve a function that nothing replaces
Statistics about spending, which show that a library costs less per visitor than any other public service
Fear of losing the library, which the writer hopes will frighten the council into continuing its funding
Humor, which lightens the tone of the paragraph and makes the argument friendlier to readers who disagree
hardQuiz.e: The phrase invokes the ideal of a public commons, a value-based appeal.

hardQuiz.q:
Source A: "Circulation of printed books has fallen twelve percent in a decade, and library budgets should follow readers: toward screens, not shelves." Source B: "Visits to our branches rose in the same decade. People come for printing, for childcare programs, for job applications, and for the one room in town where nobody asks them to buy anything."

Compared with Source A, Source B's diction is best described as:
o: More technical and abstract, with terms of measurement that make the argument sound like a report
More hostile to its opponents, with sharp wording that treats the other source’s view as foolish
More formal in its diction, with long sentences and Latinate words that give it an air of authority
More ironic in its tone, since it describes the library’s uses in a manner that implies the opposite
More concrete and humane, listing specific uses and people
hardQuiz.e: Source B names tangible needs (printing, childcare, applications); Source A uses a general statistic and a slogan-like contrast.

hardQuiz.q: In "Young Goodman Brown," Hawthorne has the devil say that Brown's forebears were his friends and co-workers in violence. A careful reader would most reasonably conclude that this claim is meant to:
o: Be accepted as an accurate history of Salem, which the reader can use to judge the village’s character
Reveal that the devil is the narrator of the tale, since only he could know what Brown’s family had done
Prove that Brown’s father was a villain, so that Brown’s decision to join the meeting is justified
Provide a realistic account of Puritan life, in which cruelty toward outsiders was common in every family
Show that the traveler is unreliable in every statement, so that nothing he says can be trusted at all
Function as a temptation whose truth cannot be verified, so its power depends on Brown's willingness to believe it
hardQuiz.e: The devil is a tempter whose claims serve his purpose; the story keeps their truth unverifiable, which makes Brown's belief the crucial act.

hardQuiz.q: Which of the following most accurately describes the difference between Hawthorne's ambiguity in "Young Goodman Brown" and Poe's ambiguity in "The Fall of the House of Usher"?
o: Both authors state plainly that the events were imaginary, and each one differs only in how he explains the dream
Hawthorne’s story is allegorical and Poe’s is realistic, so that only Hawthorne’s ambiguity has a moral purpose
Poe’s ambiguity concerns the moral of the tale, while Hawthorne’s concerns only the order in which things happen
Hawthorne’s narrator is first person while Poe’s is third person, which explains why Poe’s tale is more doubtful
They are identical in kind, because in each story the central event may be a dream and the narrator says so
Hawthorne questions whether events occurred at all, while Poe questions whether the narrator's perceptions can be trusted
hardQuiz.e: Hawthorne leaves open whether the night happened ("Had Goodman Brown fallen asleep...?"); Poe's first-person narrator is emotionally colored, leaving his perceptions open to doubt.

hardQuiz.q: Which feature of Irving's narration most clearly distinguishes the narrator of "Rip Van Winkle" from a straightforward historian?
o: His use of citations to older Dutch records, which gives each historical claim a source the reader can check
His objective tone, which never allows the narrator to comment on the characters or the events he describes
His comic exaggeration and mock-heroic comparisons, which signal that he is performing the role of historian
His reliance on documents and eyewitness reports, which he quotes at length to establish what truly occurred
His use of the first person, which makes him a participant in the story’s events and not a distant recorder
His refusal to describe characters in any detail, which leaves the reader to imagine them from their actions
hardQuiz.e: The narrator's persona is playful and satirical, undermining the authority he affects.

hardQuiz.q: In "The Fall of the House of Usher," the narrator reads aloud from a romance whose sounds seem to echo within the house. Which interpretation best accounts for the effect of this device on the story's themes?
o: It collapses the distinction between fiction and reality, mirroring the collapse of the narrator's and Usher's grasp of what is real
It lightens the tone with humor, offering the reader a break from the dread that has built up through the story
It demonstrates that the house is not haunted, since each sound has a natural cause within the romance being read
It shows that the narrator is an author, so that the reader understands why he has so much interest in the book
It is an unrelated digression that delays the climax and has little connection with the themes of the main plot
It proves that Roderick is a liar who has invented his sister’s illness in order to keep the narrator in the house
hardQuiz.e: The embedded story's events seem to come true, dissolving boundaries between narrative and reality.

hardQuiz.q: In "The Eve of St. Agnes," the final stanzas return to the Beadsman and Angela. Which reading of this return is best supported by the poem's structure?
o: It reveals that the lovers were captured by the household and punished, so that the poem ends in defeat
It shows that the Beadsman is the poem’s true hero, since his prayers have made the lovers’ escape possible
It frames the lovers' escape within a world of age, death and cold piety, giving the romance a sense of transience
It introduces a new conflict between the lovers and the Baron, which the poem leaves unresolved at its close
It undermines the lovers’ love as false by showing that those who remain behind are more faithful to the saint
It resolves the family feud by showing that the household accepts the lovers’ flight and wishes them happiness
hardQuiz.e: The coda mirrors the cold opening and places the lovers' warmth against mortality.

hardQuiz.q: Which of the following is the most defensible claim about the use of symbolism in the unit's prose texts?
o: Symbols in these stories have a single fixed meaning that each author states plainly, so there is little to interpret
Only Hawthorne uses symbols to carry meaning, while Poe and Irving rely on literal description and plain narration
Objects like Hawthorne's ribbon and staff, Poe's fissure and Irving's tavern sign carry meanings that depend on their context and can be read in more than one way
Symbols in these tales are mainly decorative, adding atmosphere without affecting the meaning of the story
Symbols appear only in the poetry of the unit, since prose of this period favored realism and plain statement
Symbols in these tales are explained by the narrators, so that the reader’s task is only to accept what is said
hardQuiz.e: Each symbol is context-dependent and open to interpretation, which is why textual evidence is needed.

hardQuiz.q: A student claims that Irving's story is ultimately about the persistence of private life amid public upheaval. Which detail offers the strongest support?
o: Rip meets the ghosts of Hendrick Hudson’s crew and drinks their liquor, which shows how far the mountain lies from the village
Rip’s old inn now carries a portrait of George Washington in place of the king, which shows how the village has changed
Rip's primary concern on returning is his family and identity rather than the political upheaval, and he settles into storytelling
Rip’s village is Dutch in its customs and speech, which shows that the tale concerns a local community and not the nation
Rip’s dog Wolf is the only creature in the story that welcomes him, which shows that Rip’s loyalties are private ones
Peter Vanderdonk, the village historian, confirms the legend of the mountain, which shows that local tradition outlasts events
hardQuiz.e: Rip's focus on personal bewilderment and eventual domestic comfort supports the claim.

hardQuiz.q: Which of the following best explains how Poe's diction in describing the House of Usher contributes to the story's effect?
o: Concrete scientific terms give the description an objective air, so the narrator seems to record the house without feeling
Dialect gives the passage a regional flavor, which roots the house in a particular place and in the speech of its people
Colloquial phrases create a casual tone, so that the horror of the house seems ordinary to the narrator
Abstract, intensifying words like 'insufferable' and 'melancholy' attribute emotion to the setting, so the atmosphere seems to act on the narrator
Short, simple words create a sense of speed, which makes the narrator’s approach to the house seem hurried and tense
Technical terms from architecture dominate the passage, and the narrator therefore reports the house with a builder’s eye
hardQuiz.e: Emotionally loaded abstractions produce a pervasive dread that attaches to the setting.

hardQuiz.q: Which statement best describes how Twain's tall tale exploits the conventions of oral storytelling?
o: The narrator hesitates and corrects himself often, so that the story seems to be a hesitant memory and not a performance
The narrator uses scientific terms to explain the jay’s behavior, so that the absurd events seem to be a report of fact
The narrator refuses to give details of the cabin and the jays, which leaves the audience to imagine the scene for itself
The narrator warns the audience not to believe him, which tells them that the story is a joke before it begins
The narrator uses archaic diction that gives the tale the dignity of a legend and lifts it above ordinary speech
The narrator treats absurd claims with deadpan seriousness, uses dialect and builds toward an increasingly ridiculous scene, as in a told story
hardQuiz.e: Deadpan exaggeration, dialect and escalation are staples of the tall tale.

hardQuiz.q: Consider the sentence from Hawthorne's conclusion: "Often, awaking suddenly at midnight, he shrank from the bosom of Faith." What does the sentence most suggest about the effect of the forest experience?
o: Brown is cured of his doubts by his night in the forest and returns to Faith with a renewed and certain trust
Faith is angry with Brown for what he did in the forest, and he draws away from her because of her reproach
Brown's suspicion survives into his intimate life, so the damage is not only public but domestic
Brown becomes more affectionate toward his wife, as though he had learned from the night how easily he might lose her
Brown has forgotten the events of that night, which now seem to him only a strange dream that he wishes to avoid
The sentence is purely descriptive of a nightly habit and adds nothing to the story’s meaning or to Brown’s character
hardQuiz.e: The detail extends the consequence into the most private area of his life.

hardQuiz.q: In what way does Keats's use of the Spenserian stanza in "The Eve of St. Agnes" most significantly reinforce the poem's content?
o: Its brevity matches the poem’s plain style, since each stanza is short enough to be read quickly and without effort
Its elaborate, flowing rhyme scheme and lingering final line match the poem's sensuous, dreamlike richness
It imitates the rhythms of ordinary speech, so the poem seems to be a conversation between the speaker and the reader
It creates a comic effect, since the long final line seems to deflate the solemn feeling of each stanza
It gives a sense of fragmentation, since each stanza ends abruptly and so breaks the continuity of the narrative
It prevents any narrative from developing, so the poem is a series of pictures and does not tell a continuous story
hardQuiz.e: The interlocking rhymes and extended final line support the lush, lingering mood.

hardQuiz.q: Which of the following would be the most persuasive thesis for an essay comparing Hawthorne and Poe?
o: Hawthorne and Poe are both American writers of the nineteenth century, and each of them composed short fiction for magazines
Hawthorne wrote about Puritans and their sins while Poe wrote about decaying aristocrats, and the two differ in setting
Both authors wrote about dark subjects such as guilt, madness and death, and their works unsettle the readers of their time
Both authors use settings to externalize inner turmoil, but Hawthorne locates the source of evil in social and spiritual hypocrisy while Poe locates it in psychological and familial decay
Both authors are interesting, since each uses symbols and settings that readers continue to study and to discuss today
Hawthorne’s story is longer than Poe’s, and this allows him to develop his characters and his symbols more fully
hardQuiz.e: A strong comparison identifies a shared technique and a precise, defensible difference.

hardQuiz.q: Irving's phrase "petticoat government" is best understood as which rhetorical choice?
o: A literal description of the colonial government, which was then administered largely by the wives of its officials
A symbol of the Revolution, in which the petticoat stands for the colonists’ rejection of their king’s authority
An allusion to a historical event, the Petticoat Rebellion, which the original readers of the tale would have known
A humorous metaphor that borrows political terms for a domestic situation
A euphemism for a crime that Rip’s wife committed against him, which the narrator prefers not to name outright
A technical term from the law of the period that describes a household governed by the wife
hardQuiz.e: The phrase applies the vocabulary of government to the household, a mock-heroic comparison.

hardQuiz.q: Which feature of "Young Goodman Brown" most strongly supports a reading of the story as allegory?
o: The setting in a particular village, which gives the story a historical and local character that a general fable lacks
The use of dialogue between the characters, which keeps the action moving and lets each speaker reveal who he is
The story’s brevity, which allows the author to keep the reader’s attention fixed on a single sequence of events
The story’s historical period, which is carefully fixed by details of dress and speech that the author provides
The story’s use of the first person, which makes the narrator a character whose reliability the reader must judge
Characters and objects whose names and attributes (Faith, the serpent staff, the ribbon) correspond to abstract moral ideas
hardQuiz.e: Allegory pairs concrete elements with abstract meanings; the names and symbols here do so.

hardQuiz.q: In "The Fall of the House of Usher," the narrator's decision to flee the house after Madeline's appearance primarily serves which function in the story's structure?
o: It reveals that the narrator is a coward who lacks the courage to help his friend, and so it shapes his character
It provides an outside witness to the collapse, allowing the final image to be described while preserving the narrator's role as observer
It resolves the story’s romantic plot, since the narrator’s flight allows Madeline and Roderick to die together in peace
It introduces a new conflict between the narrator and the house, which the story leaves unresolved after he escapes
It shows that the narrator is the true villain, since he was present at every event and is therefore to blame
It indicates that the narrator caused the collapse of the house by disturbing the vault where Madeline had lain
hardQuiz.e: He escapes so that he can report the house's destruction, completing the frame.

hardQuiz.q: Which of the following best explains why Irving includes a postscript from the fictional historian in which he affirms the story's truth?
o: It extends the mock-historical frame and gives a final, tongue-in-cheek assurance
It corrects the story’s errors and gives a more reliable account of what the legend said about Hendrick Hudson
It adds a serious political argument about the American Revolution that the story itself had only hinted at before
It reveals that the story is a forgery, so that the reader must reconsider everything the historian has said
It changes the story’s ending, so that Rip returns to the mountain and does not remain in his village
It introduces a second narrator who disagrees with the first and so makes the reader doubt the story’s truth
hardQuiz.e: The postscript maintains the comic pose of historical authority.

hardQuiz.q: What is the most significant way in which "The Haunted Palace" functions within "The Fall of the House of Usher"?
o: It interrupts the plot with comic relief, since the poem’s imagery is so exaggerated as to seem a parody of grief
It introduces a new character, a king whose palace stands for the house and whose fate the story will later repeat
It offers a compressed allegory of Usher's mind that foreshadows the house's and his own ruin
It describes a historical event, the fall of an ancient dynasty, which Usher says that his family had once suffered
It is a hymn praising the house and its family, which Usher composed in a happier time and now sings with pride
It explains why Madeline is ill, since the poem tells how her sickness came from a curse laid upon the house
hardQuiz.e: The poem's descent from splendor to horror mirrors Usher's mental decline and prefigures the ending.

hardQuiz.q: A student claims that Twain's tall tale is, among other things, a satire of human behavior. Which element offers the strongest support?
o: The jay's absurd persistence and the jeering audience of jays mirror human stubbornness and mockery
The mention of a cabin that stands empty and abandoned, which shows how the jay’s labor has gone unseen
The use of dialect in the narrator’s speech, which shows how the miner’s language differs from the writer’s own
The mention of a miner who tells the story, which shows that the tale comes from a man who has seen jays
The mention of an owl that watches the jays from a tree, which shows that nature is indifferent to their labor
The mention of an acorn, which is the object the jay drops into the hole and which shows his simple purpose
hardQuiz.e: The animals' behavior is rendered in human terms, which implicitly comments on people.

hardQuiz.q: In "Rip Van Winkle," which statement best describes the relationship between the story's humor and its treatment of historical change?
o: The humor mocks the American Revolution as foolish and vain, so that Rip’s sleep appears the wisest way to live through it
The humor is unrelated to the theme of historical change, since the jokes concern only Rip’s marriage and his idle habits
The humor celebrates war and the heroes of the Revolution, whose deeds the narrator praises in an extravagant tone
The humor is bitter and angry, since the narrator resents the changes that the Revolution has brought to the village
The story contains no humor in its account of Rip’s return, which the narrator describes with serious and tragic feeling
The humor softens the upheaval of the Revolution by viewing it through an ordinary man's bewilderment
hardQuiz.e: Comedy renders historical change human-scaled and gentle.

hardQuiz.q: Which of the following is the most accurate description of the way Hawthorne handles the question of Faith's fate in the forest scene?
o: He declares that she is lost to the devil, so that Brown’s despair at the end of the scene is entirely justified
He confirms that she is saved by her faith, so that Brown’s later doubts are shown to be mistaken and unjust
He leaves unresolved whether she is truly present or a figment of Brown's fear, which keeps the story's central uncertainty alive
He shows that she is the devil in disguise, which accounts for Brown’s horror at seeing her among the converts
He reveals that she is a witch who has deceived her husband, so that his withdrawal from her is justified
He ignores her fate in the forest and returns to it only in the last paragraph, where he mentions her briefly
hardQuiz.e: Brown's last glimpse and the morning's evidence leave Faith's role open.

hardQuiz.q: In "The Eve of St. Agnes," the contrast between the Beadsman's cold, ascetic prayer and Madeline's chamber of warmth and color most directly presents which tension?
o: Between wealth and poverty, as the cold of the chapel contrasts with the rich furnishings of the castle’s great hall
Between youth and political power, as the young lovers defy a household governed by older and more powerful men
Between city and country, as the lovers’ flight takes them out of the castle and into the wild landscape beyond
Between spiritual renunciation and sensuous, earthly love
Between science and religion, as the Beadsman’s prayers are set against Porphyro’s scheming and practical resourcefulness
Between reason and madness, as Madeline’s dream of her lover disturbs her judgment and leads her to a rash decision
hardQuiz.e: Keats juxtaposes ascetic devotion with sensual romance.

hardQuiz.q: Which of the following best distinguishes the way the unit's authors use setting to shape theme?
o: Hawthorne uses a symbolic wilderness, Poe a personified house, Irving a folkloric mountain, Keats a richly sensory chamber, and Twain a cabin as comic stage
All of the authors use the same kind of setting, an isolated place that separates the characters from ordinary life
None of the authors uses setting thematically, since each of them chooses a background merely to place the action
Only Poe uses setting to express theme, since the other authors treat their settings as a neutral background
Only the poem uses setting to shape theme, since a prose story lacks the space to develop one in detail
Setting in all of these texts is realistic only, and it serves chiefly to establish the time and place of the action
hardQuiz.e: Each setting is tailored to its work's tone and theme.

hardQuiz.q: A student wants to argue that the narrators in the unit shape readers' sympathies. Which pair provides the clearest contrast in narrative stance?
o: Hawthorne’s and Poe’s, because both use a first-person narrator who is a participant in the story’s events
Twain’s and Keats’s, because both use dialect to give the narrator an air of rustic honesty and good humor
Irving’s and Twain’s, because both are third-person narrators who observe events from a distance without comment
Keats’s and Hawthorne’s, because both are poets whose narrators remain apart from the events they describe
Irving's amused historian, who invites affectionate laughter at Rip, and Poe's anxious observer, who invites dread
Poe’s and Twain’s, because both are historians who present their tales as accurate records of events that took place
hardQuiz.e: The tone and reliability of the narrators shape how readers feel.

hardQuiz.q: Identify the person being spoken to in: “Madman! I tell you that she now stands without the door!”
o: The narrator
Madeline
A servant
The family physician
Himself alone
The house
hardQuiz.e: Usher is speaking to the narrator, who has been reading aloud to him.

hardQuiz.q: In “The Fall of the House of Usher,” the pronoun “she” in “she now stands without the door” refers to
o: The narrator’s wife
A servant
A figure from the romance being read
Usher’s mother
Madeline
The house itself
hardQuiz.e: Usher believes his entombed sister Madeline has come to the door.

hardQuiz.q: In “The Eve of St. Agnes,” the pronoun “his” in “while his frosted breath, / Like pious incense from a censer old, / Seem’d taking flight for heaven” refers to
o: Porphyro
Angela’s husband
The priest of the chapel
The Baron
Madeline’s father
The Beadsman
hardQuiz.e: The Beadsman’s cold breath rises like incense as he prays.

hardQuiz.q:
Which of the following devices is (are) present in: “a staff, which bore the likeness of a great black snake, so curiously wrought that it might almost be seen to twist and wriggle itself like a living serpent”?
I. Simile
II. Allusion
III. Hyperbole
o: I only
II only
III only
I and III only
I, II, and III
I and II only
hardQuiz.e: “like a living serpent” is a simile and the snake evokes the serpent of Eden (allusion). The description is vivid but not an exaggeration.

hardQuiz.q:
Which of the following devices is (are) present in: “a sharp tongue is the only edged tool that grows keener with constant use”?
I. Metaphor
II. Paradox
III. Alliteration
o: I only
I and II only
II only
I and III only
III only
I, II, and III
hardQuiz.e: The tongue is metaphorically an edged tool; the idea that use sharpens it is witty but not a paradox in the strict sense, and there is no meaningful alliteration.

hardQuiz.q:
Which of the following devices is (are) present in: “the vacant eye-like windows”?
I. Personification
II. Imagery
III. Onomatopoeia
o: I only
II only
III only
I and III only
I and II only
I, II, and III
hardQuiz.e: The house is given eyes (personification) and the phrase appeals to the visual sense (imagery).

hardQuiz.q:
Which of the following devices is (are) present in: “Like pious incense from a censer old”?
I. Simile
II. Imagery
III. Irony
o: I only
II only
III only
I and II only
I and III only
II and III only
hardQuiz.e: The breath is compared to incense with “like,” and the image is visual and olfactory. There is no irony in the line.

hardQuiz.q:
Which of the following devices is (are) present in the description of Rip’s reaction to the Revolution: “there was one species of despotism under which he had long groaned, and that was—petticoat government”?
I. Irony
II. Metaphor
III. Understatement
o: I only
II only
III only
I and II only
I and III only
I, II, and III
hardQuiz.e: The mock-political language is ironic and “petticoat government” is metonymy, a garment standing for a wife’s rule; the line is not understated.

hardQuiz.q:
Which of the following devices is (are) present in: “The deep and dark tarn at my feet closed sullenly and silently over the fragments of the ‘House of Usher’”?
I. Personification
II. Alliteration
III. Hyperbole
o: I only
II only
III only
I and III only
I, II, and III
I and II only
hardQuiz.e: The tarn “closed sullenly,” attributing a mood to water (personification), and “deep and dank” and “sullenly and silently” repeat sounds (alliteration).

hardQuiz.q: Based on the passage, which of the following would Rip Van Winkle most likely agree with?
o: Hard work is the foundation of good character
A person should have time to enjoy company and idleness
Wives should manage the finances of a household
Political change is the most important event in a person’s life
Rip’s neighbors are lazy
Land ownership requires constant toil
hardQuiz.e: Rip prefers fishing, hunting and neighborly conversation to farm work and takes political change lightly.

hardQuiz.q: Based on the passage, which of the following would Dame Van Winkle most likely disagree with?
o: Scolding her husband for his idleness
The need to repair the fences
The importance of providing for the children
Doing household chores
Rip’s habit of avoiding his farm work
The usefulness of a thrifty housekeeper
hardQuiz.e: She constantly berates Rip for neglecting his duties, so she would oppose his idleness.

hardQuiz.q: Based on the passage, which of the following would Roderick Usher most likely agree with?
o: The narrator’s visit will cure his illness, since only a friend could relieve a sickness so closely tied to the mind
His sister’s illness has no effect on him, for he regards her as a person quite apart from his own concerns
The family’s name is of little importance, and he is content to see the house and its line come to an end
The house and its family are bound together in a fatal way
Music is a poor comfort to a mind as troubled as his own, and he has abandoned all hope of relief from it
Plants and stones cannot feel, and so the house and its surroundings cannot influence a person’s fate
hardQuiz.e: Usher believes in the sentience of the house and links it with his family’s fate.

hardQuiz.q: All of the following are true of Rip Van Winkle EXCEPT:
o: He enjoys helping his neighbors
He avoids household chores
He is a favorite with children
He is eager to farm his own land
He is sociable in the village
He sleeps for many years
hardQuiz.e: Irving stresses his aversion to work on his own farm.

hardQuiz.q: All of the following are true of the village after Rip’s sleep EXCEPT:
o: Nicholas Vedder is still alive
The portrait on the sign has changed
Rip’s wife is dead
His daughter is grown and married
The old inn has changed
Rip’s gun is rusted
hardQuiz.e: Nicholas Vedder has died; his gravestone is seen in the churchyard.

hardQuiz.q: All of the following are descriptions of the stranger Rip meets in the mountains EXCEPT:
o: A short, stout old man with a grizzled beard
A man in the antique Dutch dress of the previous century
A tall, slender man in modern dress
A man with a grizzled beard and bushy hair
A man carrying a keg who beckons Rip to help him
A man who silently signals Rip to follow him up the ravine
hardQuiz.e: The stranger wears old-fashioned Dutch clothing, so “modern dress” is false.

hardQuiz.q: All of the following are used to characterize the traveler in “Young Goodman Brown” EXCEPT:
o: His carrying a Bible
His resemblance to Brown
His staff that looks like a snake
His fine, grave dress
His traveling in the forest at night
His claim that he knew Brown’s ancestors
hardQuiz.e: He carries a staff, not a Bible.

hardQuiz.q: All of the following are true of the house of Usher EXCEPT:
o: It is old and decayed
It has a visible fissure
It has a vault
It is surrounded by a tarn
It stands in a cheerful valley
It has vacant, eye-like windows
hardQuiz.e: The setting is bleak and gloomy, not cheerful.

hardQuiz.q:
Which of the following lists the events of “Rip Van Winkle” in the order they occur?
I. Rip meets the stranger carrying a keg
II. Rip returns to a changed village
III. Rip sleeps for twenty years
o: I, II, III
II, I, III
III, I, II
II, III, I
III, II, I
I, III, II
hardQuiz.e: Rip meets the stranger, drinks the liquor and sleeps, then returns to the changed village.

hardQuiz.q:
Which of the following lists the events of “Young Goodman Brown” in the order they occur?
I. Brown meets Goody Cloyse
II. Brown leaves Faith at the doorstep
III. Brown sees the pink ribbon fall
o: I, II, III
III, I, II
II, I, III
II, III, I
I, III, II
III, II, I
hardQuiz.e: He leaves Faith, meets Goody Cloyse on the road, then sees the ribbon.

hardQuiz.q:
Which of the following lists the events of “The Fall of the House of Usher” in the order they occur?
I. The narrator reads the “Mad Trist”
II. Madeline is entombed
III. The house falls into the tarn
o: I, II, III
III, I, II
II, III, I
II, I, III
I, III, II
III, II, I
hardQuiz.e: Madeline is entombed, the narrator reads the “Mad Trist,” and then the house falls.

hardQuiz.q:
Which of the following lists the events of “The Eve of St. Agnes” in the order they occur?
I. Porphyro enters the castle
II. Madeline prepares for sleep
III. The lovers flee

III, I, II
I, III, II
II, III, I
I, II, III
III, II, I
