workedExamples.title: Identifying the Rhetorical Situation
workedExamples.prompt: A retired general publishes an op-ed in a national newspaper the week after a controversial military budget vote, urging Congress to reconsider. Identify SOAPSTone.
steps: Speaker: a retired general — someone with firsthand military authority, lending ethos
Occasion: the recent, controversial budget vote (this is the exigence)
Audience: Congress and newspaper-reading citizens who influence public opinion
Purpose: to persuade Congress to reconsider the budget decision
Subject: the military budget vote and its consequences
Tone: likely urgent and authoritative, given the speaker's background and timing
workedExamples.answer: Speaker=retired general (ethos); Occasion/exigence=the budget vote; Audience=Congress/public; Purpose=to persuade reconsideration; Subject=the budget vote; Tone=urgent, authoritative.

workedExamples.title: Naming and Explaining an Appeal
workedExamples.prompt: A nonprofit's ad says: 'Dr. Elena Ruiz, a pediatric surgeon with 20 years of experience, warns that delaying this legislation will cost children's lives.' Identify the appeals at work and their effect.
steps: Ethos: citing Dr. Ruiz's credentials (pediatric surgeon, 20 years) establishes her authority on the subject
Pathos: 'cost children's lives' evokes fear and urgency about vulnerable children
Logos is comparatively weak here — no data or statistics are cited
Effect: combining a credible expert's warning with emotionally charged stakes makes the claim feel both authoritative and urgent
workedExamples.answer: Primarily ethos (credentials) blended with pathos ('cost children's lives'), creating an authoritative and emotionally urgent warning.

workedExamples.title: Analyzing a Repetition Device
workedExamples.prompt: 'We shall fight on the beaches, we shall fight on the landing grounds, we shall fight in the fields and in the streets, we shall fight in the hills.' Identify the device and its effect.
steps: The phrase 'we shall fight' repeats at the start of each clause — this is anaphora
The repetition builds escalating intensity and resolve as each new location is added
The listing of locations (beaches, grounds, fields, streets, hills) suggests total, unwavering commitment
Effect: the device creates a rhythmic, almost unstoppable sense of determination, rallying the audience
workedExamples.answer: Anaphora ('we shall fight...'), which builds escalating resolve and rallies the audience through relentless repetition.

workedExamples.title: Analyzing Diction and Syntax Together
workedExamples.prompt: Compare: (A) 'The company terminated 200 employees.' (B) 'Two hundred families lost their livelihoods overnight.' Explain the rhetorical effect of the difference.
steps: Sentence A uses formal, corporate diction ('terminated,' 'employees') that feels clinical and distanced
Sentence B uses emotionally charged, concrete diction ('families,' 'livelihoods,' 'overnight') that personalizes the impact
Syntax: both are short declarative sentences, but B's word choices shift the emotional register dramatically
Effect: identical facts can be framed to minimize (A) or amplify (B) emotional impact purely through diction
workedExamples.answer: Diction alone shifts the tone from clinical/distanced (A) to emotionally personal and urgent (B), despite reporting the same event.

workedExamples.title: Turning Evidence into Commentary
workedExamples.prompt: Evidence: 'A 2023 study found that students who read 20 minutes daily scored 15% higher on reading assessments.' Write one sentence of commentary (not summary) using this evidence to support the claim that schools should mandate daily reading time.
steps: Summary would just restate the finding — that's not enough on its own
Commentary must explain WHY this evidence supports the specific claim about mandating reading time
Connect the statistic to the argument's stakes: what does a 15% gain mean for struggling readers specifically?
Example commentary: 'This 15% gain shows that even a small, consistent daily habit can meaningfully close achievement gaps — exactly the kind of low-cost intervention schools should be mandating.'
workedExamples.answer: Commentary example: 'This 15% gain shows even a small daily habit can meaningfully close achievement gaps — exactly why schools should mandate it.'

workedExamples.title: Writing a Concession and Rebuttal
workedExamples.prompt: Claim: schools should eliminate final exams. Write a one-sentence concession followed by a one-sentence rebuttal.
steps: Concession: acknowledge a fair point on the opposing side, e.g., that final exams can measure retention of a full semester's material
Rebuttal: explain why the writer's position still holds despite this valid point
Concession example: 'Final exams can, admittedly, reveal whether students retained material over a full semester.'
Rebuttal example: 'But a single high-stakes test rewards short-term cramming over the deep, lasting learning it claims to measure.'
workedExamples.answer: Concession: exams can measure semester-long retention. Rebuttal: but they reward cramming over the deep learning they claim to test.

workedExamples.title: Synthesizing Two Sources into One Point
workedExamples.prompt: Source A: 'Remote work increased reported employee satisfaction by 22%.' Source B: 'Companies with remote policies saw a 30% drop in office lease costs.' Write one synthesis sentence using both sources to support the claim that companies should adopt permanent remote work.
steps: Identify what each source contributes: A = employee benefit, B = financial benefit
A strong synthesis sentence combines them into ONE argument, not two separate summaries

Draft: 'Beyond the well-documented 22% rise in employee satisfaction (Source A), companies adopting remote work have also cut office lease costs by 30% (Source B) — evidence that the shift benefits both employees and the bottom line.'
This models proper citation-with-commentary, using two sources to build one unified point
workedExamples.answer: Example: 'Beyond the 22% rise in employee satisfaction (Source A), remote companies cut lease costs by 30% (Source B) — benefiting both employees and the bottom line.'

workedExamples.title: Writing a Device-to-Effect Sentence
workedExamples.prompt: A passage uses short, fragmented sentences ('No warning. No time. Just silence.') to describe a disaster's onset. Write a full rhetorical analysis sentence connecting this syntax to its effect.
steps: Identify the device: fragmented, staccato syntax
Identify the specific effect: mirrors the abruptness and disorientation of the disaster itself
Connect it to purpose: this makes the reader feel the shock the writer wants to convey, rather than just describing it
Draft: 'The fragmented syntax — “No warning. No time. Just silence.” — mimics the abruptness of the disaster itself, plunging the reader into the same disorientation the writer wants them to feel.'
workedExamples.answer: Example: 'The fragmented syntax mimics the disaster's abruptness, plunging the reader into the same disorientation the writer wants them to feel.'

workedExamples.title: Building a Nuanced Thesis
workedExamples.prompt: Prompt: 'Is competition beneficial to society?' Write a qualified, sophisticated thesis (not a simple yes/no).
steps: An absolute thesis ('competition is always good') is less sophisticated than a qualified one
Identify a meaningful condition under which the claim holds or doesn't

Draft: 'While competition drives innovation in economic markets, it becomes destructive when applied to systems — like healthcare or education — where cooperation, not rivalry, best serves the public good.'
This thesis is specific, arguable, and shows nuance by distinguishing between contexts
workedExamples.answer: Example: 'Competition drives innovation in markets, but becomes destructive in systems like healthcare or education, where cooperation better serves the public good.'

workedExamples.title: Fixing a Comma Splice and Checking Parallelism
workedExamples.prompt: Revise: 'The committee reviewed the proposal, they approved it unanimously, and are moving to sign, seal, and finalizing the contract.'
steps: First, identify the comma splice: 'reviewed the proposal, they approved it' joins two independent clauses with only a comma
Fix with a period or semicolon: 'The committee reviewed the proposal; they approved it unanimously.'
Next, check the list 'sign, seal, and finalizing' — 'finalizing' breaks parallel structure with 'sign' and 'seal'
Corrected: 'The committee reviewed the proposal; they approved it unanimously and are moving to sign, seal, and finalize the contract.'
workedExamples.answer: 'The committee reviewed the proposal; they approved it unanimously and are moving to sign, seal, and finalize the contract.'

workedExamples.title: Map the rhetorical situation with SOAPSTone
workedExamples.prompt: A retired general publishes an op-ed the week Congress debates the defense budget, urging lawmakers to fund veterans' health care before new weapons systems. Break down the rhetorical situation.
steps: Speaker: a retired general - high ethos on military matters, and a credible critic of defense spending priorities.
Occasion: the budget debate this week (kairos - a moment when the argument can actually influence a decision).
Audience: members of Congress and the voters who watch them, especially those who claim to support the troops.
Purpose: to persuade lawmakers to prioritize veterans' health funding over new weapons.
Subject: defense budget priorities. Tone: likely firm, disappointed, and morally serious.
workedExamples.answer: The general leverages insider ethos and precise timing (kairos) to press a 'support the troops' audience toward a specific budget choice.

workedExamples.title: Analyze an appeal, not just label it
workedExamples.prompt: A passage reads: 'I have buried men I trained. I have written the letters home. When I tell you this policy costs lives, I am not speculating.' Identify and analyze the appeal.
steps: The appeal is primarily ethos, reinforced by pathos.
The short, first-person clauses establish direct personal experience, positioning the speaker as a witness rather than a pundit.
'Buried men I trained' and 'written the letters home' carry heavy emotional weight, but their function is to authorize the claim that follows.
The final sentence converts that authority into a logical claim ('not speculating'), so the reader accepts the causal assertion.
Effect: the audience is inclined to trust the speaker's judgment and treat disagreement as callous.
workedExamples.answer: The writer builds credibility through lived experience and channels emotion into it, making the subsequent causal claim hard to dismiss.

workedExamples.title: Explain the effect of syntax and repetition
workedExamples.prompt: A passage: 'They took the land. They took the language. They took the names of the children and gave them new ones.' Analyze the rhetorical effect.
steps: The repeated subject-verb opening ('They took') is anaphora.
The parallel structure and mounting specificity (land, language, names of children) create a cumulative, escalating rhythm.
Asyndeton-like brevity - short, unconnected sentences - makes each loss land as a separate blow.
The final clause extends the pattern with an added consequence ('and gave them new ones'), breaking the rhythm to emphasize the deepest violation.
Effect: the passage builds a sense of relentless, systematic dispossession and moral outrage.
workedExamples.answer: Anaphora and parallel short sentences accumulate force; the broken final clause spotlights the gravest loss.

workedExamples.title: Name a precise tone and track a shift
workedExamples.prompt: A passage begins with wry, detached observations about a city council meeting ('another Tuesday, another three-hour debate about parking'), then shifts to: 'But behind the tedium, a family was about to lose its home.' Analyze the tone.
steps: Opening tone: wry and detached - the diction ('another Tuesday,' 'tedium') and the mundane subject signal amused impatience.
The pivot word 'But' marks a deliberate tonal shift.
The second sentence drops the irony for plain, weighty diction ('lose its home').
The shift reframes the 'tedium' as a moral failure of attention, not just boredom.
Effect: the reader is moved from detached amusement to discomfort, and the writer's real concern is revealed.
workedExamples.answer: The tone shifts from wry detachment to sober concern at 'But,' turning a joke about bureaucracy into an argument about consequences.

workedExamples.title: Turn summary into commentary
workedExamples.prompt: A student writes: 'The author notes that 60 percent of the town's water pipes are over a century old.' Add commentary that connects this evidence to a claim that the town has under-invested in basic infrastructure.
steps: Restate the evidence briefly (already done): 60 percent of pipes are 100+ years old.
Ask: what does this figure prove about the claim?
Connect: pipes that old are well past their design life, so a majority-aged system reflects decades of deferred maintenance.
Extend: this supports the claim that spending was diverted elsewhere while a core service decayed.
Result sentence: 'That most of the system predates living memory is not a quirk of history but evidence of sustained neglect: for generations, the town chose not to replace what it could not see.'
workedExamples.answer: Commentary explains that an aging majority of pipes demonstrates long-term deferred investment, directly supporting the under-investment claim.

workedExamples.title: Build a qualified thesis and outline the reasoning
workedExamples.prompt: Prompt: Should high schools start later in the morning? Draft a defensible, qualified thesis and a three-part line of reasoning.
steps: Take a position, but qualify it: later start times help most, but not without trade-offs.

Thesis: 'High schools should push start times to at least 8:30 a.m., because the sleep benefits for adolescents are well documented, provided districts adjust bus schedules and after-school activities to avoid shifting the burden onto working families.'
Sub-claim 1: adolescent biology - later melatonin release makes early starts counterproductive for learning.
Sub-claim 2: measurable outcomes - districts that shifted later report better attendance and fewer car crashes.
Sub-claim 3: the concession - transportation and childcare costs are real, so the policy must include a plan to manage them; this makes the argument more persuasive, not less.
workedExamples.answer: A qualified thesis plus a three-part line of reasoning (biology, outcomes, and a managed concession) gives the essay a clear spine.

workedExamples.title: Organize a synthesis paragraph by your claim
workedExamples.prompt: Synthesis prompt on whether cities should offer free public transit. You have Source A (ridership data), Source C (a budget analysis), and Source E (an equity argument). Draft one body paragraph organized around your claim.
steps: State your sub-claim first: free transit is justified primarily as an equity measure, and the fiscal cost is manageable.
Bring in Source E to establish the equity stakes: low-income residents spend a disproportionate share of income on fares.
Bring in Source A for support: pilot cities saw the largest ridership gains among riders who had previously walked long distances or skipped trips.
Bring in Source C to answer the obvious objection: the revenue loss is a small fraction of the transit budget and is partly offset by lower fare-collection costs.
Close the paragraph by tying the three back to your claim: the sources together show a targeted benefit at a bearable price.
workedExamples.answer: The paragraph leads with the writer's claim and recruits three sources to support and defend it, rather than summarizing each in turn.

workedExamples.title: Write a strong rhetorical analysis thesis
workedExamples.prompt: You are analyzing a commencement speech in which the speaker repeatedly contrasts 'the job you take' with 'the person you become,' uses self-deprecating anecdotes, and ends with a direct charge to the graduates. Draft a thesis.
steps: Do not list devices. Ask: what is the speaker doing overall, and to what end?
The speaker is redefining success for an audience anxious about careers, and lowering the stakes of failure.
Name the key moves that serve that purpose: the repeated antithesis, the humbling anecdotes, the closing charge.
Combine into an arguable claim about strategy and effect.

Thesis: 'By repeatedly setting external achievement against internal growth and undercutting his own resume with stories of failure, the speaker reframes success as character rather than career, freeing an anxious graduating class to take risks - a redefinition his final direct charge asks them to act on.'
workedExamples.answer: The thesis states what the speaker does (reframes success, lowers the cost of failure) and to what effect, previewing the analysis.

workedExamples.title: Use concede-then-counter in an argument
workedExamples.prompt: You are arguing that public libraries should expand evening hours. A reader objects that staffing costs are already strained. Write a concede-then-counter passage.
steps: Acknowledge the objection fairly and specifically: 'The concern about staffing is legitimate; many library systems have cut positions over the past decade and cannot simply add shifts.'
Grant that it constrains the solution: 'Any expansion must be designed around that reality rather than ignoring it.'

Counter by limiting the objection's force: 'But evening demand is concentrated in a few branches and a few hours, so a targeted extension - two branches, three nights a week - would cost far less than a system-wide change.'
Add support: 'Pilot programs elsewhere covered the cost by shifting, not adding, hours, opening later and closing later on those nights.'
Return to the thesis: 'A narrow, evidence-based expansion answers the staffing worry instead of being defeated by it.'
workedExamples.answer: The passage concedes the staffing point, then narrows the proposal so the objection no longer defeats it, strengthening the writer's credibility.

workedExamples.title: Revise a wordy sentence for the MC 'writing' skill
workedExamples.prompt: Revise: 'Due to the fact that the committee was not able to reach a consensus decision, it was decided that the vote would be postponed until a later date.'
steps: 'Due to the fact that' is padding for 'because.'
'consensus decision' is redundant; 'consensus' or 'agreement' suffices.
'it was decided that' is passive and vague; name the actor or drop it.
'postponed until a later date' is redundant; 'postponed' already means to a later time.
Assemble the concise version.
workedExamples.answer: 'Because the committee could not agree, it postponed the vote.'

workedExamples.title: Analyzing Twain's anthropomorphism in "Baker's Bluejay Yarn"
workedExamples.prompt: In a well-developed paragraph, explain how Twain uses anthropomorphism and Jim Baker's point of view to advance a theme in "Baker's Bluejay Yarn".
steps: Claim: Twain gives the bluejays human speech and behavior, and lets Jim Baker narrate in a folksy voice, to suggest that human effort and pride can be as absurd as the jay's.
Evidence: choose the knothole tale (the jay dropping acorns into the hole) and one line of Baker's confident, dialect-heavy commentary; cite with author, title and page.
Commentary 1: explain that anthropomorphism makes the jays' failure feel like a human one, so the joke doubles as a metaphor for futile effort.
Commentary 2: explain how Baker's serious, sincere tone (indirect characterization) juxtaposed with the ridiculous story creates humor and irony and builds his credibility.
Link: tie back to purpose. Twain uses humor to reflect on the foolishness in human society of his time (1835-1880).
workedExamples.answer: Twain uses anthropomorphism and Baker's sincere voice to turn a comic animal story into a commentary on human folly. When the jay keeps dropping acorns into the knothole, its stubborn effort mirrors human persistence in the face of futility, and the juxtaposition of Baker's earnest tone with an absurd tale invites the reader to laugh at both. The humor therefore serves Twain's purpose: to gently mock human pride.

workedExamples.title: Allusion and setting in "Young Goodman Brown"
workedExamples.prompt: In what ways is Hawthorne's use of setting and allusion in "Young Goodman Brown" significant? Answer in one cohesive response with evidence.
steps: Claim: Hawthorne moves Brown from Puritan Salem into a dark forest and layers in Biblical allusions to show that evil hides inside the very community that claims to be godly.
Setting evidence: contrast the ordered village and Faith's pink ribbons with the shadowy forest path; label the mood and the words that create it.
Allusion evidence: the traveler's serpent-like staff (Eden) and the forest communion; explain what each reference suggests about temptation and hypocrisy.
Commentary: explain how setting and allusion together push Brown's shift from trusting to distrustful and support the theme of lost faith.
Link: end on Hawthorne's critical view of Puritan hypocrisy and the story's ambiguity.
workedExamples.answer: Hawthorne uses the shift from the ordered village to the dark forest, along with allusions such as the serpent-like staff, to argue that evil is hidden inside Puritan society itself. The setting shows Brown moving away from the safety of community, while the Biblical references frame his choice as a moral fall. By the end, Brown's lasting distrust proves how much damage suspicion of others can do.

workedExamples.title: Which device? Answering a “which is present” question
workedExamples.prompt: Which literary device is present in: “A tart temper never mellows with age, and a sharp tongue is the only edged tool that grows keener with constant use”?
steps: Identify the comparison: a tongue is compared to an edged tool without using like or as.
Rule out simile (no like/as), personification (the tongue is not given human traits), and hyperbole (not an obvious exaggeration).
Name the device: metaphor. Explain the effect: it warns of Dame's constant scolding and helps the reader sympathize with Rip.
workedExamples.answer: Metaphor. Irving compares a scolding tongue to a tool that only gets sharper with use, characterizing Dame Van Winkle as harsh and unchanging.

workedExamples.title: Word in context: vocabulary from Rip Van Winkle
workedExamples.prompt: In “Rip Van Winkle”, Irving describes Dame Van Winkle as a “termagant.” What does the word most nearly mean, and how do you know?
steps: Read the sentence and note the context: Dame scolds Rip and is described as having a tart temper.
Guess a meaning from context (a scolding, bad-tempered woman), then check against the definition: violent, overbearing, quarrelsome woman.
Choose the answer that matches in both meaning and tone (negative), not a mild word like 'merchant' or 'neighbor'.
workedExamples.answer: A violent, overbearing, quarrelsome woman. The scolding context and negative tone show it is an insult.

workedExamples.title: Chronology: ordering events in Usher
workedExamples.prompt: Put these Usher events in order: the house collapses; the narrator arrives; the narrator reads the Mad Trist; Madeline is entombed; Madeline appears at the door.
steps: Start with the narrator's arrival in response to Roderick's letter.
Madeline appears to die and is entombed in the vault.
Days later the narrator reads the Mad Trist; sounds match the story; Madeline appears; the house collapses.
workedExamples.answer: The narrator arrives; Madeline is entombed; the narrator reads the Mad Trist; Madeline appears at the door; the house collapses.

workedExamples.title: Speaker and addressee: “Madman! I tell you that she now stands without the door!”
workedExamples.prompt: Identify the speaker and the person being spoken to, and explain what the line shows.
steps: Speaker: Roderick Usher, screaming in terror as the narrator finishes reading.
Addressee: the narrator (his friend), who has been reading the Mad Trist.
Interpretation: Roderick has heard Madeline escaping the tomb, confirming the story's fusion of fiction and reality.
workedExamples.answer: Speaker: Roderick. Addressee: the narrator. It shows Roderick's terror and that the noises match Madeline's return.

PART_A.q: In SOAPSTone, 'Purpose' should always be phrased as:
o: An infinitive verb phrase ('to persuade...')
A single noun
A yes/no answer
A date
PART_A.e: Purpose is phrased as 'to ___,' describing the intended effect.

PART_A.q: An appeal to the speaker's credibility is called:
o: Ethos
Pathos
Logos
Kairos
PART_A.e: Ethos is the appeal to credibility and character.

PART_A.q: 'Either we act now, or all is lost' with no middle ground presented is a:
o: False dilemma
Hasty generalization
Valid syllogism
Antithesis
PART_A.e: Presenting only two extreme options is a false dilemma.

PART_A.q: Repetition of a phrase at the START of successive clauses is:
o: Anaphora
Epistrophe
Chiasmus
Antithesis
PART_A.e: Anaphora is repetition at the beginning of clauses.

PART_A.q: 'The city was a furnace in July' is an example of:
o: Metaphor
Simile
Personification
Understatement
PART_A.e: A direct comparison without 'like/as' is a metaphor.

PART_A.q: A word's emotional association, beyond its literal meaning, is its:
o: Connotation
Denotation
Syntax
Register
PART_A.e: Connotation is the emotional association attached to a word.

PART_A.q: Restating what evidence says without explaining its significance is:
o: Summary
Commentary
A thesis
A rebuttal
PART_A.e: Restating without analysis is summary, not commentary.

PART_A.q: Acknowledging a valid opposing point before returning to your argument is a:
o: Concession
Rebuttal
Thesis
Fallacy
PART_A.e: A concession acknowledges a fair opposing point.

PART_A.q: The synthesis essay requires citing a minimum of how many sources?
o: Three
One
Five
Zero
PART_A.e: At least three provided sources must be cited.

PART_A.q: The rhetorical analysis essay primarily analyzes:
o: HOW a writer builds their argument
WHETHER the reader agrees with the topic
The writer's biography only
Grammar errors only
PART_A.e: Rhetorical analysis focuses on the writer's rhetorical choices, not the reader's opinion of the topic.

PART_A.q: The 'O' in SOAPSTone that refers to the circumstances prompting the text is:
o: Occasion
Organization
Objective
Opinion
PART_A.e: Occasion is the time, place, and situation that gives rise to the writing.

PART_A.q: An appeal to the audience's emotions is:
o: pathos
ethos
logos
kairos
PART_A.e: Pathos moves the audience through feeling.

PART_A.q: Repetition of a phrase at the end of successive clauses is:
o: epistrophe
anaphora
antithesis
asyndeton
PART_A.e: Epistrophe repeats at the END; anaphora repeats at the beginning.

PART_A.q: 'The pen is mightier than the sword' relies on:
o: metonymy (pen for writing, sword for force)
hyperbole
litotes
personification
PART_A.e: Metonymy substitutes a closely associated thing for the concept.

PART_A.q: A writer's attitude toward the subject is the passage's:
o: tone
mood
thesis
exigence
PART_A.e: Tone is the writer's stance; mood is the reader's felt atmosphere.

PART_A.q: 'This proposal is a recipe for disaster' uses:
o: a metaphor
a simile
an allusion
understatement
PART_A.e: 'Recipe for disaster' compares the proposal to a recipe without 'like' or 'as.'

PART_A.q: A claim of value asserts that something is:
o: good or bad, right or wrong
true or false
required by policy
caused by another event
PART_A.e: Value claims render judgments against a standard.

PART_A.q: 'Because we have always done it this way, we should continue' is the fallacy of:
o: appeal to tradition
false dilemma
ad hominem
hasty generalization
PART_A.e: Longevity alone is offered as justification.

PART_A.q: A synthesis essay must use at least how many of the provided sources?
o: three
one
five
all of them
PART_A.e: The AP synthesis prompt requires citing a minimum of three sources.

PART_A.q: A rhetorical analysis essay should focus on:
o: how the writer argues and to what effect
whether the writer is correct
the analyst's own opinion of the topic
the writer's biography
PART_A.e: Analysis explains the rhetorical choices and their purpose.

PART_A.q: 'It is not unlikely that the plan will succeed' is an example of:
o: litotes
hyperbole
anaphora
chiasmus
PART_A.e: Understatement by double negation is litotes.

PART_A.q: Two independent clauses joined by only a comma create a:
o: comma splice
fragment
parallel construction
subordinate clause
PART_A.e: Fix with a period, semicolon, or coordinating conjunction.

PART_A.q: 'She likes to run, to swim, and biking' violates:
o: parallel structure
subject-verb agreement
pronoun agreement
comma usage
PART_A.e: The items must match in form: 'to run, to swim, and to bike.'

PART_A.q: An extended metaphor is:
o: a single comparison developed across a passage
a comparison using 'like' or 'as'
a brief reference to a famous text
two unrelated metaphors
PART_A.e: It governs a stretch of text with one comparison.

PART_A.q: The 'given-new' principle advises starting a sentence with:
o: familiar information and ending with the new point
the newest information
a transition word
a quotation
PART_A.e: Leading with the known creates flow.

PART_A.q: 'While the cost is real, the safety benefit outweighs it' is an example of:
o: concede-then-counter
a straw man
circular reasoning
an appeal to authority
PART_A.e: It grants a point, then limits its force.

PART_A.q: Reasoning from a general principle to a specific case is:
o: deductive
inductive
analogical
circular
PART_A.e: Deduction applies a general rule to a particular instance.

PART_A.q: A periodic sentence:
o: delays the main clause until the end
states the main clause first
has no subordinate clauses
is always short
PART_A.e: Delaying the main idea builds suspense and emphasis.

PART_A.q: On a multiple-choice writing question, the best answer is usually the one that is:
o: clearest and most concise
most formal
longest
most detailed
PART_A.e: AP MC writing items reward economical, precise language.

PART_A.q: 'Government of the people, by the people, for the people' primarily uses:
o: parallelism
hyperbole
allusion
irony
PART_A.e: The matched prepositional phrases create balanced, emphatic parallel structure.

PART_B1.q: 'You can't trust his economic plan, he dropped out of college' is an example of:
o: Ad hominem-style reasoning
Valid logos
Antithesis
Epistrophe
PART_B1.e: Dismissing an argument based on the person, not its content, echoes ad hominem.

PART_B1.q: 'Ask not what your country can do for you—ask what you can do for your country' is:
o: Chiasmus
Simile
Hyperbole
Personification
PART_B1.e: This reverses grammatical structure across clauses — chiasmus.

PART_B1.q: A long, breathless sentence packed with clauses tends to create a sense of:
o: Accumulation or momentum
Simplicity
Silence
Blunt finality
PART_B1.e: Long, layered sentences often build accumulation or momentum.

PART_B1.q: A claim asserting something SHOULD be done is a claim of:
o: Policy
Fact
Value
Tone
PART_B1.e: Policy claims argue for or against a course of action.

PART_B1.q: Organizing a synthesis essay strictly source-by-source is generally:
o: A weakness, resembling summary rather than argument
The ideal structure
Required by the prompt
Impossible to avoid
PART_B1.e: Source-by-source organization tends to produce summary instead of argument.

PART_B1.q: A rhetorical analysis essay focusing on 2-3 well-developed strategies rather than 6+ shallow ones is generally:
o: A stronger approach
A weaker approach
Against the rules
Irrelevant to quality
PART_B1.e: Depth over breadth typically produces stronger analysis.

PART_B1.q: An argument essay thesis that just restates the prompt is considered:
o: Underdeveloped — it isn't the writer's own specific position
The strongest possible thesis
Required by the rubric
Impossible to avoid
PART_B1.e: A thesis must be the writer's own specific, arguable claim.

PART_B1.q: 'I bought milk I forgot the eggs' with no punctuation between clauses is a:
o: Run-on sentence
Comma splice
Sentence fragment
Correct sentence
PART_B1.e: Independent clauses joined with no punctuation form a run-on.

PART_B1.q: A senator opens a floor speech with 'I have read every page of this bill.' The statement primarily builds:
o: ethos, by claiming diligence and firsthand knowledge
pathos, through emotional appeal
logos, through statistical evidence
kairos, through timing
PART_B1.e: Asserting personal effort and knowledge strengthens credibility.

PART_B1.q: 'Either we fund the arts fully or we abandon our culture entirely.' This commits:
o: a false dilemma
an ad hominem
a hasty generalization
circular reasoning
PART_B1.e: Two extremes are presented as the only options.

PART_B1.q: A passage of long, clause-heavy sentences is followed by 'It didn't work.' The syntactic contrast:
o: emphasizes the blunt conclusion after elaborate build-up
confuses the reader
signals a quotation
introduces a source
PART_B1.e: The short sentence lands hard because of what precedes it.

PART_B1.q: A writer describes a policy as 'a bridge to nowhere, built with borrowed money and painted to look finished.' This is:
o: an extended metaphor developing one comparison
a simple simile
litotes
a rhetorical question
PART_B1.e: The bridge comparison is developed across the sentence to shape judgment.

PART_B1.q: An author supports a broad claim about national reading habits with a single anecdote about her nephew. The evidence is:
o: relevant but insufficient
irrelevant
sufficient and representative
a fallacy of relevance
PART_B1.e: One case cannot establish a general trend.

PART_B1.q: A passage shifts from a bitter tone in describing a loss to a hopeful tone in proposing a remedy. The best analytical move is to:
o: identify the shift and explain how it repositions the audience toward action
label the whole passage 'emotional'
note only the first tone
treat the shift as an error
PART_B1.e: Tonal shifts usually mark a turn in the argument's strategy.

PART_B1.q: 'We should adopt this reform; studies from three states show it lowered costs' is reasoning that is primarily:
o: inductive, generalizing from evidence to a recommendation
deductive, from a first principle
circular
an appeal to authority
PART_B1.e: It moves from data in particular cases toward a general policy claim.

PART_B1.q: A columnist writes about a ballot measure 'with three days left before the polls close.' This clause establishes:
o: kairos - the urgency that makes the argument worth making now
the writer's ethos
a logical fallacy
a concession
PART_B1.e: The timing signals a narrow window for the argument to matter.

PART_B1.q: Which is the stronger rhetorical analysis thesis?
o: To make readers feel complicit in the problem, the writer shifts to second person and stacks concrete examples of everyday waste.
The writer uses second person, examples, and repetition.
The passage is about environmental waste.
The writer is an experienced journalist.
PART_B1.e: It names what the writer does and to what effect, not just which devices appear.

PART_B1.q: 'The reason the bill failed is because the votes were not there' should be revised to:
o: The bill failed because the votes were not there.
The reason for the bill's failure is due to a lack of votes.
The bill failed due to the reason that votes were lacking.
Because of the reason of votes, the bill failed.
PART_B1.e: 'The reason ... is because' is redundant.

PART_B1.q: A writer grants that a new fee 'will burden some small businesses' before arguing the fee is still justified. This move:
o: is a concession that strengthens the writer's credibility
abandons the argument
is a straw man
is circular reasoning
PART_B1.e: Acknowledging a real cost before countering it shows fairness.

PART_B1.q: 'And the debt grew, and the interest compounded, and the options narrowed' uses:
o: polysyndeton to convey relentless accumulation
asyndeton
anaphora
antithesis
PART_B1.e: Repeated 'and' slows the reader and stacks up the consequences.

PART_B1.q: A synthesis essay that spends one paragraph each summarizing Source A, B, and C, then gives an opinion, has fallen into:
o: the summary trap
over-quotation
citing too few sources
an informal tone
PART_B1.e: Synthesis must organize around the writer's own claims, using sources as evidence.

PART_B1.q: 'You can't take his budget seriously; he's never balanced a checkbook' is:
o: an ad hominem
a false dilemma
a red herring
an appeal to tradition
PART_B1.e: It attacks the person instead of the budget.

PART_B1.q: A writer chooses 'crowd' in one paragraph and 'mob' in the next for the same group. This signals:
o: a deliberate shift in the writer's attitude toward the group
a grammatical error
a citation
a concession
PART_B1.e: The connotative jump from neutral to threatening is a rhetorical choice.

PART_B1.q: For a 40-minute rhetorical analysis essay, analyzing three strategies in depth will generally:
o: score higher than listing eight strategies with no analysis
score lower for lack of coverage
earn full marks automatically
fail to address the prompt
PART_B1.e: The rubric rewards developed analysis over identification.

PART_B1.q: A colon is used correctly in:
o: The plan has one flaw: it assumes cooperation.
The plan has: one flaw, an assumption.
The plan has one flaw; it assumes cooperation, and more.
The plan: has one flaw.
PART_B1.e: The clause before the colon is complete, and the colon introduces the explanation.

PART_B1.q: An argument essay with two thoroughly analyzed examples will usually score higher than one with:
o: eight briefly mentioned examples
one analyzed example
a single statistic
no examples
PART_B1.e: Development and reasoning outweigh the number of examples.

PART_B1.q: 'The committee released their report' contains an error in:
o: pronoun-antecedent agreement ('committee' is singular: 'its')
verb tense
parallel structure
punctuation
PART_B1.e: Collective nouns acting as a unit take singular pronouns in formal American usage.

PART_B1.q: A rhetorical question such as 'How long will we wait?' functions to:
o: press the audience toward the implied conclusion
gather information
introduce a source
concede a point
PART_B1.e: The implied answer advances the argument.

PART_B2.q: Read: 'Every year, thousands of families lose their homes not to disaster, but to paperwork.' Identify the rhetorical device used and explain its effect in 2-3 sentences.
PART_B2.sa: This is antithesis/juxtaposition — contrasting 'disaster' with 'paperwork' in parallel structure. The effect is to make an ordinary, bureaucratic cause (paperwork) feel as devastating and urgent as a natural disaster, provoking outrage that something so mundane causes such serious harm.

PART_B2.q: A student's synthesis essay quotes all four provided sources at length but includes no original commentary connecting them to a thesis. Explain the specific weakness in this approach in 2-3 sentences.
PART_B2.sa: This approach turns the essay into a summary of sources rather than the writer's own argument. Without commentary connecting each citation to a specific claim, the reader cannot see how the evidence supports any particular position — the essay lacks a genuine line of reasoning.

PART_B2.q: Explain why a 'qualified' thesis (e.g., 'X is true, except when...') is often considered more sophisticated than an absolute, all-or-nothing thesis. Answer in 2-3 sentences.
PART_B2.sa: A qualified thesis acknowledges that an issue is more complex than a simple yes/no answer, showing the writer has considered exceptions or context. This nuance demonstrates deeper critical thinking than an absolute claim, which can seem oversimplified or naive about real-world complexity.

PART_B2.q: Explain the difference between summary and commentary in an essay's body paragraphs, and why commentary matters more for a strong argument. Answer in 2-3 sentences.
PART_B2.sa: Summary restates what evidence says, while commentary explains why that evidence matters and how it supports the thesis. Commentary matters more because it builds the actual line of reasoning connecting evidence to argument — without it, evidence sits unexplained and the essay reads as description rather than persuasion.

PART_B2.q: Read: 'The report is 300 pages long. I doubt anyone on the council has finished it. And yet we are asked to vote tonight.' Identify ONE rhetorical strategy in this passage and briefly explain its effect.
PART_B2.sa:
Strategy: the three short, escalating sentences (with a pointed 'And yet') build to an implied accusation.
Effect: the clipped syntax and the final concessive turn make the council's readiness to vote seem hasty and irresponsible, positioning the audience to distrust the process without the writer stating that outright.

PART_B2.q: Read: 'We were promised a park. We got a parking lot. We were promised jobs. We got a press release.' Identify the primary device and explain its effect.
PART_B2.sa:
Device: anaphora combined with antithesis ('We were promised X / We got Y').
Effect: the repeated structure creates a drumbeat of broken promises, and each pairing sets an expectation against a disappointing reality, building cumulative indignation and framing the authorities as unreliable.

PART_B2.q: A writer argues for later school start times using (1) a study of adolescent sleep biology and (2) a personal story about her own exhausted teenager. Briefly explain which piece of evidence is stronger for a broad policy claim and why.
PART_B2.sa:
The sleep-biology study is stronger for a broad policy claim because it is systematic and generalizable: it speaks to adolescents as a group rather than one household.
The personal story is relevant and adds vividness and pathos, but by itself it is insufficient to support a district-wide policy; it works best as illustration alongside the study.

PART_B2.q: Read the thesis: 'The author uses ethos, pathos, and logos to persuade the reader.' Explain why this is a weak rhetorical analysis thesis and rewrite it more effectively for a passage in which a scientist warns a general audience about an environmental risk.
PART_B2.sa:
It is weak because it only lists appeals; it makes no arguable claim about what the writer is doing or to what end, so the essay has nothing specific to prove.
Better: 'By translating technical data into everyday consequences and adopting the measured tone of a reluctant witness, the scientist makes the risk feel both credible and personally urgent to readers who distrust alarmism.'

PART_B2.q: Briefly explain the difference between a concession and a refutation, and give a one-sentence example of each responding to the claim 'Remote work hurts collaboration.'
PART_B2.sa:
A concession grants that an opposing point has merit; a refutation directly answers it and shows why it fails.
Concession: 'It is true that spontaneous hallway conversations are harder to replicate remotely.'
Refutation: 'But teams that adopted structured async updates and weekly in-person planning days reported collaboration scores equal to or above their pre-remote levels, so the loss is a design problem, not an inherent one.'

PART_B2.q: Read: 'Some say the museum should charge admission to cover costs. They have a point: budgets are tight. But a fee would keep out exactly the families the museum most wants to reach.' Identify the structural move and explain its effect.
PART_B2.sa:
Structural move: concede-then-counter. The writer states the opposing view, explicitly grants it ('They have a point'), then pivots with 'But' to a limiting objection.
Effect: conceding first makes the writer seem fair-minded and reasonable, which strengthens ethos, so the reader is more receptive to the counterargument that follows.

PART_B2.q: A synthesis prompt provides six sources on public transit funding. A student writes an essay that quotes all six but never states a position of their own. Briefly explain the main problem and how to fix it.
PART_B2.sa:
The main problem is that the essay summarizes and compiles sources instead of advancing the student's own argument; the sources are not doing work in service of a claim.
Fix: draft a defensible, qualified thesis first (a clear position), then organize body paragraphs around the student's sub-claims, bringing in whichever sources support each and using disagreements between sources to sharpen the argument.

PART_B2.q: Revise this sentence for concision and explain the two changes: 'Due to the fact that the data was incomplete, it was decided by the committee that the study would be repeated.'
PART_B2.sa:
Revision: 'Because the data was incomplete, the committee repeated the study.'
Change 1: 'Due to the fact that' is wordy padding for 'because.'
Change 2: 'it was decided by the committee that the study would be repeated' is a passive, roundabout construction; naming the actor ('the committee repeated the study') is shorter and clearer.

PART_C.q: Synthesis prompt: Read three sources (not shown here) on whether cities should invest in public transit over highway expansion. Write a well-developed paragraph taking a specific position, citing at least two of the sources by letter, using commentary (not summary) to connect the evidence to your claim.
PART_C.sa: Sample high-scoring paragraph: 'Cities should prioritize public transit investment over highway expansion, both for economic and environmental reasons. Source A's finding that transit-oriented cities saw 18% lower per-capita transportation costs demonstrates that transit investment directly benefits residents' wallets, not just abstract policy goals. Source C's data on reduced congestion further supports this: fewer cars on the road means highway expansion would only temporarily relieve traffic before induced demand fills the new lanes again. Together, these sources reveal that highway expansion treats a symptom while transit investment addresses the underlying cause — car dependency itself.'

PART_C.q: Rhetorical analysis prompt: A passage describes a scientist's decades-long campaign to warn the public about a public health risk, using short sentences in moments of urgency and long, layered sentences when describing the science. Write a paragraph analyzing this syntax choice and its effect on the passage's persuasive purpose.
PART_C.sa: Sample high-scoring paragraph: 'The writer's deliberate contrast in syntax mirrors the emotional register of each moment. In urgent passages — such as describing the scientist's warnings being ignored — short, clipped sentences (“No one listened. Years passed. The risk grew.”) create a sense of mounting frustration and crisis. By contrast, when explaining the underlying science, the writer shifts to long, layered sentences that unfold methodically, mirroring the patient, evidence-based nature of scientific inquiry itself. This contrast reinforces the passage's central purpose: to show that urgent human stakes were being met with too-slow, methodical institutional response, and that the reader should feel that same frustration.'

PART_C.q: Argument prompt: 'Is it more important for schools to teach practical skills or critical thinking?' Write a well-developed paragraph defending a specific, qualified position, using at least one well-developed piece of evidence.
PART_C.sa: Sample high-scoring paragraph: 'While practical skills like budgeting or coding have clear immediate value, schools should prioritize critical thinking, because it is the skill that allows students to adapt as practical demands change. Consider how quickly job-specific software skills become obsolete — a student trained narrowly in one program may find that knowledge useless within a decade, while a student trained to analyze problems, evaluate evidence, and reason through unfamiliar situations can adapt to whatever tools or careers emerge next. This does not mean practical skills are worthless; rather, critical thinking is the foundation that makes practical skills transferable and durable rather than narrowly disposable.'

PART_C.q: Rhetorical analysis prompt: A passage opens with a personal anecdote about the writer's grandmother losing her home, then pivots to statistics on foreclosure rates, then closes with a direct call to action. Write a paragraph analyzing how this structural progression builds the writer's persuasive purpose.
PART_C.sa: Sample high-scoring paragraph: 'The passage's structure moves deliberately from pathos to logos to a direct appeal, building persuasive momentum at each stage. Opening with the grandmother's story humanizes an otherwise abstract policy issue, ensuring the reader is emotionally invested before any data appears. The subsequent foreclosure statistics then lend logical weight to that emotional foundation, transforming a single sympathetic anecdote into evidence of a systemic problem. Finally, the closing call to action capitalizes on both the emotional and logical groundwork already laid, asking the reader to act only after they have been made to feel the stakes personally and understand them broadly — a structure that makes the final appeal far more persuasive than if it had opened the passage.'

PART_C.q: The passage below is the opening of a speech by a mayor announcing budget cuts. Write a rhetorical analysis thesis and a paragraph analyzing ONE strategy. PASSAGE: 'I ran for this office promising more. Tonight I have to explain less. Every family in this room has sat at a kitchen table and made a list of what stays and what goes. Tonight the city sits at that table with you.'
PART_C.sa:
Thesis: By pairing a blunt admission of broken promises with an extended domestic metaphor, the mayor recasts painful cuts as a shared, familiar act of household budgeting, seeking to defuse anger and position herself alongside residents rather than above them.
Analysis of the kitchen-table metaphor: The mayor moves from the abstract ('budget cuts') to a scene every listener knows - a family deciding 'what stays and what goes.' The metaphor does two things. First, it normalizes the cuts as an ordinary, responsible act rather than a failure, since every household does it. Second, the final sentence ('the city sits at that table with you') collapses the distance between government and governed, casting the mayor as a fellow participant in a hard but honest process. The plain, parallel syntax ('what stays and what goes,' 'promising more / explain less') reinforces the tone of candor. The combined effect is to make the audience more likely to accept the cuts as unavoidable and the mayor as trustworthy despite the reversal.

PART_C.q: Write an argument essay thesis and a body paragraph in response to this prompt: 'Some argue that students learn more from failure than from success. Take a position, qualify it, and defend it.'
PART_C.sa:
Thesis: Failure teaches durable lessons that success rarely does - but only when it is followed by honest reflection and a real second attempt, which means schools should build in structured chances to fail, analyze, and retry rather than treating every setback as final.
Body paragraph: Consider how students actually respond to a failed project versus a smooth one. After success, most move on without examining why it worked; the process stays invisible. After failure, the specific point of breakdown is exposed - a flawed assumption, a skipped step, a misread of the audience - and that specificity is what makes the lesson stick. But the reflection is not automatic. A student who fails a test and simply feels ashamed learns only to dread testing. The lesson lands only when the failure is paired with a diagnosis ('you misapplied the formula here') and a genuine opportunity to redo the work. This is why the strongest version of the claim is conditional: failure is a better teacher than success, but only inside a system that treats failure as data and gives students the time and the second attempt to use it. Classrooms that grade only final products waste the very failures that could teach the most.

PART_C.q: Read this two-source scenario for a synthesis task and write a defensible thesis plus one body paragraph. SOURCE A: A study finds that four-day school weeks cut district transportation and utility costs by 15 to 20 percent. SOURCE B: A follow-up finds that in districts with many low-income families, the fifth day previously provided meals and supervision that families then had to arrange themselves, often at a cost.
PART_C.sa:
Thesis: A four-day school week can deliver real savings for districts, but adopting it without replacing the meals, supervision, and instructional time the fifth day provided simply shifts costs onto the families least able to absorb them; districts should move to four days only if they fund a robust fifth-day program for students who need it.
Body paragraph: The case for the four-day week rests on the savings Source A documents: a 15 to 20 percent reduction in transportation and utility costs is not trivial for a strained budget, and proponents argue those dollars can be redirected to teacher pay or classroom resources. But Source B reframes what that saving represents. The fifth day was not merely an expense; for many families it was infrastructure - guaranteed meals and a safe, supervised place for children while parents worked. When the day disappears, those needs do not; they are transferred to families, who must pay for childcare or lose work hours. In that light, part of the district's 'savings' is really a transfer of cost from the public budget to private households, and disproportionately to low-income ones. A responsible four-day policy therefore has to include a funded fifth-day option - meals, care, and enrichment - so that the reform reduces total cost rather than merely relocating it.

PART_C.q: Analyze the rhetorical function of syntax and tone in this passage from an essay about social media. Write a thesis and one analytical paragraph. PASSAGE: 'We were told it would connect us. It connected us to everyone and everything, all at once, without pause, without weight, a firehose of the world aimed at a single face. We adjusted. We told ourselves this was normal.'
PART_C.sa:
Thesis: Through a shift from a short, plain opening to a long, breathless, unpunctuated middle sentence and back to two flat, resigned sentences, the writer enacts the very overwhelm being described, then lets the deflated closing tone imply a quiet indictment of how easily we accepted it.
Analytical paragraph: The passage is built on a deliberate rhythm. It opens with a short, clean sentence ('We were told it would connect us') that states a promise. The second sentence then runs long and accumulative - 'everyone and everything, all at once, without pause, without weight, a firehose of the world' - with the asyndeton and piled phrases denying the reader any rest, so the syntax reproduces the sensory flood it names. The metaphor 'a firehose of the world aimed at a single face' fixes that abstraction in a physical, almost violent image. Then the writer drops back to two short, affectless sentences: 'We adjusted. We told ourselves this was normal.' The tonal fall - from vivid to numb - is the argument. The plainness of 'this was normal' reads as bleak understatement, implying that the real problem is not the firehose but the ease with which 'we' normalized it. The syntax makes the reader feel the overload; the flat ending makes the reader complicit in accepting it.

PART_C.q: Write an argument essay thesis and body paragraph in response to: 'Evaluate the extent to which anonymity online does more harm than good.'
PART_C.sa:
Thesis: Online anonymity does more good than harm on balance, because the abuses it enables - harassment and disinformation - are better addressed through platform design and enforcement than through unmasking users, while the goods it protects, dissent and disclosure by vulnerable people, cannot be preserved any other way.
Body paragraph: Start with the strongest case against anonymity: it lowers the cost of cruelty. People say things behind a pseudonym they would never say under their own name, and coordinated anonymous accounts spread falsehoods at scale. That harm is real and should not be minimized. But the remedy of requiring real identities would not remove the incentive to harass or deceive; it would remove the protection anonymity gives to the people who most need it. A worker documenting unsafe conditions, a citizen of an authoritarian state, a teenager seeking help about abuse - each depends on being able to speak without their name attached. Real-name policies have repeatedly failed to reduce toxicity while measurably chilling this kind of speech. The better tools target behavior rather than identity: rate limits, friction on resharing, reputation systems, and consistent enforcement against harassment. These reduce the harms without sacrificing the goods. Anonymity is not costless, but the costs are manageable in ways that its benefits are not replaceable.

PART_C.q: Read this scenario and write a synthesis thesis plus one body paragraph. SOURCE A: A city that made downtown bus routes free saw a 30 percent ridership increase, mostly among riders switching from long walks or skipped trips. SOURCE C: A budget review of the same city found the lost fare revenue equaled 4 percent of the transit agency's budget, partly offset by eliminating fare-collection equipment and staff. SOURCE E: A transportation researcher argues that fares function as a regressive tax, since low-income riders spend a far higher share of income on transit.
PART_C.sa:
Thesis: Free downtown transit is justified primarily as an equity measure and is fiscally sustainable at the scale these sources describe, so cities with similar route structures should adopt it while monitoring for crowding and budget drift.
Body paragraph: The three sources fit together into a single case. Source E establishes the principle: because low-income riders spend a disproportionate share of their income on fares, a flat fare operates as a regressive tax, and removing it delivers its largest relative benefit to the riders who need it most. Source A shows that principle playing out in practice - the 30 percent ridership gain came 'mostly among riders switching from long walks or skipped trips,' meaning free service expanded access rather than merely subsidizing trips people would have taken anyway. Source C then answers the obvious objection about cost: the forgone revenue is only 4 percent of the agency budget and is partly recovered by scrapping the machinery and labor of fare collection. Taken together, the sources support a targeted, affordable policy: not universal free transit, but free service on the routes where the equity payoff is highest and the revenue loss is small enough to absorb.

PART_C.q: Analyze how the writer uses evidence and reasoning in this passage. Write a thesis and one analytical paragraph. PASSAGE: 'Critics say a wealth tax is unworkable because the rich will hide assets. Perhaps some will. But we already tax property, and homeowners do not bury their houses in the yard. The question is not whether evasion is possible - it always is - but whether a workable version can raise real revenue. Norway's experience suggests it can.'
PART_C.sa:
Thesis: The writer defuses a strong objection not by denying it but by reframing the standard of judgment - shifting the question from 'is evasion possible?' to 'can a workable version still raise revenue?' - and then supplies an analogy and a real-world case to meet that lower, more honest bar.
Analytical paragraph: The passage models concede-then-counter. It states the objection plainly ('the rich will hide assets') and immediately grants part of it ('Perhaps some will'), which builds credibility. The reasoning then does the real work. The homeowner analogy ('do not bury their houses in the yard') argues that we already levy hard-to-hide asset taxes successfully, implying that partial evasion does not doom a tax; the analogy's strength depends on how comparable real estate is to financial assets, which the writer glosses over, so it persuades more by common sense than by rigor. The key move is the explicit redefinition of the question - conceding that 'evasion is possible - it always is' - which lowers the bar from 'perfect' to 'workable and revenue-raising.' Finally, the reference to Norway supplies an empirical case to satisfy that redefined standard. The evidence is thin (one country, no figures), but within the reframed question it is enough to shift the burden back onto the critics.

PART_C.q: Write an argument essay thesis and body paragraph in response to: 'Some say that requiring community service for graduation teaches civic responsibility; others say mandatory service is a contradiction in terms. Take a position.'
PART_C.sa:
Thesis: Required community service is worth keeping, but only if schools treat it as a structured learning experience - with reflection, choice, and connection to coursework - rather than a box-checking hour count, because the version most schools run teaches compliance while the version done well can genuinely build civic habits.
Body paragraph: The objection that mandatory service is a contradiction has force: service compelled under threat of not graduating is, in a narrow sense, not voluntary, and a student filing paperwork for 40 grudging hours learns mainly how to satisfy a requirement. But this describes a bad implementation, not an inherent flaw. Consider the difference between a program that assigns students to sort donations in silence and one that lets them choose an issue, work with an organization over a semester, and then write and discuss what they saw. The second is still required, yet it exposes students to problems and people outside their usual world and asks them to make sense of the experience - which is how civic dispositions actually form. Plenty of valuable learning is required: we do not call required reading a contradiction. The real question is whether the requirement is designed to produce reflection and agency or just hours. Schools should redesign service programs around choice and reflection, and defend the requirement on the grounds that, done well, it works.

PART_C.q: Analyze the rhetorical situation and one major strategy in this passage. Write a thesis and one analytical paragraph. PASSAGE (from a letter by a nurse to a state legislature, during a debate on staffing ratios): 'You will hear today from hospital administrators with spreadsheets. I come with a different document: the list, in my head, of patients I could not get to in time. I am not here to argue about margins. I am here to tell you what a twelve-to-one ratio feels like at 3 a.m.'
PART_C.sa:
Thesis: Writing as a frontline nurse to legislators who will also hear from administrators, the writer contrasts two kinds of 'document' - the administrators' spreadsheets against her remembered list of patients - to reframe the debate from a financial question into a moral and experiential one that only she can testify to.
Analytical paragraph: The rhetorical situation is a contest for the legislators' frame of reference: the nurse knows her audience will hear a cost-focused case from administrators, so her strategy is to pre-empt and recategorize it. She does this with a pointed antithesis of evidence: 'administrators with spreadsheets' versus 'a different document: the list, in my head, of patients I could not get to in time.' By calling her memory a 'document,' she claims evidentiary standing for lived experience and implies the spreadsheets leave something crucial out. The short, declarative sentences ('I am not here to argue about margins. I am here to tell you...') refuse the administrators' terms outright and assert her own. The closing detail - 'what a twelve-to-one ratio feels like at 3 a.m.' - converts an abstract policy number into a felt, specific scene the legislators cannot claim to know. The combined effect is to position a vote against staffing ratios as a choice to value margins over the concrete human cost she alone in the room can describe.

PART_C.q: Write an argument essay thesis and body paragraph in response to: 'Evaluate whether it is more important for a leader to be respected or to be liked.'
PART_C.sa:
Thesis: For a leader with real authority over others' work and welfare, being respected matters more than being liked, because respect survives hard decisions while likability does not - but a leader who is respected and cold will still fail, so the goal is respect first, warmth close behind.
Body paragraph: The case for respect over likability becomes clear at the moment a leader has to do something unpopular: cut a project, hold someone accountable, deliver bad news honestly. A leader who has optimized for being liked has spent their credibility avoiding exactly these moments, and when forced into one, they either flinch or lose the goodwill they were protecting. A respected leader can make the same hard call and have it received as fair, because respect is built on consistency, competence, and honesty rather than on pleasantness. That said, respect without any warmth curdles into fear or distance, and people withhold information and effort from leaders they do not trust to care about them. So the priority is not respect instead of being liked but respect as the foundation, with warmth as what makes that foundation livable. A leader should be willing to be disliked in the short term for a decision that is right, and should earn back regard through how consistently and humanely they lead over time.

PART_C.q: Read this passage and analyze how diction and imagery shape the reader's view of the subject. Write a thesis and one analytical paragraph. PASSAGE (describing a new highway interchange): 'They call it an improvement. It is a knot of concrete flung over what used to be a neighborhood - ramps looping like tossed rope, a shadow underneath where a park was promised and a gravel lot delivered.'
PART_C.sa:
Thesis: Through loaded diction ('knot,' 'flung,' 'shadow') and a controlling image of the interchange as carelessly discarded rope, the writer converts an official 'improvement' into a symbol of disregard for the community it displaced.
Analytical paragraph: The passage opens by quoting the official label - 'an improvement' - only to dismantle it. The word 'knot' frames the structure as a tangle rather than a solution, and 'flung over what used to be a neighborhood' assigns the action carelessness and violence, as if the interchange were thrown down without regard for what was beneath it. The simile 'ramps looping like tossed rope' extends that idea: rope that is tossed is rope no one is carefully placing, so the engineering is made to look haphazard and indifferent. The final clause turns to a broken promise with plain, damning parallelism: 'a park was promised and a gravel lot delivered.' The 'shadow underneath' is both literal and figurative - a darkened space and a sign of what the project cost. None of this argues explicitly that the interchange was a mistake; the diction and imagery do the arguing, leaving the reader with the impression of a community treated as something to build over.

PART_C.q: Write a synthesis thesis and body paragraph. SOURCE A: A survey finds most teachers believe handwriting instruction improves early literacy. SOURCE B: A controlled study finds children who learned letters by typing recognized them as well as those who learned by hand, but those who wrote by hand were faster at composing short sentences months later. SOURCE D: An education budget analysis notes that dropping handwriting frees roughly 15 minutes of daily instructional time in early grades.
PART_C.sa:
Thesis: Elementary schools should keep a reduced but deliberate amount of handwriting instruction, because the evidence links it to later composing fluency even though it is not essential for letter recognition, and the instructional time it costs can be trimmed rather than eliminated.
Body paragraph: The sources point toward a middle position rather than either extreme. Source A shows strong teacher belief in handwriting, but belief alone is weak evidence, so the controlled findings in Source B matter more. Source B splits the question: for the narrow task of recognizing letters, typing worked just as well, which undercuts the argument that handwriting is indispensable for basic literacy. But the same study found a lasting advantage for hand-writers in composing sentences months later - a higher-order skill that matters more for real writing. That suggests the value of handwriting is not in learning the alphabet but in building fluency that transfers to composition. Source D supplies the practical constraint: handwriting instruction costs about 15 minutes a day. Given Source B, cutting it entirely would trade a documented composing benefit for reclaimed time. The reasonable synthesis is to keep a focused, shorter handwriting block - enough to preserve the fluency effect - and reclaim part of the 15 minutes for other instruction.

PART_C.q: Analyze how the writer builds and then complicates their argument in this passage. Write a thesis and one analytical paragraph. PASSAGE: 'For years I argued that reading fiction makes people more empathetic. The studies seemed to show it. Then better studies showed less. Now I think the honest claim is smaller and stranger: fiction does not reliably make us kinder, but it gives us practice at holding a mind that is not our own - and that practice has to be worth something, even if we cannot yet measure what.'
PART_C.sa:
Thesis: By narrating his own retreat from a strong claim to a smaller, qualified one, the writer uses intellectual honesty as a rhetorical strategy: conceding that the evidence weakened makes his revised, more modest claim about fiction more credible than the original.
Analytical paragraph: The passage is structured as a public change of mind, and that structure is the argument. The writer first states the bold version ('reading fiction makes people more empathetic') and the support ('the studies seemed to show it'), then immediately undercuts it with 'Then better studies showed less.' Conceding that the evidence turned against him costs him the strong claim but buys credibility: a reader trusts someone who follows the data even when it is inconvenient. He then offers a deliberately deflated replacement - 'smaller and stranger' - and qualifies it heavily ('does not reliably,' 'has to be worth something,' 'even if we cannot yet measure'). The hedging is not weakness here; it signals that the writer is claiming only what he can defend. The final phrase leans on a modest appeal ('practice at holding a mind that is not our own') that asks the reader to grant intuitive value rather than proven effect. The effect is a persuasive humility: the argument is more believable precisely because it admits its own limits.

PART_C.q: Write an argument essay thesis and body paragraph in response to: 'Some argue that people should be free to say anything short of direct incitement; others argue that some speech does enough social harm to justify limits. Take a position, qualify it, and defend it.'
PART_C.sa:
Thesis: The near-absolutist position is closer to right - the government should restrict speech only in narrow, well-defined categories - because the power to ban 'harmful' speech is far more dangerous in practice than the harms it would prevent, though private institutions may and should set stricter norms for their own spaces.
Body paragraph: The strongest argument for broader limits is that some speech - sustained harassment, dehumanizing propaganda - measurably damages people and public life, and it feels perverse to protect it. That harm is real. But the question is not whether the harm exists; it is who gets the power to decide what counts as harmful enough to ban, and how that power will be used over time. History is not reassuring: speech restrictions have repeatedly been aimed at dissidents, minorities, and unpopular movements far more than at the powerful. A rule broad enough to catch genuine propaganda is broad enough to catch protest the government dislikes. This is why the limits should be narrow and category-based - incitement, true threats, defamation - rather than a general 'social harm' standard. It does not follow that anything goes everywhere: a university, an employer, or a platform can and should enforce stricter standards within its own community, because those bodies lack the state's coercive power and their rules can be left by exit. The line I am defending is about government force specifically, and there the case for restraint is strong.

PART_C.q: Analyze the rhetorical strategy of this passage and its likely effect on a skeptical audience. Write a thesis and one analytical paragraph. PASSAGE (opening of an essay urging suburban homeowners to support denser housing): 'I know what you are picturing. A tower next to your fence. Traffic. Strangers. I pictured the same thing, in the same house, for the same reasons. Then my daughter, a nurse at the hospital you are proud to live near, could not afford to live within forty minutes of it.'
PART_C.sa:
Thesis: The writer disarms a hostile audience by voicing their fears in their own words before revealing shared membership in the group, then delivers a single concrete, sympathetic example that reframes density as a question of whether valued workers can live nearby.
Analytical paragraph: The passage's strategy is preemptive identification. Rather than arguing against the audience's objection, the writer states it for them - 'A tower next to your fence. Traffic. Strangers.' - in clipped fragments that match how the fear actually feels. Then comes the pivot: 'I pictured the same thing, in the same house, for the same reasons.' By placing himself inside the audience (a fellow suburban homeowner who shared their instinct), he removes the usual grounds for dismissing a pro-density argument as coming from an outsider or an ideologue. The final sentence does the persuasive work with one example chosen for maximum sympathy: 'my daughter, a nurse at the hospital you are proud to live near.' It ties the abstract housing debate to a specific, admired person the audience already values, and to a place they take pride in, so that opposing density starts to look like opposing the nurse. For a skeptical reader, the combined effect is to lower defenses (he is one of us, he understands) and then to reframe the issue from 'protecting my neighborhood' to 'can the people we depend on live here.'

PART_C.q: Write a synthesis thesis and body paragraph. SOURCE A: A meta-analysis finds that later school start times are associated with modest gains in attendance and test scores and a measurable drop in teen car crashes. SOURCE B: Interviews with parents in hourly-wage jobs describe morning childcare gaps created when elementary schools shift earlier to free buses for later high school starts. SOURCE E: A district that implemented later high school starts without changing elementary schedules reported the benefits with far fewer complaints.
PART_C.sa:
Thesis: Districts should move high school start times later, because the health and safety benefits are well supported, but they should do so without pushing elementary schools earlier, since the version that shifts the burden onto working parents of young children is both avoidable and the main source of backlash.
Body paragraph: The three sources map cleanly onto a single recommendation. Source A supplies the case for later high school starts: not a dramatic effect, but a consistent one across studies - better attendance and scores and, more concretely, fewer teen car crashes, which is a serious safety gain. Source B identifies where such policies go wrong. To free up buses for a later high school run, some districts move elementary start times earlier, which opens a morning childcare gap for exactly the parents least able to cover it - those in hourly jobs who cannot flex their schedules. That is a real cost, and it falls unevenly. Source E shows the cost is not inherent: a district that changed only the high school schedule captured the benefits Source A describes 'with far fewer complaints.' The synthesis, then, is not 'later starts, yes or no' but a design choice: adopt later high school starts, budget for the transportation cost of leaving elementary schedules alone, and avoid the trade that turns a health policy into a hardship for working families.
